Mr. Speaker, it is with a good deal of reluctance tha/t I have decided to take part in this debate, and when I look into the difficulties connected with my speaking at this stage, I realize that they are two-fold. First of all, coming into the discussion after various hon. gentlemen who from both sides of the House have contributed well-prepared addresses on the question at issue, it may be thought that it will be impossible for me to avoid falling into tedious repetition. Secondly, I may say that I intend to discuss the matter not as a partisan, but from the general standpoint of public and provincial interest. I may assure you, Sir, that I will not worry the House with quotations, and I will not roam through a mass of engineering technicalities, because I am not conversant with that side of the question, and it would not affect the point of view which I take in regard to this matter. As it iE necessary for the proper presentation of my views that I should deal with the history of the road, I will, with the permis-

sion of the House, make an analytical sketch of the discussion which took place in the House when the legislation providing for the construction of the National Transcontinental railway was enacted and how the work was executed. And I will then come to the report of the commissioners and endeavour to point out what is the duty of the Government in that regard.
When the legislation creating the National Transcontinental railway was brought down in 1903, the Government met with a very hostile opposition from many quarters. First of all, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company could not view without apprehension the invasion by a competitor of the territory- of which they had at the time a practical monopoly, and those who were friendly to this national corporation claimed that it was not fair for the Government of Canada to use public money and to pledge the credit of the country to create a competitor to a private concern. They contended also that the Canadian Pacific railway had done much for the development of our western country and that it was nothing but just that it should be allowed to reap the benefit of its long years of expenditure. To this line of argument the Government of the day answered that it was true that the Canadian Pacific railway had done much for Canada, but that Canada had done its share for the Canadian Pacific railway. It was true that through the campaign of literature carried on by the company, immigrants had been induced to take up the land of our western country; but at the same time the development of that country was such that the Canadian Pacific could not give satisfaction to the western part of Canada, and that the creation of another company would not bring undue competition to bear upon the Canadian Pacific railway, which was unable to face alone the development of our western prairies.
Then, the Government of the day had to face the opposition of the Tory party. It has been said that the duty of the Opposition is to oppose, and the Tory Opposition of that time did their best to oppose the idea of Canada's building a transcontinental railway. The opposition of the Tory party assumed many aspects. Some hon. gentlemen of the Opposition claimed that the construction of the-Grand Trunk Pacific railway should terminate on the shores of the Great Lakes. Others thought that if the Grand Trunk Pacific had to be built it would be better to build it from Winnipeg
to North Bay and there link it up with the Grand Trunk railway system. Other members of the party, having at their head the late member for the county of Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), contended that if it were necessary to build a National Transcontinental railway, it would be better to build, as a substitute for the project of the Government, a line running into our colonization territory so as to connect it with other lines of railway running south to north from the St. Lawrence river. Not only had the Liberal Government of 1903 to meet the opposition of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and those who were friendly to it; not only had they to meet the opposition of their opponents in this House, but they had to face also the opposition of one of their own friends. The Hon. Mr. Blair, who up to that time had been Minister of Railways and Canals, severed his connection with the then Government because he held the view that it would be unfair to the Intercolonial railway if the Government should build a railway which would parallel the Intercolonial railway, and which would be leased to another company. Mr. Blair was in favour of extending the Intercolonial railway over the Canada Atlantic from Montreal to Parry Sound so as to compete as a Government-owned railway for the traffic of the West.
He claimed that building the road as the Government intended to build it involved an unwarranted expenditure, that it was useless for the Government to enter upon such an undertaking, that the railway would traverse a barren country, that the road would never make expenses. It was said that the Government had not sufficient data to go on with such a huge undertaking. If any hon. member will read the debate that preceded the adoption of the law creating the National Transcontinental railway, he must admit that this is an accurate synopsis of it. The Government of the day claimed that this opposition was not well founded. They had every confidence in the future of this country; they thought that the time was ripe for Canada, in justice to our western farmers, to secure for them an outlet for their produce to the markets of the world. At the same time, they so designed the railroad that it would do justice not only to the West but also to the Bast; not only to the new country west of lake Superior, but also to the old provinces that at first constituted the Dominion of Canada. You hear very often that there are men in this country who think that Canada begins on the shores of the Atlantic

and ends on the eastern shores of lake Superior. On the other hand, you have some Canadians who are under the impression that Canada begins only west of lake Superior. In my own province, there is a class of politicians who, on the public platform and by every other means, trying to arouse prejudice, claim that the province of Quebec, being one of the oldest and being inhabited by descendants of the French race, should not welcome immigration to our shores because the greater the immigration the sooner we shall see the province of Quebec completely outvoted; for, of course, in this country the majority must rule and must enact the laws. I belong to the province of Quebec; I am proud of my province and of my race; but, thank God, I do not want to stop the development of this country. Canada should do her utmost to develop the western part of our country, and it is only just that she should give to those who have come to throw in their lot with us every opportunity for success; we must not give them any reason to regret that they have come to work hand in hand with us. But at the same time, the older provinces have a right to be heard, to secure at least justice from the central Government of Canada. The National Transcontinental railway was designed to provide an outlet for the produce of the West, to afford that competition with the Canadian Pacific railway for which the farmers had been asking, to open new regions in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick, and to keep the trade of our great western country for the benefit of the whole of Canada. That was the design of the National Transcontinental railway; but when the Government of that day submitted this measure to the consideration of Parliament, the faith of their Administration was pledged. It was not only the policy of the Liberal party and Government, but it was enacted as the law of this country. It was and is a contract entered into by the Parliament of Canada on one side and the Grand Trunk Pacific on the other side. The Government of Canada represented the provinces. What was the reason that we submitted to the electors of this country in the general election of 1904 for accepting that policy? The reason, Sir, was that every province was having its share of justice. It is true that the money of the country was being spent to create an outlet for the West; but the contract entered into with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company was acknowledged and accepted by the electorate of Canada because every province 
and every part of the electorate was receiving its share of justice.
I shall not discuss what was to be the cost of the National Transcontinental railway, and the reason is very clear. I claim that in 1904 the principle of the construction of the road was accepted by the electorate. From 1904 to 1908 the Government of the day had begun the expenditure of the money, and everybody in this country realized that the road was going to cost more than the original estimate. But it was an issue in the general election of 1908. We went before the electors and discussed that single question. What was the motto of the campaign ? ' Let Laurier finish his work; let the Government finish their work; let the Government go on with the expenditure; because what this country requires is a railway built according to the conditions of the contract and of the law enacted by the Parliament of 1903.' I do not defend this measure because it is a measure of the late Administration; I defend it as it has been enacted and as the work has been proceeded with, because it is in accordance with the contract agreed to by Parliament. The Minister of Justice, speaking in this Chamber, said that there was a contract in reference to the pension fund, and that it had to be respected. If it was only right that that contract should be respected, as the hon. Minister of Justice said, have I not a right to say that the contract entered into with the Grand Trunk Pacific should also be respected by this Government? The same principle and the same reasoning are involved. But there are other reasons. The road has been paid for partly out of the surplus of the different administrations and partly by the selling of bonds unloaded on British investors. What induced the British investors to buy those bonds? It was because a contract had been entered into by the Parliament of Canada guaranteeing the bonds and the construction of a first-class railroad. Yet this Government of 1914 are degrading the road; and are they not also degrading the value of the securities held by the British bondholders? This is the first time that I have seen an administrator-although the Government of the day claim to be masters of this country, they are only its administrators-appointed to manage the affairs of an estate, doing his utmost to degrade the asset which has been confided to him to administer. What a feeling of security the spreading of this report will engender in the minds of bondholders all over the -world ! The ministers on

the Treasury benches may claim that they are spreading this report broadcast to show what kind of administrators their predecessors were; they may claim that it is in the public interest; but how can it be in the public interest to create a false impression abroad that the Government of this country have indulged in bribery and wasteful expenditure of the public money? What benefit will that be to the community? None whatever.
There is another phase of the question with which I wish to deal. Not only have the bondholders' securities been degraded by this Government, but the different provinces are not being treated fairly. When the different provinces entered into Confederation they gave to the central Government all their sources of revenue and kept themselves all the departments which involved expenditures. That is why, at different times, provincial governments have come to the central Government and asked for a better repartition of the revenues of the country. They have made their case so clear that the Government at Ottawa had to enact legislation giving a bigger proportion of the taxes to the provinces. The revenues of the provinces are small compared with the revenues of the Dominion, but their expenses are great. When the legislation creating the Northern Transcontinental railway was enacted, the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, having every confidence that the compact would be kept to the letter, incurred great expenses in surveying land and creating villages, so that they' would be in a position to help in the development of this country when the railroad was in operation. Do you think for one minute, Mr. Speaker, that the Government of the province of Quebec would have gone to the expense they have incurred at La Tuque, and all the other villages along the line, if they had believed that with a change of Government the railroad would also be changed, and that instead of these villages being on the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific, they would be only on a local line carrying practically no through traffic? I say no, not for a moment would they have incurred that expense. Since I have had the honour of occupying a seat in this Chamber, I have seen members from the Maritime provinces stand up to defend the rights of their provinces, and lately I have heard one of the representatives of the province of Prince Edward Island asking that the law
be set aside in order that Prince Edward Island should retain its present representation in this House. The members from the Maritime provinces were fighting for the rights and prerogatives of their provinces, and no one denied them that right. When the members from the province of [DOT]Ontario claimed their rights and pointed out the duty of the Government towards their province, no one denied them that right. Nor was any dissatisfaction expressed when western members claimed certain rights for their provinces. But every time that a member from the province of Quebec stands up to assert the rights of his province, immediately you will hear, or see in the press, that that man is raising a race cry, or is indulging in peanut politics. I claim that the province of Quebec has as much right as any other province in this Dominion to be treated fairly. I do not claim that it should be given favours. No. All we are asking for is justice-justice for every part of this country.
Through this bargain, the people of the West were afforded the outlet for their products which they were demanding. Does any one contend that when this Government decided to degrade the road, justice was done to Ontario, to Quebec, or to the Maritime provinces? Certainly not. This contract was enacted by Parliament, on the understanding that the people of Canada would be treated fairly according to its terms, and the Government in ea deavouring to destroy what Parliament did in 1903 is renegade to its duty. That is npt what this Government was elected for. In 1903 the Parliament of Canada enacted this legislation; in 1904 the electorate of Canada sustained the Government for passing that legislation, and in 1908 the people of Canada, knowing that the expenditure was larger than at first estimated, imposed on the late Administration the duty of continuing the work. Under these circumstances Mr. GuteMus and Mr. Lynch-Staunton, or Staunton-Lyneh, have no right to come here and for a fee of $65,OCO to impeach the Parliament of 1903 and the opinion of the electorate of Canada in 1904 and 1908. If the present Government wanted to repeal this legislation, why did they not bring forward a measure to do so in 1912, in 1913, or in 1914? They knew that even their supporters would not sustain them on such a proposition; they knew that under our democratic system such conduct could

lead to nothing but anarchy. Why did not the Government, before degrading the road, consult the electorate and get their approval? They dare not do so, because they knew the people would not sustain them. In spreading broadcast the report of this commission, which was made for the definite purpose of inuring their opponents in the public mind, do not they know that they are creating a precedent which may be bad for them when they leave office? They will not be long in power; they are sowing the wind now, and later they will reap the whirlwind. Since they came to office there are some acts of administration which they have carried out, and which are dear	to	them, but	do they think
they will ;be satisfied, if after having, in their opinion, done the best for the country their successors should cancel the legislation they have enacted? On the 4 p.m. whole, the electors of Canada are an honest people; there may be individual exceptions, but on the whole, I assert that the electors of Canada are . actuated by good principles. When the Liberals were defeated on the 21st of September, 1911, the people of Canada said to the Tory party, administer the affairs of the country according to your own ideas, but the people gave the Tory party no mandate to destroy what had been in existence. They were charged to develop this country, not with Turning (its ctedit; they were charged to make the country prosperous- prosperity they did not bring to the country, but they should have at least remained within the lines of their mandate. If the Tory party could do nothing for the prosperity of the country, they should at least not have destroyed that which they had been charged to keep intact.
To the Prime Minister, who has been listening to my remarks, I say: there are in Canada a large number of electors who put their confidence in the Conservative party now in power, because they thought that under the right hon. gentleman they would have a clean, honest, and progressive government. Does the right hon. gem tlernan think he has respected the confidence of the people by appointing -a commission, such as we are now discussing, and becoming responsible for his party's press bureau sending false statements broadcast throughout the country, twelve months before the report was presented to Parliament, so as to create the false impression that the country had been swindled 
out of $40,000,000, when on the report being presented it is found .that it does not corroborate such assertions? It is not fair to the country, it is not fair to Parliament, it is not fair even to the right hon. gentleman himself that such an attempt should have been made to mislead the people. I know that we cannot force certain hon. gentlemen on the Government benches to have confidence in the Opposition, but above party politics, and above the desire to remain in office, there is -the public interest which should always be respected.
With these few remarks, I hope that the report as it is now will be the vindication of the late Administration; and let me hope that before it is too late the Government will come back to the old contract and will restore to the road its former degree of efficiency. If they do not do so, we will wait for them at the polls, where they will receive their condemnation, because the contract must be adhered to as is was signed and concurred in by Parliament in 1903, and, approved by the people of this country in 1904, and in 1908.

Mr. Speaker, eleven years ago the Government of the day came to this Parliament with a proposition that the time had arrived in the history of Canada when we should enter upon the construction of a second transcontinental railway. They submitted to Parliament an agreement made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of Canada and containing in its recital a statement of the reasons which had induced the Government to enter upon that enterprise and to ask the Canadian people to provide the funds necessary to carry it into effect.
It is perhaps just as well for us, in the inception of our consideration of this question, to see what was the original idea in regard to this enterprise. I read from the contract made on the 29th day of July, 1903, between the Government of the day and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company:
Whereas, having regard to the growth of population and the rapid development of the production and trade of Manitoba and the Northwest territories, and to the great area of fertile and productive land in all the provinces and territories as yet without railway facilities, and to the rapidly and expanding trade and commerce of the Dominion, it is in the interest of Canada that a line of railway, designed to secure the most direct and economical interchange of traffic between eastern Canada arid the provinces and territories west of the Great Lakes, to open up and develop the northern zone

of the Dominion, to promote the internal and foreign trade of Canada and to develop commerce through Canadian ports, should he constructed and operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion from ocean to ocean, and wholly within Canada.
That is the germ of the proposition put forward at that time toy the Liberal1 party and approved on the repeated occasions on which the electorate were called upon to discuss it.
Although we have this report, ridiculous in its character, mischievous and false in its allegations, put before the Canadian people at this juncture, there never was a time during the last six years when any Conservative of responsibility was prepared to take the position that this transcontinental railway should not be constructed where and when it was proposed to be constructed by the Liberal party. We are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that, when this proposition came before Parliament, the then Premier of Canada told the Canadian people that the railway would cost only $13,000,000, and that the then Minister of Finance said that it would cost only $61,000,000. Led us consider for a moment the truth of these allegations and how far this question of cost entered as an element into the consideration of Parliament when it passed that Act in 1903. Every one knew that the northern part of Canada between Winnipeg and Quebec and between Quebec and Moncton had undeveloped resources of the greatest possible extent. General information was to be had in the various departments of the Government in regard to this, and the statement of Mr. Schreiber is to the effect that there existed in regard to tihe condition of that part of the country preliminary reports made by surveyors such as Sir Sandford Fleming. From that information Mr. Schreiber gave to the Minister of Finance of that day estimates upon which the latter based his figure of $61,000,000. Every one in Parliament at that time knew the conditions under which the estimate was made. Every one knew that no test pits had been sunk, that no experimental surveys of the land had been made as to the location of the road and so as to arrive at definite figures. Therefore no one would be able to say within $10,000,000 whatthe road would actually cost. Although the Conservative members in all the intervening years have declared that the present leader of the Opposition stated that the cost of this railway was to be only $13,000,000, every one of them knew that the leader of the Opposition 144
was only speaking of the interest upon the cost as estimated by Mr. Schreiber. But hon. gentlemen opposite did not accept these figures. What did they say? My hon. friend the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), a member of the present Cabinet, told the country at that time that the railway would cost $73,000,000. My hon. friend the member for Peel (Mr. Blain) told the country that it would cost $100,000,000. The late Minister of Railways, the Hon. Mr. Haggart, said that it would cost $125,000,-
000.	The hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter) said that it would cost $150,000,000. You, Mr. Speaker, then gave an opinion in regard to its cost. You knew that it would cost more than $13,000,000 or $61,000,000. You said that it would cost $125,000,000. You were not deceived. It was stated by a prominent member of the Opposition of that day, the hon. member for West Toronto (Sir Edmund OsleT), that tl e railway would cost $200,000,000. The right hon. gentleman who leads the Government to-day said that the railway would cost anywhere from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000 and that on account of the four-tenth per cent grade, it was impossible to tell in advance within $10,000,000 of what it would cost. When we went to the people in 1904, my right hon. friend's organization in the province of Nova Scotia declared tthat Ithis railway would cost $130,000,000. In the election of 1904, every Conservative who asked the support of the electorate, pled with the people that they should oppose the Government because it would put an untold burden upon his constituents, and every Conservative quoted figures in dollars and cents to show just how great a burden was to be placed upon his constituents as the result of the construction of this railway. What occurred? The cost was not the issue; that question was not worrying Parliament at that time, because Parliament had before it the fact that the Intercolonial railway of Canada, running from Quebec to Sydney, had cost the people of this country $78,953 per mile, and was aware of the cost of railways in the United States and other countries. In New South Wales, railways not of this high standard cost $64,000 per mile; in Germany, $107,000; in France, $126,000; in Russia, $83,000; in Austria, $87,000. In Great Britain, with her expensively prepared road beds, the average cost is $272,000 per mile. These data were quoted in Parliament in 1903, and Parliament and the country knew that the cost of this enterprise would be very great, and they accepted that responsibility.



What position did the leader of the Government, then leader of the Opposition, take at that time? Was it cost that he was inveighing against? Not at all. He said this railway should be built from sea to sea, so that our ocean ports on the Atlantic -at the termini of this much-abused Quebec and Moncton section-should be developed, and that the lines should be owned by the Government. The slogan of the Opposition then was not cost, it was: Are we to have a Government-owned railway or a railway-owned Government? That was the question on which they went to the people. So, when these hon. gentlemen complain of being deceived about the cost, there is not a man of them who was here in 1903 but knows that he is drawing a red herring across the trail, that on the discussion of this report he is attempting to bolster up the most ridiculous document ever presented to a free Parliament; and he laughs in his sleeve when he talks of cost and argues that the estimates of 1903 were the important point. Did not the people of Canada know?
Mr. 8EXSMITH: No.

My hon. friend did not believe his leader if he did not know. In 1904 the people of Canada declared that they wanted a new transcontinental railway built with the object and according to the terms set forth in the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. And the Government of that day was returned. They initiated the construction of the road. Here and there, in the intervening years, we heard some discussion about the question. In 1908, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), now Minister of Trade and Commerce, gave his estimate of the cost of the Transcontinental. Speaking in this House, he said that the cost would be $155,000,000. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), speaking in this House in 1908, said that, exclusive of the cost of terminals, the construction of this railway would involve an expenditure of $114,000,000, as estimated by his engineers. The present leader of the Government (Mr. Borden) in 1908 estimated- and this was when very little had been done in the way of construction-that the cost of the road would be $161,724,185, or, adding the cost of terminals estimated at $5,000,000, the cost would be in round numbers $167,000,000. These were the statements made to Parliament by members on either side previous to the general elections of 1908. And the Government that went to 
the people in that year making these statements as to the cost of the railway was overwhelmingly sustained and returned to carry on the enterprise which they had inaugurated.
I have attempted to deal frankly with this question of cost, for there never was a greater bugaboo than the statements of hon. gentlemen opposite on this question. The party organs discussing the eloquent speech of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) cannot but admit its masterly character, but they say he failed to deal with the question of the cost of the enterprise. Now, I wish to meet that question squarely as proposed by my hon. friends on the other side; and I have shown that no Conservative in Parliament was deceived on this question of cost in 1903, 1904 or 1908, that all parties in this House before going to the country for confirmation of their position estimated that the cost of the railway would be from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000. But on the 30th of September, 1910, four years ago, Mr. MacPherson, now assistant to the chairman of this commission, estimated the cost of the road at $143,000,000, or $78,000 a mile. On the 10th of March, 1911, Mr. Gordon Grant, then and now chief engineer of the road, estimated the cost at $145,339,000 or $80,565 a mile, not including the cost of terminals. That is the estimate that was given when the Liberal party went out of power in 1911. When hon. gentlemen opposite came into power that course was entered upon which has led to the bringing down of this report. An estimate was prepared by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) in February, 1912, which he submitted to Parliament, declaring that the cost of the road since they had come into power had gone up to $171,000,000, or $95,000 a mile. In other-words, while Mr. Gordon Grant, the chief engineer, who has the confidence of this Government, declared under Liberal rule that the cost was going to be $145,000,000, hon. gentlemen opposite to the injury of the country, jumped the estimated cost to $171,000,000. Then after a year of their own Administration, on the 18th of April, 1913, they changed the estimated cost again, bringing it down to $161,307,800. But in that amount is included $16,000,000 for terminals and other expenditures, the amount of which has been determined solely and exclusively by this Government. So, you have the exact result as to the cost of this railway what it was placed at 'by the Liberal party in March, 1911, $145,000,000; for if you deduct from the $161,000,000 the

amount of money that has been spent or is being provided for by this Government in regard to terminals, $16,000,000, you have an estimate for the road of $145,000,000. The result of all this is that, with the exception of the abnormal estimate in February, 1912, the object of which is now apparent, and with the same engineer responsible for every dollar of the money that has been paid on this Transcontinental for the last six years in office to-day, you have the estimated cost as put forward by the Liberal party four years ago absolutely sustained. So, I assert without fear of contradiction, that at no time since the inception of this road, since there were given to the public estimates made by engineers dealing with this question after full examination had been made, has the expectation and asserion of the Liberal party upon this question been shown to be untrue or false in any particular, nor has it been shown that the country had been misled by one iota in regard to the matter. The Canadian people in 1903-4, in 1908 and in 1911 declared in favour of a second transcontinental railway and declared that that railway was not inaugurated one moment too soon; and I assert that there is not a man of any responsibility on the Government side who holds his seat here to-day who was prepared to go to the people in 1911 and declare that Sir Wilfrid Laurier had done wrong when he asked the people in 1904 to build this railway.
In 1908 we had the scandal election; that was the time when charges of all kinds were hurled against the Government of the day. The aftermath of the activities of that period were statements made upon irresponsible platforms and in the nondescript press throughout the country as to the enormous corruption that was going on in connection with the construction of the Transcontinental railway.
When hon. gentlemen on the other side have nothing else to talk about, they allow their imaginations to run riot, and they make absolutely irresponsible assertions in regard to this question on the platforms and in the press. When by a curious turn of fate they were given the responsibility of dealing with the affairs of this country, they tried, through the Morine commission, to make good the charges that had been hurled against the late Administration; but when Morine made his exit, when the investigation being conducted by the commission of which he was the chairman met with a sudden death, hon. gentlemen found themselves upon the horns of a 144i
dilemma. They had to invent something new along the same line; so, they said, here is the Transcontinental railway; we will proceed to appoint <two commissioners about whose opinions we have absolutely no doubt. We will pick out men this time who know their business, and we will provide conditions under which they will bring in some kind of a report which we can use as political material. They disregarded altogether the effect of such a report upon the credit of the country. I am sure that many hon. gentlemen who sit opposite know, from the advice which they have received from business men in their constituencies and elsewhere throughout the country, that a great mistake has been made in connection with this report. The hon. Minister of Finance does not sleep on any easy bed these times; by every mail communications from London and elsewhere tell him of the gross error that was made by this Government in sacrificing Canada's credit in order to make good their pre-election assertions. Why did hon. gentlemen not have a parliamentary investigation if they believed that an investigation was necessary? Why did they not appoint a special committee of the House of Commons to deal with the matter, and to deal with it in the clear light of day?
My hon. friends have no confidence in themselves; and, being afraid to trust themselves to dp the partisan work, they got two partisans to do it for them. Why was not a Royal Commission of judges appointed? Why did not hon. gentlemen opposite, if they believed that there was .any wrongdoing in connection with this matter, select from the bench of Canada men who are absolutely free from any suspicion of partisan taint, and ask them to investigate the whole matter and bring in a report, the statements contained in which would be considered of some value? My hon. friends could not find anybody on the bench who would suit them, and they selected their own commissioners. They were hand-picked men.
At North Bay, in the constituency of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, lived Mr. Gutelius. Born in the United States, and having been 17 years in this country, Mr. Gutelius, although occupying positions on different railways of this country, did not think enough of Canada or of British institutions to take out his naturalization papers. 'Well,, says the Minister of Railways, I have a proposition to

make to you, Mr. Gutelius. You go on this board and investigate the Transcontinental rail-way construction; do the thing right, according to my taste, and when you get through I will make you general manager of the Intercolonial railway at a salary of $20,000 a year. All I want you to do is to become a British subject and prepare this report as I would like it prepared. That was a very tempting offer. My hon. friend the Solicitor General said: Why make'this imputation with regard to Mr. Gutelius when the hon. ex-Minister of Railways 0noted Mr. Berry? I will tell you why. There is a great deal of difference between a witness giving evidence and an alien coming into this, or any other British country and working under a commission from the Crown in which he .has not sufficient confidence to swear allegiance to. After Mr. Gutelius was appointed, he became naturalized and entered upon this work.
And what about Mr. Staunton? Will any hon. gentleman on the other side say that Mr. Lynch-Staunton was not a partisan? There is not a man. in the province of Ontario who does- not know that Mr. Lynch-Staunton. has been one of the most active and aggressive Conservative partisans in the province for a long period of years. Whenever the Ontario Government wanted to obtain legal services they sent for Mr. Lynch-Staunton.

That was because
of his ability.

That may be right;
I am not saying anything about Mr. Lynch-Staunton's ability; but I am saying that, the Government having intimated that they were going to have a close and rigid investigation into the circumstances connected with a certain matter, and that they were going to appoint a non-partisan and impartial body to conduct that investigation, the members of it, no matter how able they might be, should not be men who at the same time are in the pay of the Tory party.

He is a good Irishman,
too.

I do not know
whether he is of the same stripe as the Minister of Militia and some other hon. gentlemen opposite; of course, in the estimation of some hon. gentlemen, the question as to whether or not he is a good 
Irishman would depend on whether he came from the North or from the South. I am afraid a good many other gentlemen on the other side would not think very much of the Irish party of Mr. Lynch-Staunton, so far as I have any knowledge of it. But while he was conducting this alleged investigation he was in the pay of the Ontario Government. He went to Detroit in February of last year and appeared before the International Joint Waterways 'Commission as counsel for the province of Ontario; so that while drawing his $25,000 from this Government for his services in connection with this commission he was being well paid by the Ontario Government for the specific services which I have mentioned. Is there a man in this House, is there a man anywhere, who knows the ethics of matters of this kind, who thinks that Mr. Lynch-Staunton was an absolutely impartial gentleman who would approach the consideration of this matter with that judicial feeling which ought to be possessed by any man, who undertakes to perform such an important duty for the Government of the country? Everybody knows that the suggestion of his being impartial is absurd, in view of the facts which I have stated.
These two gentlemen were selected to save the face of the Conservative party after the failure of Morine, and what they have given to this country is not a judicial finding or determination, but a political pamphlet, nothing more or less. It is no wonder that my friend Mr. Cahan, the former leader of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia, and a close personal friend of the present leader of the Government, not only took the advantage of the occasion of his addressing a body of students in Montreal to denounce this tribunal, its ex parte proceedings, its methods of dealing with important public questions and its utter disregard of the rights of the public, but, being specially interviewed, sent broadcast throughout this country his disapproval, as .a Conservative, of the farce that has been enacted before the Canadian people in the appointment of these men and their utilization as commissioners to investigate the construction of the National Transcontinental railway.
Whom would you have appointed?

I have already intimated to my hon. friend that the proper course would have been to have had at least a parliamentary investigation or, fail-

mg that, to have appointed a royal commission of judges.

You admit it should
have been done anyhow; that is the great point.

That is very clever.
I will admit this, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative party, after the Morine episode, saw that they were in a hole, and as they had talked so much in regard to the question of the Transcontinental expenditure and corruption, it would never have done for them to have appointed judges or to have had a parliamentary investigation in the broad light of day. There was only one thing for them to do and that was to appoint these men whom they especially selected, and especially provided in advance that these men would make the report which they did, and as to that there can be no possible question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I desire to say that that statement is absolutely without foundation.
Mr. MACDONALD Which statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member
stated that the Government had provided in advance the character of report which these gentlemen would make.
I did not say that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I so understood him.

I did say that this Government were in a position, that in order to save their faces they picked out two men whom they knew would make a report upon this question that would, as far as it could, save the faces of the Conservative party. That is what I isaid.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I desire to isay that the
Government knew nothing of the kind.
My right hon. friend did not know .anything of the kind?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
Then my hon. friend has the audacity to suggest to this House-
Order, ordeT.

Not at all; that is
within order. If I cannot say that an hon. member has the audacity, I would like to know what I can say.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have only to say that according to some very well established English rules, the word ' audacity ' is hardly parliamentary.

I would like to be
sure as to that. You have rather developed some new rules in regard to narrowing down the rights of the Opposition to use language in regard to this Government, and I would like to have some authority. If I cannot say that this Government has audacity, I would like to know how I can discuss their acts in regard to any question.
If audacity is not a quality that we are permitted to attribute to a Government whose acts we are discussing, what is it that one can say in regard to them? Nerve, temerity, or what other expression can I employ? If the leader of the Government did not know all about Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Staunton beforehand, there were other members of his Government who did know what kind of a report they were going to bring in, and I am sure ;my right hon. friend, whose denial I am bound to accept, can only speak for himself, because there are some other members of his Govern-nient into whose minds he cannot enter. My right hon. friend cannot question the assertion which I make, that there were members of the Government, who when Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Lynch-Staunton were appointed, knew the kind of report they would bring in and what they were going to say.
Mr. BORDEN I desire to say, as my hon. friend has appealed to me, that I do absolutely question that.
You only question it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. member said I could not question it.

My right hon. friend is not omniscient, and his knowledge in regard to governmental matters is confined,
I am sure, to matters that come within has own purview. I think he will toe bound to admit that there are members of his Government who have thoughts and conceptions in regard to matters that he cannot fathom.
After all these preliminary investigations, after all these questionings, after all this bartering with the American citizen who transferred his allegiance and provided this report for a permanent salary of $20,000 a year, after all that, when you get the document, the commissioners have not the audacity or nerve to allege that there had been any corruption in regard to the construction of the railway. You can search the report from end to end to find the slight; est allegation of corruption in connection

with the construction. Other things they did say. They went beyond the purview of the Order in Council appointing them to declare that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister of this country did not know what lie was talking about. Where do they do that? When they declare that this line of railway from Quebec to Moncton should never have been built. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister was a strong supporter of the proposition that the line from Quebec to Moncton should be built. My right hon. friend in his own constituency, in a manifesto which he issued in newspapers throughout the province of Nova Scotia, previous to the election of 1904, declared that he was the best friend of the Maritime provinces, he wanted to build this railway from Quebec to Moncton; but he wanted to build it as a Government work.
He said so in St. John.

So that when these
commissioners undertook to say in the report, as they did say, although they were not asked to do so by the Order in Council, that:
In our opinion this section should not have been constructed at all. If one-third of the money had been expended on the Intercolonial railway it would have provided all the trunk line facilities for the province of New Brunswick which would be required for many years
They said they knew more than the Prime Minister about the matter.
Is the province of New Brunswick the only province by the sea? My right hon. friend and I come from a province which has some pride in its place in this Confederation. We have been wont to look forward in after days to a condition under which there shall come to us there, at the entrance of this Dominion-the outgoing place and the incoming place of Canaida-the trade of all this country behind. A local road in New Brunswick? Is that what the Premier told the people of our province in 1904? Let me give you what he did say in Halifax on October 28, dealing with the charge that he was not the great friend of Halifax and its port and that he was not actually in favour of this Quebec-Moncton section. He said:
My friend the Minister of Finance spoke of some remarks of mine speaking- at the Empire Theatre on the 7th of the month referring to the Quebec-Moncton section of the road.
If Mr. Fielding meant to state that I was opposed to the building of a shorter line between Moncton and Quebec he stated that for. which he never had and has not now the slightest warrant.

That is where my right hon. friend stood in 1904, and that is where he still stands. What was said by Mr. T. E. Kenny, an old member of this House and the first colleague of my right hon. friend. Speaking in Halifax in October, 1904, Mr. Kenny said:
We should vote for Borden and O'Mullin supporters of a party pledged to build a road across the continent as a great work with its termini on the Pacific and on the Atlantic in Canadian ports.
And how was that railway ever going to get down to Canadian ports by a shorter route if it had not been built from Quebec to Moncton? My right hon. friend issued a manifesto which appeared in the Halifax Herald of October 26, in which he said:
The Government, (that is, the Liberal Government) seeks to impose upon the people liabilities amounting to at least $150,000,000.
Just fancy these gentlemen whose souls are vexed over this question, of cost.
Their leader knew what he was talking about. In 1904 he told the people of Nova Scotia that the road would cost $150,000,000 under conditions which absolutely failed to safeguard our national interest. My right hon. friend said: I am in favour of the principle of a new transcontinental railway stretching from sea to .sea. I am a better friend to you than is my opponent, because I want to have a Government-owned railway, not a railway-owned Government. And yet this commission that he appointed-I do not think he really did appoint it, and I think he is ready to disclaim his responsibility for it-this commission says that that section should never have been built at all, although the reference never asked their opinion on that point. The commissioners further say:
This commission does not think that the National Transcontinental railway should have been constructed east of L6vis which was done at a cost of $35,000,000
While there may be some reason for the construction of a railway through the timber districts in the eastern portion of the province of Quebec, the construction of the railway from Edmundston to Moncton was not justifiable because of the lack of local business along this line which two years of operation has already proved.
That statement shows that the commissioners not only were reckless in their inquiry into facts, but did not know what they were talking about as regards conditions in the eastern part of the Dominion. Mr. Gutelius had nothing to do with railroading in eastern Canada previous to his appointment as commissioner. If Mr. Staunton ever came to the Maritime prov-

luces, and had a glimpse of the line extending eastward and of the seaports, I think he came down there impregnated with the narrow view which has already been expressed by isome hon. gentlemen, that there should have been a railroad constructed from Cochrane to Winnipeg so that all the traffic in the winter months might come down through the province of Ontario and go on to Boston and other American ports. That would have been a nice thing for the eastern seaports	of	this	Dominion. Splendid
Canadianism that! The commissioners did not care a snap whether the terminals of the Transcontinental were in Canada or not. They were perfectly willing that all the great trade of the West in the winter months should be drained down through the province of Ontario and on to Boston and New York. These gentlemen dealt with something they had no business to deal with. They declared that the present Prime Minister did not know what he was talking about in 1904 when he declared that the eastern section should be built and that it -would be a good thing for Canada. The Prime Minister stands for that to-day. He would not dare to go into Nova Scotia and say that for all the days to come we in our little province are not to share in the development of this great Hinterland; that the Transcontinental line shall not bring the trade of the West to the eastern ports of this country. Out in British Columbia to-'day guarantees, assistance and subventions are given with a lavish hand, and for what purpose? To get one more transcontinental railway into that province? To get four. The Grand Trunk Pacific is already going to Prince Rupert, but the assistance of this Gov-eminent and of the provincial Government is given for the purpose of getting the Canadian Northern railway to make its terminus at Port Mann. British Columbia can have four transcontinental terminals, but poor Nova Scotia is told by Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton, who are bigger than governments and bigger than the Premier of this country, that the Government and the Prime Minister of this country do not know what they are talking about, and that Nova Scotia cannot have this railway-that the line east of Ldvis should not have been constructed.
I am sure that my right hon. friend agrees with me on that phase of the report, and I think he will agree with me on another phase; that he and his Government are responsible for every dollar that was spent
in connection with the construction of the Transcontinental since September 30, 1911. There can be no question about that. The exhibits furnished with this report give a statement of the cost of the road up to September 30, 1911-not money, mark you, that has been actually paid out at the time, but the amount of work done and the value of it as estimated by the engineers. Taking all this work, I find that the total amount done up to September 30, 1911, was $108,730,700. A very large proportion of that amount had not been paid out at that time. The payments were made subsequently, and a most conservative estimate would show that no more than $95,000,000 was paid out by the late Government previous to their going out of power. If the estimate made by this Government as to the cost of the road is correct, then this Government is responsible for an expenditure of at least $67,000,000. This commission takes everything that was done down to the date of the report as if the late Government was responsible for it all. Have gentlemen opposite been so very careful in regard to this matter? Take for instance the cost of grading. The amount spent for grading up to September 30, 1911, under the late Government, was $64,706,000; and taking the estimated cost of grading, which is $107,000,000, it will be seen that this Government has spent $42,359,000. This Government, its officials, and its commissioner are responsible for that payment. Not only that, but they are rseponsible for the final settlement with the contractors. They were the men who had to settle with the contractors, and if there was any improper classification, if there was any unususal expenditure in any department, the men that had to O.K. those .accounts, whose certificates had to be obtained before a single dollar was paid, were the chief engineer and the present commissioner; so that for every dollar expended after September 30, 1911, this Government is entirely responsible. What was the oondit'on of affairs at that time? Length of road, 1,804 miles; 1,866 miles of grading Lad been completed and 1.659 miles of track laid down; bridges were completed to the extent of 82.75 per cent.; telegraph lines had been built on 982 miles of the road; cost of the road per mile up to that date, $63,700. All that is included in the expenditure of $108,000,000, and the payment of a large portion of that amount was still held in reserve, That phase of the situation has been entirely ignored by the commission.

Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: Who signed the contracts?

What contract are you talking about?
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: All the contracts that were let.

Do you not know ? It does not make any difference who signed the contracts; the question of how much should, be paid under the contract was a question to be determined by this Government.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER [DOT] They could not determine the terms of a contract already let.

Could they not? The amount that was to be spent under the contract could only be determined since 1911 by this Government and its friends.
Mr. A. DeWITT FOSTER: The Teport has only been in for about two weeks, and the Government could not have known two years ago what was in that report.

I knew the -hon. member did not know what he is talking about. What I am saying is that since 1911 Mr. Leonard, the appointee of the Government, and he alone, could determine what money was to be received by anybody. The fact is that if this railway has cost $161,000,000, at least $65,000,000 of that will have been spent entirely and solely upon the responsibility of the Conservative Government, who have been in control of that enterprise since September, 1911, and it is just as well the country should know that.
Why have these commissioners dragged in every possible item in order to make the expenditure seem large? The hon. member for St. Hyacintbe (Mr. Gauthier) very ably pointed out the injury which was being done to Canada by these misrepresentations. Why did. the acting Minister of Railways want to add the cost of the Quebec bridge to the cost of the Transcontinental railway? Why did he try to make out that the Quebec bridge was part and parcel of that railway project? Why did be try to make it be believed that if it were not -for the Transcontinental railway the Quebec bridge would never have been considered? I had the curiosity to look up something about the history of the Quebec bridge, and I find that the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) speaking at a banquet in Quebec in 1907, declared that the Conservative, party and not the Liberal party was entitled to credit for the in-
ception of the Quebec bridge. He told his listeners that the Conservative party had promised it, and he said:
The Quebec bridge has been promised us by important Conservatives. That promise was not kept, and that was an error. The electors should always insist upon the accomplishment of any promise made, and they should prefer that fewer promises should be made and these carried out.
Who said that?

The Hon. Mr. Pelletier said that, speaking at a banquet given to the Prime Minister. Then Mr. Monk, the late Minister of Public Works, speaking in tlie Transcontinental railway debate said:
I mention this because I have always been favourable to the Quebec bridge project, and the Conservative-party, as members of this House are well aware, were committed to assist in the construction of this bridge before IS 96.
Therefore, hon. gentlemen opposite, in discussing this matter, will please remember that on no less authority than the Postmaster General and the former Minister of Public Works, the Conservative party promised the construction of the Quebec bridge long before there was 5 p.m. any thought of a transcontinental railway.
Seven years before.

Yes. Let us look at one or two other features of this report. For the sake of carrying out the real purpose of this commission, Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton did not confine themselves to an error of half a million dollars here and there. They refer in one place to the money which was ' unnecessarily expended in building the railway east of the St. Lawrence river.' It worried these two great economists and statesmen to think that this national railway should have its termini on Canadian soil. They say that without including the section east of the St. Lawrence river, at least $40,000,000 was needlessly expended in the building of the road. I defy any man to go through this report from beginning to end, and, taking the figures set out by these two gentlemen that they total up more than $28,392,000. In some cases they refer to alleged engineering mistakes, or to wooden trestles having been used instead of steel, and they give specific instances which they repeat after including their cost in the totals; but taking every possible suggestion they make, they are between nine million dollars and ten

million dollars away above anything they have given details for. They speak of $40,000,000 having been needlessly expended, when, on their own figures, it is only a little over $28,000,000; but $10,000,000 is nothing to these gentlemen when the fair name of Canada is to be defamed for party purposes. Let me give another illustration of this. They say in this report that the classification prescribed in the contracts was ignored, and that the contractors were overpaid $3,300,000 on improper classification. But, taking the very figures they themselves give, their computation is $37,082 too much.
Whenever they speak of the Transcona shops they say that they are entirely too big; that only half the money need have been spent on them, and they always refer to them as having cost $4,500,000. But take the estimate of Mr. Grant, the chief engineer, as to the cost of construction, which you will find in these very exhibits, and his last statement shows that the cost of these Transcona shops would be $4,238,000, and not $4,500,000, so that these commissioners are $260,000 wrong there. Then, with regard to the Winnipeg terminals, you find that according to the engineers' statement of the cost up to date, these commissioners are $1,642,000 too high. All through, this report is grossly misleading. Why should these two gentlemen proclaim to the world that $40,000,000 might have been saved, when, after all, their star chamber investigation, after all their ex parte dealing with witnesses, browbeating them and distorting and misrepresenting the facts, the total amount they could gather together by the grossest exaggeration was only $30,000,000. But, when they wanted to carry out their object and to defame the country, $10,000,000 is a bagatelle to them. These gentlemen state that the alleged engineering mistakes on this railway cost the country $9,945,000, and it does seem to me that in regard to this question of engineering mistakes, hon. gentlemen opposite have, wittingly or unwittingly, misled the public mind to a very great degree. The suggestion is made that the commission were the people who decided what ought to be paid to a contractor. As a matter of fact, the commission had nothing to do with the matter, except to pay the amount certified by the chief engineer. This is what the statute says upon the subject. I am reading from chapter 71, section 18:
No money shall be paid to any contractor until the chief engineer has certified that th* work for or on account of which it is claimed has been duly executed and that such money is due and payable, nor, until such^ certificate has been approved by the commissioners.
Therefore, before any contractor on the Transcontinental railway could be paid for assembled rock or for solid rock, he had first to have a valuation made by the resident or district engineer. Their reports would have to go to the chief engineer, who was responsible for the ultimate determination as to how much was to be paid. The chief engineer would send the account to the commissioners, who had nothing whatever to do with the classification except to certify the account. There is not in this House an hon. gentleman of the legal profession who, after reading that section, .would dare to assert that, unless the chief engineer of the commission wrongfully and knowingly certified to a wrong amount, it would be possible for the commission to pay a single dollar improperly to any contractor. What were the other conditions? While this railway was being constructed in this northern land, from Cochrane east to Moncton, west to Winnipeg, resident engineers and district engineers were on the ground. These men were all young Canadians, many of them fresh from college, on the threshold of life, ambitious to succeed, knowing that unless honesty and integrity were the qualities they possessed, they could never come to the front in their profession. The district engineers and the resident engineers, who saw every ton of stone blasted and every shovelful of earth removed, were the men who could determine whether an excavation should be classified as loose earth, as common rock, or as solid rock. These were the men who sent the reports to Ottawa. Unless this House is prepared to believe that not merely the district engineers and the resident engineers but every chainman, every rodrnan, and every transit man, who saw what kind of material was coming out and who knew whether it should be classified as solid rock or as common excavation, were criminals, then there is not the slightest justification for this huge item of $9,000,000. Hon. gentlemen, for party purposes and in the heat of party argument will make suggestions against the Government of the day and hold it responsible for things, for which perhaps on examintion they will find no justification for their assertions. Any hon. gentleman who approaches this question of classification with a fair mind knows that the men who were on the work would know

whether or not there was wrongdoing. If he is prepared to say that these men were criminals, then I am sorry for him because I do not believe they were. Not only would they need to be criminals, but the chief engineer himself would need to be a criminal. He has been in that position for the last five years. Hon. gentlemen opposite must have confidence in him or they would not continue him in this position. He has certified to every dollar that has gone out of the public treasury of this country for the construction of this railway since the autumn of 1909. Hon. gentleihen know that that statement is absolutely true and cannot be controverted. The chief engineer for two years previous to the Liberal party going out of power certified to every dollar paid to any contractor or to any man for work done on the Transcontinental railway. Yet my hon. friends opposite let loose their dogs of war; they assert throughout this country that $9,000,000 were taken wrongfully out of the public treasury by this public servant, whom they recognize as being competent and honest and whom they continue in office until this very day certifying to every dollar that is paid out. Was ever a more grotesque position presented to the people of any country than the one held by hon. gentlemen opposite in regard to this matter?
Who appointed the subordinates? It is on record in the public documents of this country that every man appointed under the regime of Mr. Lumsden was recommended by him. Every man appointed since Mr. Grant became chief engineer was recommended by Mr. Grant. These men had toiled in the northern wilds; they had been engaged in this pioneering and preliminary work and had done their duty. They had received the ratification of the Government of the day previous to 1911 and the ratification of this Government every day and every hour .through the chief engineer. Then Mr. Gutelius goes out and inspects the work. He looks at a cut and says: Why, the man that was here when this cut was made does not know anything about it. It is true that the stone that was blasted and the earth that was removed are now lying in an embankment perhaps hundreds of feet away; but I am Mr. Gutelius; I know more about it than the man who was here, or than Mr. Col-lingwood Schreiber or Mr. Kelliher or Mr. Woods or Mr. Gordon Grant. I know more about it than they do, although they went over all this territory and looked at every bit of excavation where any exception was 
taken to the classification. They formed their opinions, they certified to every dollar; they paid the money. I know more, says Mr. Gutelius, than all these gentlemen do, although I am only coming here four or five years after the line has been built and when trains are running over it. After the snows of the winter have come and melted away in the spring and after all the changes that come with nature's changes have come and gone, still this great man, Mr. Gutelius, knows more than all these people. Of course Mr. Lynch-Staunton does not know anything about engineering; he does not pretend to do so. Mr. Gutelius, I am told, knows something about engineering. He comes before the Canadian people and says: Although all these men were toiling and working on that railroad, I know more about it than they do, though I never saw the material, and in regard to high classification, ploughable clay and overbreak, he said these men had allowed $3,362,000 too much and a lot of items peculiarly within the knowledge of the engineer constructing the road should be entirely wiped out. Then he totals up all the alleged mistakes of these men who have been working on that railway for seven long years having everything certified to by responsible men and particularly by the chief engineer, whom the Premier of this country continued in office, and whom he proclaimed to the world as an honest man. The people of Canada are asked to believe this Mr. Gutelius who says that he has examined the work and that $9,000,000 might have been saved by these men. After all that, the people of Canada are asked to believe this grotesque proposition -that this man, Gutelius, could blow into this country after ali this was over and proceed to tell where $9,000,000 might have been saved. I say this proposition is so ridiculous that all that is necessary is to let the clear light of day shine upon it in order that we may understand it.
Now, Mr. Grant went over this question before. Mr. Grant was the arbitrator to determine these things. And this is what he says as to the value of the examination that could be made of a cut from which material had been taken. I quote from the evidence in the Lumsden investigation-Appendix to the Journals, of the House of Commons, volumn xlv, page 535:
Q. You told us, Mr. Grant, that even with very experienced engineers making a very cursory and very superficial examination of cuts, such an examination as Mr. Lumsden has described to us as made by the arbitrators in the first arbitration, would be insufficient to form

any opinion that would be at all reliable?-A. Oh, I don't think any engineer unacquainted with the work can go into those cuts now and they have been done for two or three years and form a judgment without considering very carefully what he is doing, and questioning the engineer who is on the ground, and getting all the information from him that is possible and also examining the material in the fill that came out o,f that cut, because when you go in a cut you see the sides, you don't see the material that is taken out of it.
The effect of that answer is to show that the men who came along inspecting in after days would have to get back to the engineer who was there when the work was done. So, the question was naturally asked Mr. Grant:	*
Q. While acting as assistant district, engineer or as inspecting engineer or as chief engineer, did you ever acquire any knowledge that would lead you to suspect the good faith of any of the engineers classifying?.-A. I did not.
Q. There may have been some errors of judgment, but you are satisfied that there was no bad faith on the part of the engineers classifying?.-A. I am perfectly satisfied. The proof of that is that the same men are on the line to-day, and if I suspected them of bad faith they would not be there.
In face of that testimony of the gentleman whom this Government hold out to the people as the responsible man who is to carry on this construction, of what use is it of Mr. Gutelius and Mr. Lynch-Staunton to come here with this party report, this political pamphlet, intended to misrepresent the political history of this country?
Another point in this connection should be noted. We have heard a good deal about classification. Hon. gentlemen have talked a good deal about that and have told us just where this country was losing three or four million dollars. Who ever heard of 'assembled rock'?-they ask. But Mr. Gordon Grant said that there were to be found in the Laurentian range, two particular districts, F and B, in which this material was to be found, which could only [DOT]be described as ' assembled rock ' and must be classified accordingly. I will just give Mr. Grant's evidence. I may say, we have heard a good deal about the McArthur contract. Having had the opportunity to go from Fort William to Winnipeg over this line, it seems to me that if bon. gentlemen opposite had wished to arrive at a fair conclusion in regard of this matter some of them at least would have taken a trip over that part of the road. There they "will find conditions which involve railway work of the heaviest kind to be found anywhere in Canada except in the Rocky mountains.

Not even excepting the
Rocky mountains,

Yes, the heaviest
kind of work. Here is Mr. Gordon Grant's evidence, page 534:
Now on the McArthur contract-if you do not know of course you will tell us so-can you give us an idea of the proportion of ledge rock and of assembled rock-A. Well, so far as I am concerned, this question of over-classification to me is a tempest in a teapot, and to illustrate that let me take the McArthur contract: there have been 15,200,000 yards of material moved on that contract.
Q. 15,200,000?-A. Somewhere about that. About 6,300,000 yards of solid rock. Now, about
350.000	yards of that is assembled rock and no more. Therefore if the whole mass were disputed, which would be absurd, you would not have much to kick about.
Q. Out of 6,300,000 yards of rock there is only how much of assembled rock?-A. About
350.000	yards.
Q. About 350,000 yards?-A. That is all they can dispute.
Q. And there is no dispute about the rest of the rock? The only dispute is about assembled rock?-A. So if you turned the whole thing into loose rock, which I say would he absurd, on the face of it, you would not have more than
300.000	yards to kick about.
Here is the duly accredited chief engineer of the Transcontinental Cbmmission recognized by this Government and held up to the Canadian people as responsible for every dollar spent on that line-and to he there, I suspect, until it goes into operation-who declares that this whole question of over-classification, which is being made the basis of misrepresentation in this report, is nothing but a tempest in a teapot.
Oh, oh.

Of course, my hon. friend knows more about it than Mr. Grant does. Now, let me quote from page 547, with regard to this question of assembled rock:
Q. Now, where you have found assembled rock, as I understand on district B there were very large quantities of assembled rock, and that assembled rock is taken out would It be feasible to put that with a slope similar to ledge rock when that is removed ? A. No, it would not; It would not be safe to do so, because assembled rock as you know consists largely of boulders, and that material won't stand up for any length of time on a slope of J to 1. It will for a certain time, but it is not safe. Therefore for the sake of safety all slopes on assembled rock cuts had to be flattened out to 1, and in many cases to 1J to 1, which of course increased the quantities to a very much greater amount than was estimated.
Q. I suppose wherever this assembled rock existed, the portion outside the theoretical slope for ledge rock would probably be greater

than that within the slopes, wouldn't it ? A. Yes, in the case of 1J to 1 slope it would practically double the quantity.
Q. Could that have been foreseen in any way, Mr. Grant ? A. No, it could not.
Q. Is there any fault to be attributed to anybody in connection with it ? A. None whatever.
Now, I referred a short time ago to the fact that $60,000,000 of the cost of this Transcontinental Tailway lies at the door of hon. gentlemen opposite. If they wanted to economize, if they wanted to reduce this amount of expenditure, the estimate of which they have given to the country, the power is with them. One would think, to hear them talk, that the Liberal party were still in power controlling the construction of the Transcontinental. But it is two years and a half since the Liberal party went out of office and their responsibility ceases. Hon. gentlemen opposite, through their officials, are the mm who have to certify the payments for contractors. Not only must Mr. Grant certify, but their specially .appointed commissioner, Mr. Leonard, who does not seem to please the Winnipeg Telegram, but who has the confidence of the members of the Government, and who is supposed to be especially the watchdog of the treasury in this matter, must certify to everything. We have heard a great deal of the McArthur contract. I was surprised, on looking over the Auditor General's Report, to find that this Government was paying out money with a liberal hand. In the financial year ending March 31, 1913, they had paid out, largely to contractors, $13,766,000. When they, came into office, and so became responsible for this work, they were in this position:
They found that a large measure of security had been provided by the wise forethought of the men who were dealing with the matter when the Liberal party was in power. The final estimates had all been passe 1, every dollar of security was in the hands of hon. gentlemen opposite. This is the statement of Mr. Grant on page 539 of the report of the special committee:
Q. Well, in the matter of both over-classification and overbreak, I want to come back now to the position of the Transcontinental Commissioners. No final estimates have gone out with respect to any of this work in which there is in your opinion some over-classification and some access of overbreak allowed. There are no final estimates gone out at all?- A. There are no final estimates gone out at all.
Q. It is all subject to revision and correction?-A. Yes.

Q. Now, the Transcontinental commissioners have certain securities and guarantees. What do these guarantees consist of?-A. Practically speaking, about three times as much money as there is in dispute on any contract.
Q. So that taking the extreme view of all the classification, and of all the overbreak that is said to be allowed in excess of what ought to be allowed, the commission to-day has absolute security in cash?-A. For double the amount.
Q. For double the moment anyway?-A. Yes.
Q. And then in addition they have all the plant as security?-A. Yes.
So that when hon. gentlemen came into power they had the whole matter in their own hands. If there was over-classification; if any one of the hon. gentlemen on the other' side who talked so loudly in the House and out of the House previous to September 30, 1911, knew that any contractor had obtained money improperly, he and his party could have seen that the country got it back. Have we heard of anything of that kind? No; hon. gentlemen have gone along paying out money to M. P. and J. T. Davis

the gentlemen whose names have been bandied about in this House during the last ten days by hon. gentlemen on the other side. Last year this Government paid to M. P. and J. T. Davis upon contracts 7, 8 and 9 something like $869,000.
Then there was Mr. Fauquier. Our friend the Solicitor General the other night, when the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) was speaking, referred to what Mr. Fauquier had said about mass. For curiosity-and I may say that I am going to watch the Solicitor General very closely in future when he quotes evidence-I referred to the evidence of Mr. Fauquier, and I found not the slightest suggestion of any kind to warrant the assertion of the Solicitor Gen' eral in that regard. In fact, Mr, Fauquier told the commission that if they wanted to find out all about this matter, they should subpoena his brother, who had the documents and all the information in his office. But they did not subpoena his brother, and his evidence was not obtained. To Mr. Fauquier hon. gentlemen opposite paid out, down to March, 1913, $529,000; in fact, reference to the Auditor General's Report will show that hon. gentlemen opposite went on paying money to these contractors every day from the time they came into power, without questioning the payments in any way whatever. It was a case of the responsibility of the Administration on the one hand and the exercise of political claptrap on the other; hen. gentlemen went on paying money to these contractors without attempting for one moment to stand by their political claptrap game wherein they

alleged that the country should be protected in regard to this matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not permissible to apply the words 'political claptrap' to hon. members of the House.
I have spoken in a general way about the Conservative party throughout the country who are playing a political claptrap game with regard to this matter. I think I can make that assertion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the words were applied to anything which took place outside this House, they would not be unparliamentary, but it is not permissible to apply them to members of the House.
