I spoke of the Conservative party applying the claptrap game as a whole on the one hand, and of the responsibility of these gentlemen holding the reins of power, on the other. These gentlemen, who had to see to it that the Administration of this country was carried on, holding in their hands security for double the amount of any sum that is alleged to have been misspent, went on paying these (contractors without protest, on the certificate of the chief engineer of the road. Further than that, they paid to one contractor more than the amofunt provided |for by the award of the arbitrators. They do this on itbe one hand, and on the other hand they carry out this political claptrap business of talking about the country losing $40,000,000 in the construction of this road.
I want to make another citation with regard to the question of grades and the statement made by the chief engineer, Mr. Grant. He was asked the advantage of building the road up to a high standard, to which he replied that it would be a paying proposition, while the adoption of the lower standard would result in a loss, and a failure to earn the expense of running the road. I need not go into this question in detail; the hon. ex-Minister of Railways went into it at great length, and I would be taking up time unnecessarily if I were to make further reference to it.
Let us analyse some of the other assertions made by these gentlemen, in order to see how anxious they were to find some grounds for alleging over-expenditure. They said there was no necessity for building engine houses so permanently; that had cheaper engine houses been built, the oountry could have saved $800,000. With that divine inspiration which they assume in dealing with this whole question, they
say that only four station houses were needed in the whole of that northern country between Moncton and Quebec. This terrible Railway Commission, the report alleges, had the temerity to build sixteen stations, and because 'they did so, the country lost $204,000. What does Mr. Lynch-Staunton know about freight sheds and station houses? What does he know about how many station houses should be constructed in that northern country, or what kind of freight sheds should be built? Yet he has the unction to sign his name to a report which tells the country that $300,000 would have been saved if cheaper freight sheds had been built. Here is another amusing thing. Eighty-pound i-ails were used in the construction of the road. There is no reason why our friends opposite, if they were sincere in their desire to be true accountants and wanted to do what they talked about when they had no responsibility, should not have ordered that 65-pound instead of 80-pound rails should be used in the remainder of the road. But they did not do so; they went on laying the 80-pound rails; yet they charge this terrible Railway Commission with being extravagant in using 80-pound rails in the sidings, whereas if they had used only 65-pound rails the country would have been saved $340,000.
And so the game goes on. Then these gentlemen, who were in possession of all the wisdom that ever was heard of in regard to railway construction, said: Why, what was the necessity of double-tracking certain pieces of road up there? This commission appointed by the Liberal party had the temerity actually to double-track six miles, they thought it was in the public interest to do so; but they did not know anything about it; we know all about it, they should not have double-tracked that six miles, and so would have saved the country $679,000. And so they go on along these lines, and after they have strained every possible suggestion, gone into every ridiculous hole and corner, drummed up every suggestion of a fault that could be found, they arrive at the end of their labours without being able to allege that there was any corruption on the part of anybody connected with the road, and they have to misrepresent the total of the alleged errors which they find, to the extent of $10,000,000, in order to have a good round figure to talk about in the country. Who is responsible for this report now that has been laid before Parliament by this Govern-
Oh, oh.
My hon. friends do not think that is true. I would like some hon. gentleman on the other side to say what this Government ever did for the good of Canada.
They have made you very tired.
My hon. friend from Simcoe has been as peaceful as a lamb since he sat on that side of the House. We never hear his sweet voice now, as we used to hear it when he was in opposition.
No need to now.

I can assure my hon. friend that I find myself in the best of health and am not a bit tired. I repeat, after two and a half years of Conservative rule my right hon. friend is still living in the past. All he can think of is some of the old stories he used to retail in 1908, some figments of the imagination like the yarns about the Transcontinental. He has created commissions to bring in Teports which injure Canada at home and defame her abroad. The action of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in asking this House to declare that this report is one which should be absolutely condemned as untrue and as misrepresenting the facts is one which should receive the honest consideration of every hon. gentleman in this House. There is one consolation about this matter which the people of Canada are beginning to find out and are becoming more certain of day by day, and that is that the report has no basis in fact and is purely the result of partisanship, written by partisans and written for

a party. The one result of this report will be to hurt Canada in other portions of the world where the facts are not understood as they -are here. Everybody here will soon know how little weight should be attached to this report, and I hope that every hon. gentleman in this House will do his duty to Canada by supporting the motion of my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways.
Mr. GEO. W. FOWLER (Kings and Albert):	Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman
who has just taken his seat (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) has followed the custom of the old-time lawyer who, when he had a really	bad case,
used to abuse the other side. Almost the whole of the hon. gentleman's speech was made up of abuse. He criticised gentlemen on this side of the House because they appointed a commission to lay before the people of Canada-whose trustee this Government is-the exact condition of affairs with regard to the Transcontinental railway and the tremendous expenditure of money connected therewith. That was a duty which this Government owed to the people of this country, a duty which they have well and nobly performed. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) says that this is a cheap report, that it is no good, and yet the ex-Minister of Railways spent seven hours in attempting to answer this cheap report, made by a partisan lawyer and a Yankee engineer of no aoeount whatever according to the hon. member for Pictou. Let me say that in all the history of Canada there has never been .a state paper submitted to Parliament higher in character than the report of Messrs. Staunton and Gutelius. It is -clear and concise, moderate in its tone-
Oh, oh.

-yes, and temperate in every way, showing absolutely no trace whatever of partisanship. It is strong, of [DOT]course. Why? Because the evidence on which it is based, is strong. Would you expect a watery namby-pamby report with such evidence as the commissioners had before them on which to base their conclusions? No. If they had been commissioners like the late Government would have appointed, then we might have expected a milk-and-water report, but they were not that class of men. They gave a report which is clear and concise, which covers the whole ground and there is not a word -or a line of that report that is not based .{Mr. Macdonald.{
on strong and conclusive evidence. And they published the evidence with the report. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat was not as eloquent in his peroration as lie usually is. He had such a bad case that he laboured very hard. I recognize the fact which every man in this House must recognize that we have no more eloquent speaker in this House than the hon. member for Pictou. When he has a good case it is a delight to listen to him, but I felt sorry and pained for the hon. gentleman when I isaw him labouring so hard with his case.
I could have understood some other Liberal members of this House talking blue ruin, but I thought the member for Pictou was more up-to-date. I thought he was more patriotic; I thought he had a greater regard for the welfare of Canada than to be guilty of such preaching. Has the gloom of adversity; have the cold shades of opposition, so chilled the heart of the member for Pictou that he imagines the gloom which possesses his soul, pervades the whole of Canada. I can understand that the hon. gentleman feels badly at being in opposition, because he was assured by his leader that were the Liberals returned to power in 1911 he would be one of the elect. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition will not deny, that while my hon. friend from Pictou may not have been so assured in words, he was given good reason to believe that if the elections of September, 1911, had turned out differently, he would have been taken into the Administration and had the word 'honourable ' prefixed to his name. And, Sir, my hon. friend from Pictou apparently imagines now that because his own soul is chilled with disappointment, and filled with deep and abiding gloom, his condition is that of all Canadians. The hon. gentleman need not worry about that.
The hon. gentleman speaks of browbeating witnesses, and he tells us that the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners were brought before these commissioners and browbeaten. Can you imagine Simon Napoleon Parent being browbeaten by anybody? The hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) has a very vivid imagination, but it cannot reach far enough to encompass such an idea as that. Then, there was Michael Patrick Davis, the contractor; do you imagine that a man with the brazen brow of Michael Patrick Davis could be browbeaten by a little chap like Gutelius? Such an idea is absurd. Then Mr. O'Brien was upon the stand, Mr. O'Brien the great contractor; Michael J. O'Brien. I do not know what

the ' J ' stands for, but you can call it Jeremiah if you like, and the title Jeremiah would probably fit him, because now he is in the slough of lamentations, without any friends that are any good to him. His friend was the ex-Minister of Railways. There is one thing about Mr. M. J. O'Brien that I admire, and I admire it very greatly -he understands what gratitude means. There were many contractors who reaped fortunes when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, but they have not all shown their gratitude in the splendid way in which Mr. M. J. O'Brien did, on one occasion, in South Renfrew.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight oclock.

When the House rose at six o'clock, I was referring to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald). One statement made by him was that no one was deceived as to the cost of this railway. I do not know what the hon. member means by that statement, because it contains a serious reflection upon his leader, the exPremier of this country, who stated that, not the total cost but the total burden of cost, would be $13,000,000. I had the honour of being a member of this House at the time when the right hon. the present leader of the Opposition introduced the National Transcontinental Bill, and I heard him make that statement. Will the total burden of cost of this railway upon the people of this country be only $13,000,000? It will be many times that sum; yet the hon. member from Pictou says that no one was deceived. Was it because no one believed the right hon. gentleman? Is his reputation for veracity and for business ability such that, when he makes a business statement to this House and to this country, the people do not take it at its face value? I cannot read any other meaning than that into the statement of the hon. member for Pictou. We were told by the hon. the then Minister of Finance that, not the total burden of cost but the total cost of this railway from Winnipeg to Moncton, built up to the standard of 0.4 per cent and 0.6 per cent grades, would be $61,000,000. Did the people believe that statement? According to the views of my hon. friend the member for Pictou, they could not have believed that statement, because he says: No one was deceived. When you add the interest to the cost of construction, which is the cost to the 145
people of this country, you will find that the cost will be more than four times the estimate given by the then Minister of Finance; but my hon. friend the member for Pictou says that no one was deceived with regard to the cost of this railway.
He says that the present Government is responsible for every dollar expended upon this road from that memorable 21st day of September, 1911, a black-letter day in the record of my hon. friends opposite. The hon. gentleman must think he is talking to an unintelligent public. The people of Canada are too intelligent to swallow any such stuff as that presented to them by the hon. member for Pictou. If your honour had not decided that the words ' political claptrap ' were not proper in this House,. I could find no words more suitable to characterize this statement of my hon. friend's; but as you have already given that decision, I forbear making the statement.
Every contract for the construction of this railway was let before the 21st of September, 1911. Contracts that need not have been let until perhaps even now were let before" the election of 1911. In case anything happened my hon. friends opposite wanted their friends to have the pickings. Every contract wa3 let and they were specification contracts and the price was set opposite every item in the specification. There were instances where such things as this occurred. On items for which the contractor was to get $17 per cubic yard for concrete work, he sublet the work for $7 a cubic yard, making a rake-off of $10 without doing a stroke of work. Could the new commissioners do anything in regard to it? They were absolutely powerless; they could not repudiate the contract solemnly entered into by their predecessors in office. That is why the money was expended since the coming in of the present Government and the appointment of the new commissioners. It was not the fault of the contractors that they were receiving these huge sums. There was no fraud so far as the contractors were concerned. The fault and the fraud, if there be fraud-and if there was not fraud there was the grossest ignorance and incompetence and my hon. friends can take whichever horn of the dilemma they choose-and the incompetence and ignorance lie at the door of the commissioners appointed by the late Government.
My hon. friend the member for Pictou, who I regret is not in his seat at present, tried to make out that we were opposed to the building of the Quebec bridge. The Con-

building of the bridge was mooted a number of financiers in the city of Quebec thought it would be an excellent plan to form a company to build the bridge, and they organized themselves-into a corporation, the name of which, I think, was the Quebec Bridge Company, of which Mr. Parent was the president. It was a company with large capital, not less than $1,000,000, and as they were going to build this huge bridge, the greatest that had ever been built, it was necessary to have lots of money, and they made a call upon the shareholders of the company by which they produced the magnificent sum of $40,000, 4 per cent on the capital, which amount was put in the treasury. They then elected their directors; any man who had a large amount of money was elected director with a large salary, so that long before the bridge tumbled into the river they had drawn out through the directors the whole of the original' capital. They got a subsidy from the city of Quebec; they got a subsidy from the province of Quebec, and they got a subsidy from the Dominion Government, and then they started to build the bridge. The same M. P. Davis who made $3,500,000 out of the Transcontinental railway was the gentleman appointed by the Quebec Bridge Company to build the bridge. Having started the work, they drew the subsidy from the city of Quebec, they drew the whole or a part of the subsidy from the province of Quebec, .and they drew a portion of the subsidy from the federal Government. When Davis had his substructure nearly finished, the company did not have enough money to pay him. The federal Government would not pay them any more money under the terms of the subsidy, but they had taken power to issue bonds against this bridge. They owed Mr. Davis $160,000, and they handed over to him $400,000 in bonds to pay that debt of $160,000, which meant that his bonds were worth only forty cents on the dollar. The br dge was going to cost $5,000,000 or $6,000,000; all subsidies did not amount to more than $1,750,000; there was only $40,000 of the original capital in the treasury-it had all been drawn out by the directors-so it looked as if the bonds were not going to be worth much. No superstructure had been provided for, and there was no money to build it; it looked as though that M. P. Davis was an easy mark. But those who thought so did not know their man. What happened? Mt. Parent, who was a very influential man at that time in the province of Quebec, came to IMr, Fowler.]
Ottawa and induced the late Government to guarantee the bonds of the Quebec Bridge Company for $6,000,000; so, by the stroke of a pen, by the passing of the necessary Act, the bonds which M. P. Davis had taken at 40 cents on the dollar were worth 100 cents on the dollar-the result being that M. P. Davis was in pocket the sum of $240,000-this simple, innocent M. P. Davis who had been fooled into taking $400,000 of the bonds of the Quebec Bridge Company. Is there a man on the other side of the House so innocent as to suppose for one moment that there was not a secret understanding between Mr. Davis, Mr. Parent and the Government at Ottawa when he accepted these bonds at 40 cents on the dollar, that they were to be implemented by an Act to be passed to make the bonds good? That is how M. P. Davis made $240,000 out of the people of this country.
What thoughts the Quebec bridge calls to mind. If there ever was a monument to the incompetency and to the incapacity of ia government it is the Quebec bridge. Six million dollars of the public money of this country went tumbling into the river. But that was not the worst part of it. More than seventy men-mechanics, the very pick and flower of Canadian workmen -went down to death and burial in the waters of the St. Lawrence river. Let me say that to-day those unblessed bodies are terrible witnesses of the incapacity of the late Laurier Government. What was the matter? Why did the Quebec bridge fall? It did not fall because heavy trains had crossed upon it; it did not fall from any great earthquake that had taken place or any terrible storm which carried away the Forth bridge. Sir, before it was half way across the river it fell of its own weight. It fell because of blundering, faulty construction-and who was to blame? Oh, they say, the engineer was to blame. But before the bridge fell the late Government, not that wonderful Quebec Bridge Company, had assumed the responsibility for its construction. Whom did they appoint as the supervising engineer? Tire very man who designed the bridge, Mr. Cooper, the consulting engineer for the Phoenix Bridge Company, contractors for the bridge. By reason of that man's ignorance and unfitness for his job that bridge fell and carried these men to death, and caused the destruction and loss of $6,000,000 of the public money of this country. Was it not possible for that Government to have obtained men- competent to super-

vise the erection of the bridge? There were yet living that famous band of engineers who had designed and built the wonderful Forth bridge, that triumph of engineering skill. They could have been obtained. But no, so fond at that time were out friends of the American engineer that they thought they had to go across there and secure tne very man who was the consulting engineer for the Phoenix Bridge Company. What was our loss was Mr. M. P. Davis gain. He gained $240,000 by that Quebec bridge transaction, in addition to whatever sums he may have made on the contract. That is not the only thing. Take contracts 16 and 17. By these two contracts M. P. Davis made $740,000 without ever turning a hair.
I thought the defence of the ex-Minister of Railways (Mr. 'Graham) on that was splendid. It stands out in my memory from his whole speech. Why, he said, if Davis had built the road we would have had to pay that $740,000 just the same. Was not that a splendid argument? Was it not a wonderful answer for a man who had filled the prominent position of Minister of Railways in a federal Government in this country? The only defence he could offer for a straight steal, a straight loss to the people of this country, of $740,000, was that if Mr. Davis had built these two contracts himself it would have cost that much just the same. Those tenders were called for at a time when they should not have been called for, when there was no necessity for calling for them. I say here without fear of successful contradiction, the facts show it and the fair inference to be drawn from the facts shows it irrefutably that that tender was let at the time it was let in order that some pet of the Government might be able to make .a large sum of money. There can be no question about that. No man is so innocent as not to realize that. Owing to the inaccessibility of the country tenderers naturally put their figures up. The work was to begin at once and to be completed at once. Davis puts in his tender, gets the two contracts and never goes near the place. He waits for eleven months and then sells the contract to O'Brien, Macdougall and O'Gorman for a rake-off of 10 per cent-and the commissioners agree. Who are the commissioners? Parent, the same gentleman who helped O'Brien to carry off the $240,000, the very same Mr. Simon Napoleon Parent. Ten per cent! And then they waited for months and a little work was
done. By the terms of the contract the whole contract was to be completed at a period when only twelve and a half per cent of the work had been done on 16 and nothing had been done on contract No. 17. What were they waiting for? Until Fauquier Bros, got their two contracts at either end of the work completed so that they could get in their supplies cheaply to this work and make this huge rake-off. So the contract was transferred, by the consent of the comipissioners, and Mr. M. P. Davis made his nice little rake-off of $740,000. So it is between him and his friend Parent. On the Quebec bridge he got $240,000 which, with this $740,000, makes in round figures $1,000,000 that M. P. Davis got without ever having been up there or done anything. But that is only a trifle, a trifle as light as air. What is a million dollars to a Grit contractor? It only helps him to be in a better position to open up the head of the barrel when elections come around. These were not the only transactions where Davis profited from the late Government. There was the lighting of the Cornwall canal, familiar to all of us who were members of this House in the old days when we were in the cold shades of opposition-but were not half as glum as our friends opposite, we did not cry blue ruin or think the country was going to the dogs because there was a certain obsession in the minds of the people and they allowed themselves to be governed by the party that never had the genius for government, and always made a blunder when unfortunately they got the reins of power, but it will be so long before they get them again that gentlemen sitting on the other side will all be gathered with their fathers long before. It was amusing to hear the hon. member for Pictou this afternoon bewailing the fact that this rascality in connection with the building of the Transcontinental railway had been uncovered, because of the effect it was going to have on the money markets of Europe. Yet my hon. friend from Pictou could stand in his place and say that this country was going to destruction, that the Minister of Finance of Canada could not sleep at night by reason of the awful condition financially of the affairs of this country-that would do no harm of course. I quite agree that it would do no harm, people know too well the reason for this awful wail that is going up from the other side of the House to take any stock in it or to have any confidence in it. I am glad my hon. friend has at length returned to the House. I hope he has had a good

dinner. I was lonesome without him. I wanted to see his smiling face across from me because however he may wail about blue ruin he is always smiling.
There is a small matter-but small matters like straws sometimes show which way the wind blows-the matter of farm crossings. I do not know whether reference has been made to the farm crossings in this debate, but just to give a palpable instance of the magnificently efficient way in which these commissioners handled this business I would point to the farm crossing known as Delisle farm crossing. Delisle had a farm of fifty-five acres, and he offered this farm to the commission for $3,500, little less than $70 an acre. The right-of-way agent reported that that was too much, and so they only bought 5.23 acres, for which they paid $100 an -acre, with damages of $277, and a further payment of $500 for damages. That made $1,300 altogether. The railway went across this man's farm, and it was necessary for him to have a crossing to get his cattle to water; so they enlarged the size of the culvert in order that he might drive his cattle through it. What did the enlargement of size of this culvert cost? It only cost $23,635. My hon. friend from Pictou did not observe that. The total cost, therefore, was $24,317, and they could have bought the whole farm for $3,500. There was another case, the Perron farm [DOT]crossing, but it came a little cheaper. The [DOT]extra cost was only $21,000. My hon. friend from Pictou is not the only gentleman who has made a speech in this House on this matter. I have in mind now an hon. gentleman opposite, the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Garvell). Has there ever been a subject discussed in this House upon which the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., has not been heard? I sit and listen to the hon. member for Carleton, and am amazed at the vast knowledge he possesses on every subject. I marvel, and I think e.an it be possible that one mortal mind can hold such vast stores of knowledge? He is a comparatively young man, and if he had devoted to study only those hours usually devoted, it would not be possible for him in the short time he has lived on this earth to have become the walking encyclopedia that he is to-day. Does he ever sleep, or does he spend the still watches of the night prowling about acquiring knowledge and more knowledge? We had a debate last year upon the Naval Bill. Some hon. IMr. Fowler.]
gentlemen doubtless remember it. You at least, Mr. Speaker, remember it, because you were obliged, by virtue of the high office which you hold, to sit and listen to those long, dreary speeches. It seems to me that the emoluments of that office and the dignity that pertains to it are dearly bought when you have to listen to such speeches as were made on the Naval Bill by our friends on the other side of the House. My hon. friend from Carleton made a speech on that subject, and told us all about the construction of warships, ancient and modern, from the triremes of ancient Borne to the caravels of Columbus, from the flat boats of the Bideau canal to the super-dreadnoughts of Great Britain. All were an open book to him. He not only constructed the hulls of the ships, but filled them with the magnificent machinery that propels them. He launched two units, one for the Atlantic coast and the other for the Pacific coast. He put in engines, and in the debate showed a knowledge of the building of an engine not surpassed by Parsons, the inventor of the turbine, nor by Kudyard Kipling, the writer of Mc-Andrews' Hymn.

Mr. Speaker, I hope
you will withdraw your objection, as I am enjoying the hon. .gentleman's remarks very much.

I am sure my hon.
friend is the last man to squeak; I know him too well. When it comes to agriculture, the hon. member knows all that pertains to that science. He is familiar with agriculture, from potatoes to peas, from milking a cow to grooming a horse, from the proper rotation of crops to the best soil in which to grow mushrooms. He can tell the Minister of Agriculture what sort of farm to select and where to select it. He has a thorough and complete knowledge of the subject. But the subject on which he is really at home is electricity. When he speaks on that subject you can see the veritable sparks flashing from his eye and the little blue flames playing about his corrugated brow. My hon. friend from Carleton can find nothing wrong with the conduct of the commissioners charged with the construction of the Transcontinental. Could there be any act of a Liberal Government so bad, so heinous, that my hon. friend could find

anv thing wrong with it? Or could the present Adm'nistration do anything, however good, that my hon. friend 'would not find fault with? So my hon. friend's criticism of the report of this commission is robbed of a weight that it might otherwise have, when we know that he condemned it before he read it, simp'y because it was the report of a commission appointvote on this question. In the debate of September 22, 1903, when I was addressing the House, Mr. Logan, who was then a member, put this question to me:
May I ask the hon. gentleman If he is opposed to the building of the short line between Moncton and Quebec?
I replied, and my answer is to be found in ' Hansard,' 1903, volume 5, page 12046,

I just wish to refer to one other remark that my hon. friend made in his speech the other day. I was a little surprised that you, Mr. Speaker, who are somewhat tended with regard to the rules of debate in this House did not call the hon. gentleman to order. He .said:
Any man from the Maritime provinces who will vote to sustain this report is a traitor to this country and has not the best interests of his province at heart. I will watch this vote with interest.
I hope he will watch it with interest and with principle, too. If the hon. gentleman would only vote on principle and watch with interest, I am afraid he would have to leave his party. He further said:
I want to see what attitude the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will take on this question.
I do not think the hon. gentleman really had any question in his mind as to what attitude the Minister of Marine would take, nor indeed as to what attitude every other member from the Maritime provinces, on this side of the House, would take on the question. I was a member of this House in 1903, when this Transcontinental Bill was launched; I was not afraid then to state the position I was going to take witli regard to the line from Quebec to Moncton.
I am not one of those who votes for a measure simply because it brings a temporary benefit to my province. My interest in this Confederation is not bounded by the limits of the province of New Brunswick; my interest in my country extends from* Halifax to Vancouver, and from the boundaries south to the northernmost limits of Canada. I hold that man a traitor to his country, who, for the sake of some temporary advantage to a locality, is willing to vote for a measure which he knows in his heart is not in the best interests of the whole country. The hon. gentleman need have no uneasiness as to how the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will vote; he need have no uneasiness as to how every member from the Maritime provinces on this side of the House will

speechtext:
