How does his position compare with that of my hon. friend the member for Kings and Albert? The office was there in the gift of his leader, who had the goods to deliver, of exactly the quality that my hon. friend desired. In the hands of his leader was the office that my hon. friend was looking for, that he was praying for. He put himself in the market the moment the door was open; on the first day of the fair he was on the spot. What is the matter? A story is told of an old Irishman whose wife died. Her name was Sarah Jane Hinckley. He wanted to put a tombstone over her grave. The sculptor asked him: what will be the epitaph on your wife's tombstone?
' Oh,' he said, ' I do not know; I would just like to write across the stone there " What is the matter with Sarah Jane Hinckley; she's all right." ' I suppose our Sarah Jane Hinckley from Kings and Albert thought that he was all right for the position, for anything that the Prime Minister had to offer. But unfortunately the right hon. gentleman who had the goods to deliver did not think that the hon. member had the capacity or the qualities necessary. Has the hon. member the consolation of saying that his leader did not know him? Has he the satisfaction of saying: Well, if he had known my excellent qualities better, he would have given me the office? He cannot say that. From 1908 to 1911 his leader knew him intimately, and had some knowledge of him when he was not a member of this House. He saw him perform; he knew his points; he knew all about him. He saw his gaits in his various attitudes and positions. Therefore, the excuse cannot be that the hon. gentlemen did not know my hon. firiend. The reason is that his leader knew him too well. So much the worse for the feelings and the experience of my hon. friend when he comes to discuss the feelings of a disappointed office-seeker. He is somewhat in the position of the ubiquitous Irishman who was on his trial and was told, 'Pat, do not be frightened; you will get justice.' Pat said, That is just what I am afraid of-that I will.' My hon. friend was no doubt afraid that he would get what was coming to him, because of the knowledge his leader had of him, and the unfortunate thing is that he got just what was coming to him. These are my reasons for yielding at once to the vast experience and knowledge of my hon.
friend when he comes to deal with the heart-rendings of a disappointed office-seeker.
What did the hon. gentleman tell us about the contracts that were let and the subject which we are particularly dis-' cussing upon the motion and the amendment before the House? We were told by the hon. member that there were great irregularities, and he began to point them out by showing that contracts were not properly let and that there was squandering of money and dishonesty from one end of this transaction to the other. I am sorry that the mind of the hon. gentleman is so constructed that he cannot conceive of honesty anywhere except perhaps under his own hat. Does the hon. gentleman know of anything that was irregular, anything that savoured of wrongdoing with regard to this huge undertaking from Winnipeg to Moncton? There are some men in this country who cannot conceive of anything being done honestly or in a straightforward way. They think there must be something wrong about it. I submit that, on account of the latitude allowed the hon. gentleman to discuss the motives of parties and of men, 1 am quite in order in pointing out to him the history of his party in regard	to matters of this kind.
The people of Canada have been very kind indeed to the Conservative party. If ever there was a party in Canada or anywhere in the civilized world that has had opportunities of showing what it could do for its country, it is the Conservative party of Canada. They were honoured with the confidence of the people at Confederation and remained in power until 1873 under the leadership of Sir John Macdonald. Why did they lose the confidence of the .people in 1873? Simply because when they came to manage a big transaction in which great sums of the people's money could be handled rightly or could be handled wrongly, they handled those moneys wrongly and dishonestly-they squandered and stole the money of the people. And so they were turned out of power. But, as I have said, the people were indulgent to the Conservative party, and called them back to power in 1878. But can the leopard change his spots or the Ethiopian his skin? The Conservative party were but a short time in office when they were back at their old tricks. By reason of the tactics of their great leader, Sir John Macdonald, they remained in power down to his death. And

what was the cause of his death? He died broken-hearted because of the scandals that broke out around him; the tide of corruption ran too strong against him, the conditions were such that he could not face them; he died of a broken heart because of the sins of the party he led. Why did they go out of power again? Because of the Curran bridge scandal, the Soulanges canal scandal, the McGreevy-Connolly scandal, and the thousand and one other scandals that arose in connection with their handling of the public funds. I can understand why the hon. member for Kings-Albert cannot conceive of any political party doing things honestly, for he is a lineal descendant, and fellow-workman of the party whose record I have just related.
And what have they brought home to us in the fifteen years when we were in power under our distinguished leader? We were told year after year, and day after day, by those hon. gentlemen when they were in opposition, that the moment they got into power they would throw light upon the book-keeping, the contracts and all affairs involving money in the public business of this country and they said they would rend the heavens with the disclosures they would make of the doings of our Administration. The change of government came, and every public record which could be used for the purpose of disclosure was within their control. They have been in power for two years .and a half; they have had commission after commission, searching-party after searching-party, and down to this day they have not been able to put their finger on one fifty-cent piece of the people's money spent under the Laurier Administration that was not properly used. If there is anything that they know, I, as a humble follower of the great leader of the Liberal party, and as a humble member of this party, defy them to produce it, and to show the people wherein either as a party or as individuals belonging to that party we have done anything unworthy of the cause we represent or the name our party bears. It is an easy matter to slander either an individual or a party, especially here in this House where the cloak of privilege is thrown over the shoulders of the speakers. But I challenge the hon. member for Kings-Albert to say in the open the things concerning Mr. Davis that he has said in this House-that Mr. Davis was stealing money from the treasury of Canada, that he was receiving money, improperly and with the assistance

of the commission. If he will go outside and say these things concerning Mr. Davis and the commissioners, I promise him, he will get an answer from the Supreme Court of this country that will not be to his liking. It is easy to make general statements without anything to back them up; and I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that there was not a single statement made by the hon. gentleman with regard to Mr. Davis or the commissioners that he could back up with facts. Now, I can very well leave the record of our party there. We have a leader, we have a record, we have a policy that received the commendation of the people. I think it ill becomes the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House, or any gentlemen of the party to which he belongs, to throw stones at us in view of the rickety glass house in which they themselves have lived for the last forty years.
The hon. gentleman challenged us to show any statement in this Gutelius-Staunton report that was not backed up by the evidence. Well1, Sir, this report contains the statement that money was squandered by the Transcontinental Railway Commission in 'building a double-track railway, whereas they should have built a single-track railway. I had a controversy with my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) the other night on that point. And, with his usual capacity for acrobatic performance and jumping everywhere except where he was asked to jump, the hon. gentleman avoided the point. I asked him to show where in the Act it was provided that this was to be a single-track railway. And what did he do? He produced a contract under which the contractor bound himself to build a singledrack railway. And he was cheered to the echo by the ' intelligence ' of the hon. gentlemen who sit around him, and they all said, what a masterful lawyer that young chap is. The	hon.	gentleman endeavoured to prove that Davis had a contract to build a single track railway; of course, he said, that is the law; that is what is in the statute. I submit that that is not the law, and that is not what is in the statute. I do hope that the reputation of the member for North Ontario as a lawyer does not depend upon the assertion which he made in that regard. But this assertion was followed up to-night by another along the same line made by the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the House. What is the law on this point? Chapter 71 of the Acts of 1903 very clearly and specifically

slates the power of the commission in this regard. Section 8 says.:
The eastern division of the said Transcontinental railway extending from the city of Moncton to the city of Winnipeg, shall he constructed by or for the Government in the manner hereinafter provided and subject to the terms and provisions of the agreement.
There is not a word in this section about single track railway. Here is section 15 of the same Act:
The commissioners shall have, in respect to the eastern division, in addition to all the rights and powers conferred by this Act, all the rights, powers, remedies and immunities conferred upon a railway company under the Railway Act and amendments thereto, or such general Railway Act, in so far as they are applicable to the said railway, and in so far as they are not inconsistent with or contrary to the provisions of this Act shall be taken and held to be incorporated in this Act.
My hon. friend appeared very learned the other night and got his friends to laugh because I took the point in law that there was no restriction on this commission as to what kind of railway they should build. Here is the statute from which I was quoting on that occasion, and which I stand by now. I say that the statute does no more than give the amplest power to these commissioners' to build any kind of railway they want to build. If I did have any doubt about this matter it was removed long before the hon. member for North Ontario spoke by the observations of the hon member for South Renfrew, who held this book out the other night to the Solicitor General and asked him to find in it or anywhere in the law governing this subject a provision that the road must be a single track road, and the Solicitor General, with all his ingenuity and ability to get rid of a difficulty, had to succumb to the inevitable and acknowledge that there was no such provision. What becomes of the challenge of the hon. member for Kings and Albert, directed to me as the next speaker, to point out in this report anything inconsistent with the facts and the evidence submitted? There is not in this report, from one end to the other, a particle of evidence which in the slightest degree supports the contention that only a single track railway should be built. I submit that even if the law said that a single track railway should be built, which it does not say, what was actually done is incidental to the building of any railway, that is, the making of provisions for double tracks and sidings at the termini of the road. There is, therefore, nothing at all in the point which hon. gentlemen opposite have attempted to make to the effect
that hundreds of thousands of dollars were lost in the double tracking of this road.
The hon. member foT Kings and Albert challenges us also to name one assertion made in the synopsis of the commissioners' report which is not backed up by the evidence. I want to give one more illustration, and then I am through with that part of my remarks. I wish to point out, not only to the House but to any person who may think it worth while to read my observations, that this report is not reliable because in dozens of instances statements are made which are not borne out by the facts. While I do not propose to go over the whole of these instances, I want to point out that when the evidence of any person is found to be defective in several material points, the value of the whole of his evidence is practically destroyed. Hon. gentlemen in this House who are lawyers and who have to deal with the weight of evidence, know that if a man goes on the -stand and is caught in stating what is not the fact on several points, so far as the court is concerned, while he may tell the truth in some instances, the value of the whole of his evidence is practically destroyed because he is found telling what is not true. I simply wish to apply that principle to this report, and to ask my hearers to conclude that the report is entirely unworthy of confidence. On page 6 we are told that the commissioners were wrong in their methods of inviting tenders. The report says:
The rules adopted by the commission in advertising for tenders, the unlimited security required to be furnished by the contractors, and the proposal to let the work for the most part in unreasonably large sections, resulted in only five contractors tendering for 806 miles of the railway, and eleven contracting firms secured all the work and sublet it to upwards of 100 subcontractors, who, had the work been divided into reasonably large sections and the security required In other governmental contracts only been exacted, would have in all probability competed in the bidding. As an indication of the handsome profits derived by these eleven firms, it appears that they were paid $8,800,000 in profits for that part of their work which they let to subcontractors.
For the proof of that statement we are referred to page 19. It may be tedious to you, Sir, and to the House to listen to the evidence to which we are referred, but a concise statement of facts is made on page 6 of the report, and at the foot of that page we find the words: ' See page 19.' One would therefore expect to find on page 19 of the report evidence to substantiate the charge that tenders were improperly called for. Here is page 19: ' Methods of award-

ing contracts and the consequences.' Permit me to read this evidence, and let me remind hon. gentlemen again that we expect to find on this page evidence of misconduct in respect to the calling for tenders:
As there are several important matters considered under this head, an explanation of some length is necessary to their understanding.
For construction purposes, the 1,806 miles of railway to be built was divided into 21 sections, the length and location of which will be seen on exhibit No. 9.
The commission furnished under forms (see exhibit No. 10), which included a unit price schedule for various items of work and material connected with the intended contract and named everything which the engineers thought might enter into the construction of the railway in all its ramifications. The tenderers were required to fill in the schedule with their prices per yard, per pound, etc., for excavating and furnishing material.
Before advertising for tenders the engineers made an estimate for each section of the quantities and cost of the various materials and works named in schedule expected to be moved or provided, to be in a position when the tenders were received by placing the prices mentioned in the tenders opposite these items to determine who are the lowest tenderers. A glance at the schedule will make the above quite clear.
The contractors were required to tender on a general contract to do everything towards the building of the railway excepting the supplying of the steel for the tracks, the building of steel bridges, depots, shops, warehouses, freight and fuel sheds. For some reason unknown to us although the other buildings were excluded the engine houses and section houses along the whole line were specifically included in the general contract and, for some other reason quite impossible to understand, it is provided in the contract that the prices named should not apply to engine houses and section houses. That this was deliberately done appears from the fact that the secretary drew the attention of the commissioners to the omission. Later (see 'buildings,' page 80) we will have something more to say about this peculiarity of the contract, which practically allowed the contractors to fix their own prices.
It was open to the commission to inform the tenderers of the quantities which the engineers estimated would be included in their contracts for the purpose of letting them know what the engineers thought as to the magnitude of the contract.
After consulting with Mr. Collingwood Schreiber, who strongly advised that estimates be not exhibited to the tenderers the commissioners decided that they would not give to the contractors this information, and would [DOT]furnish them only with profiles and plans. ( Exhibit No. 11.)
The contractors themselves considered that the engineers' estimates were strictly private. (Page 494.)
Where the information is not open to all it is most unfair that any one tenderer should ebtain 'inside information' because, if he knew the quantities he might put a very high price against an item on which he knew the engineers

had not estimated or had only estimated for a small quantity without any fear of the total under that head bulking so large in the entire price as to imperil his chances, or he might, as was done by Fauquier Bros., put a very low price on an item which the engineers had mistakenly estimated at a very large amount.
In awarding the general contracts the first step was to advertise for tenders. A copy of an advertisement is appended. (See exhibit No. 12.) In submitting their tenders the tenderers were to fill in in the column headed 'rate' their price for each of the 103 items enumerated.
That is the whole of the evidence on page 19. I submit to you and to the hon. gentlemen in this House that there is not one word there to substantiate the charge that tenders were improperly called for and that opportunities were given to some tenderers that were not given to others. These are at least two instances in which there is not the slightest evidence that there had been any wrong-doing as far as the commissioners were concerned.
We have a charge elsewhere in this report of the investigating commission that momentum grades should have been adopted and the statement that if they had been a great saving would have been effected. The investigators report that the commissioners and the Government were to be condemned, forsooth, because they did not follow such a course. We have the evidence furnished by the investigating commission themselves upon that very point, and what is it? Not one syllable from the officers whom the commissioners were obliged to follow and these rulings and decisions they were bound to observe, to support the contention made in this report that momentum grades should have been allowed and that they would have been equally effective and efficient in the construction of the road. Here is the evidence furnished by the commission, and I submit to you that there is no danger of their furnishing anything but what they had to; they would certainly not furnish anything favourable to the commissioners who had the construction in hand. On August 9, 1905, there is a letter to Mr. H. A. Woods, assistant chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, from Mr. D. MacPherson, the assistant chief engineer of the commission. That letter reads:
August 9, 1905.
H. A. Woods, Esq.,
Assistant Chief Engineer,	.
Grand Trunk Pacific Railway,
Montreal, P.Q.
Dear Sir,-Would you kindly send me a set of your speed and distance diagrams for cal-

culating momentum grades, giving details of weights of engines used.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) D. MaoPherson.
On August 14, there is a reply to that letter:
Montreal, Que., August 14, 1905.
Mr. D. MacPherson,
Assistant Chief Engineer,
Transcontinental Railway,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-Replying to your letter, of August 9, asking for a set of our speed and distance diagrams for calculating momentum grades. I beg to say that we have not considered momentum grades, iri any way, in our located lines, and I question the utility of doing so on grades as low as we are using.
For details of weight and engines used, I have to say that we propose to use the new Government specifications for bridges, using the ' heavy' class of engines. This I understand gives the weight of engine and tender 355,440.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) H. A. Woods. Assistant Chief Engineer.
Then there is a letter addressed to H. D. Lumsden, Esq., as follows:
November 20, 1905.
H. D. Lumsden, Esq.,
Chief Engineer,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Attached is correspondence I have had with our district engineers and with the assistant chief engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, on the subject of virtual grades.
You will see that some of our engineers are in favour of using same in certain places, and some are not. Mr. Woods is not in favour of using them.
Here is the point: Mr. Woods is the engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific, who are to take over this road under a contract when it is finished, and we have here the statement that Mr. Woods is not in favour of using momentum grades:
They are of course only suitable for undulating country and not for long stretches of couth try on maximum grades.
Engineering has been described as the art of making a dollar earn the most money, and a judicious use of virtual grades at points where the locomotive engineer has a chance to ' take a run at the grade,' would undoubtedly save money in construction and admit of the line being operated with maximum virtual grades of 0.4 and 0.6 though the actual grades would appear on the profile as steeper. Of course, if we have actual grades of 0.4 in locations where the engine can get a run at them, they can be operated as virtual grades or less slope, and the haulage capacity of the engine will be greater than on a virtual grade of 0.4. Will you kindly let me have your ruling early as to whether or not we shall use virtual grades where possible? Please return file.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd) D. MacPherson, Assistant Chief Engineer.
The reply to this letter is as follows:
D. MacPherson, Esq.,
Assistant Chief Engineer.
Dear Sir,-In reply to your letter of the 20th inst. re actual and virtual grades. I am certainly of the opinion that we must adhere to actual grades so far as our construction is concerned, and all district engineers should be so instructed. Should any exceptional cases arise they should be submitted to this office, but you must bear in mind they must be approved by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company before they can be adopted. I return herewith all correspondence.
Yours truly,
(Sgd) Hugh D. Lumsden.
That seems to be all that passed between the engineers of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the engineers of the commission in connection with this matter. The question was brought up by MacPherson, who submitted it to the chief engineer of the Transcontinental. Mr. Lumsden said that it was not in compliance with the terms of the contract, and therefore there was no use talking any further about it, and he ordered his assistant engineer to instruct the engineers from one end of the line to the other accordingly, and that was the end of it. The commission appointed to construct this road were given under the Act a chief engineer who had general control of the whole work, absolute control over the final estimates, and actual control of what should be regarded as final in connection with the whole work. When such a man gives an opinion to the commission that a certain grade is to be followed, and that there is no use talking about anything else, would it be conceivable for one moment to suppose that the commissioners, who were bound to follow that man's advice, would put up their own opinion against his and say: We will change the grade and change the contracts? Where would this work have been if the commissioners had not followed the advice of the best authority on engineering which this country put at their disposal? They were bound to follow the advice given by the chief engineer, and in following that advice they did what was right. We have heard a great deal about clap-trap this evening. My references have no bearing on the language of anyone in this House, but I submit that, so far as business is concerned, this report is clap-trap of the worst possible kind, and not deserving of the least possible attention of this House or of any respectable portion of the community to which it is supposed to be submitted.

The investigating commissioners also raise the point that the Transcontinental Commission did not follow the advice of the legal authorities of the Government, and that if they had any legal authorities themselves they did not consult them. I submit that that is not fair; it is not what I would call honest. I find here upon the record a question put to Mr. Grant which strikes me as not being a fair and proper question. Mr. Lynch-Staunton asked him the following question:
Q. You were not aware that the commissioners were asked the opinion ot a legal adviser in respect to the matter of the construction that they were putting on this assembled rock?
Mr. Grant, with the answer practically put in his mouth, says:
No, I am not aware. So far as I know, they did not.
Q. Don't you think it was poor business for them not to have asked a legal opinion?-A. I suppose it would have been better.
But all this time Mr. Staunton had in his hand the letter and the opinion which appears on page 384 of the report in respect to this very subject of classification. If there is anything wrong about the classification-I do not agree for one moment that there is-that is certainly a matter not brought home to the doors of the commissioners. They accepted the plans and specifications put in their hands by the officers of the Government. By whom were those plans and specifications prepared? They were prepared by Mr. Woods, by Mr. Butler, and by the engineer who was the adviser of the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Collingwood Schreiber. These three capable men met and prepared the plans and specifications, approved them so far as they could approve them, and handed them over to the commission as being the plans and specifications on which the road was to be built. What remained to the commissioners was simply to accept those plans and specifications and to carry out the work to the best of their ability. If there was anything wrong with those plans it was certainly not for the commissioners to correct them, but for the experts of the Government.
I wish to bring to the notice of the House a very remarkable state of affairs. At the time this contract was entered into and the plans and specifications were agreed upon, there was in the office of the Railway Department of this country, as Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals and as chief engineer of that department, a gentle-

man of very high repute as an engineer, a gentleman of learning and ability and a man of affairs in this country-Mr. M. J. Butler. Mr. Butler, of all men had knowledge, from the origin, of those plans and specifications. He had intimate knowledge of how the building of this high-class road was arrived at, he knew what advice he had given to the Government with respect to it, and the responsibility which he took upon himself in connection with preparing the plans and the advice he gave in regard to the grade to be used on the Transcontinental. It would strike you, Mr. Speaker, that a royal commission that was looking for the truth and the truth only, a commission that wanted to get at the foundation of this matter and put the facts before the people, would have called as its first witness Mr. Butler. Mr. Butler knew all about the business better than any other man in this country. But what happened? The commission sat day after day, wandered about from place to place, took photographs and snapshots of themselves on the hillsides whenever it was pleasant and sunny enough for them to be out. From the day they were appointed till they handed in this report they were wandering all over the country taking evidence here and there. Mr. Butler was available to them; he was in the city of Montreal and could have been called at any time. His evidence would certainly have been valuable to the people of this country, and would have been the best evidence, and the kind of testimony the people of this country want; but from the day the commission started until they handed in their report Mr. Butler was not examined and the people of this country and the members of this House are not given the benefit of his opinion. If the commissioners wanted to get at the real facts, why did they not call Mr. Butler, the man of all others who knew all about it and could give an opinion as to why they decided on an 0.4 per cent grade one way, and an 0.6 per cent grade the other? I do not know why they did not call him-I do not want to make any harsh statements- but, judging from the general character of this report, and the aptitude with which the facts are suppressed and the facility with which matters are put forward which are detrimental to the interests of the Liberal party, and which throw a slur on the capacity of the engineers of the National Transcontinental Commission, 1 nave the right to draw the conclusion that the evidence of Mr. Butler was kept in the background because it might throw on this whole business

a light that they could not hide under a bushel, and so the only safe thing to do was not to examine him at all. Mr. C. A. Young was the commissioner in charge of the Winnipeg end of the work, and one would naturally suppose that he would be the first man they would call as a witness. He had to deal with the matter, and he was the best evidence, because he was on the spot and knew all about it, but Mr. Young was never called, and not one word of his testimony is. printed in ths blue book. What I have said about the evidence of Mr. Butler I say about the evidence of Mr. Young, namely, that his evidence was the suppressed by these gentlemen because it would not suit the kind of instrument they were preparing, and the contract they undertook.

Worse than that, they
had a discussion with Mr. Butler, and it was never incorporated in the evidence.

I am told by the non. member that they had an opportunity of discussing with Mr. Butler what his evidence would be, and when they found it would not suit their purpose they left it out altogether. That is the kind of a report we are called upon to treat seriously.
1 wish to point out further, that so far as Mr. Lynch-Sitaunton put himself in opposition to the opinion of anybody else who had a right to give a definite and considered opinion in connection with this matter, he was found to be wrong. He put himself forward as an authority on the question of what kind of buildings should be erected, and the manner in which the railroad, with all that appertains to it, should be operated. These commissioners put their opinion against the authority, of such a man as Sir William Whyte, chosen as arbitrator by the contending parties, and Sir William Whyte turned down that opinion when it was submitted to him, and gave the nr st emphatic decision against Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton as far as concerns the operation of the road and its equipment. One would think that when the award of the arbitrator was against the opinion of the commissioners, they would accept that as being the law, as happens, in every other proceeding o.f this kind. If a judge differs from his brethren on the Bench, and he is overruled, and the majority give a decision settling what the law is for the time being, the dissenting judge does not go out and say: I am right and the others are wrong; he accepts the dictum if the majority. That was what Mr. Lynch-
Staunton should have done when the decision of the tribunal was against him, but instead of that we find him reporting to the King, as represented by the Governor General, that he still adheres to his own opinion, as against the decision of Sir William Whyte.
Then Mr. Lynch-Stauhton gave his opinion on a law point in connection with the contract, and against Mr. Staunton's opinion we have the opinion of the Minister of Justice, a gentleman of wide practice and experience on the Bench and at the Bar; the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice, than whom there is no more capable lawyer in the Dominion ; the opinion of a former distinguished Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Aylesworth, agreeing with the present Minister of Justice and the deputy minister; the opinion of Mr. A. J. Brown of Montreal, a lawyer, whose opinion I understand is of considerable weight, and the opinion of the Law Clerk of the National Transcontinental Railway Commission, and yet, when the report comes down to the House, in spite of this	array of	authority10 p.m.	against	him, Mr.	Lynch-Staunton	still adheres to hisown	legal	opinion.	Of course,	that was
done for the purpose of reflecting upon the National Transcontinental Railway Commission, and upon the late Government.
On the question of classification, I would point out that Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton seem to know very little about assembled rock. I rather think that when the people of Canada come to understand the genesis of this report, for which this country had to pay $63,000, they will reach the conclusion that while the commissioners are ignorant on the subject of assembled Took, they are very astute upon the subject of assembled falsehoods.
On exhibit 16 of volume 2 of this report, we have a diagram of what Mr. Lumsden, the chief engineer, handed out to his subordinates. He pointed out in diagram No. 1 a certain kind of rock in ledges; in diagram No. 2, rock in boulders over one cubic yard; in diagram No. 3, conglomerate rock or plum pudding stone; in diagram No. 4, detached ledge rock in mass over one cubic yard; in diagram No. 5, rock in masses of over one cflbic yard reassembled rock); in diagram No. 6, shale rock. He summarizes at the foot of the page as follows:
No. 1 is a mere matter ot measurement by the engineer.

No. 2 is a mere matter of measurement by rock measurers.
No. 3 is a mere matter of measurement by the engineers.
No. 4 is a mere matter of measurement by rock measurers.
Nos. 5 and 6. To form a judgment as to whether or not it is best removed by blasting, the chief engineer must view the work in progress or leave it to be decided by the engineer in charge, whose duty it is frequently to visit the work during its operation and be governed thereby and act accordingly.
This is signed by Hugh D. Lumsden, chief engineer, and put into the hands of his subordinates; and the commission and everybody else had to follow this report and the law as laid down there by the chief engineer. As I said already, I submit to the House and to the country that there was nothing left to the commissioners but to follow the instructions as laid down by the gentleman given to them as the man above all others who was to direct them as to what was assembled rock, shale rock or common excavation or whatever else they had to deal with in connection with this work. That being the case, I submit that no ease of any kind has been made out against the commissioners.
We have a right to suppose that, before such slanderous charges would be made against the personnel of the commission, there would be some evidence to back them up. I have no brief for the hon. gentlemen who composed that commission, and many of them personally I did not know at all. I had slight acquaintance with the commissioner from Winnipeg, Mr. Young. I believe he is a man of excellent standing in his own city; I have never heard anything to the contrary; and we have to assume until the contrary is shown that he is an honest, capable man, and, of course, as far as this commission and this evidence is concerned, there is nothing to the contrary. As far as the former premier of the province of Quebec is concerned, I submit that he can very well afford to laugh at the criticism levelled against him by hon. gentlemen opposite. He is a man of first class standing in his own province. Not only is he known in that province favourably and well, but he is known from one end of this country to the other as a big man. I submit that, when the day came for the distinguished gentlemen who led the Government of the time to find a man to take the place of Mr. Wade, it would be difficult for him to find a more capable gentleman than Mr. Parent, the exPremier of the great province of Quebec. The old adage would well apply to him in

regard to the speeches made on the other side yesterday and to-day in reference to him. I have heard him say: 'Well, on a beautiful moonlight night, you hear the dogs barking; you hear a lot of noise; but what does the moon do? The moon moves majestically on.' This gentleman, who is and who has always been of high repute in his province, can well afford to hear those barkings and move majestically on in his business and pay no attention to them. If my hon. friends opposite go outside the shelter and protection they may have in their various callings, and say anything about this gentleman, when they are brought to task, they will find that Mr. Parent is the respected gentleman that he always has been, and that his repute and standing in the country are not to be molested or maligned by cheap jack talk, such as we have heard in regard to him yesterday and to-day in this House and elsewhere.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the expression ' cheap jack talk,' as applied to hon. members, is not proper in this House.
Mr. McKENZIE; Well perhaps not, Sir.
I come now to my own province of IS ova Scotia, and refer to those hon. gentlemen who had charge of this commission. We had as the first gentleman who was made chairman of this commission the hon. Mr. Wade, who was for many years a member of this House and well known to yourself, Sir, and many other hon. members. I submit that dn his day, when he was appointed and for many years before he was appointed to this position, Mr. Wade took second place to no man in any province of the Dominion as a gentleman, a man of affairs and a lawyer. While ' he was in charge of this work, he did it well, faithfully and with great display of ability' It is a poor tribute to his memory that gentlemen opposite try, at this time, when he is silent in death, to cast reflections upon his memory by stating that he was a party to giving false information and handing out contracts in a false way and doing things for the purpose of carrying on improperly and dishonestly the affairs of the great undertaking of which he was made chairman and as regards which he had great responsibility. I submit that it is slanderous to him and that it is a pity that hon. gentlemen opposite should think it worthy of them to make such charges against a man who is unable to defend himself.
I come to the hon. gentleman from the

county of Antigonish (Mr. Mclsaac), who took the position of commissioner at the death of Mr. Wade. He does not require any defence at my hands. He was a member of this House for many years, and I submit, without disrepect or disparagement to any other member, that there was never a man in this House who more correctly and more properly behaved himself and was more respected in this House than Mr. Mclsaac. As has been pointed out to me, when it came to the finding of a successor in the great county of Antigonish, which was honoured for many years as having for its representative the distinguished gentleman who was at one time Premier if this country, the right Hon. Sir John Thompson, the mantle of Sir John Thompson fell upon the worthy shoulders of Mr. Mclsaac. He was the gentleman selected by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier to fill the position of Commissioner. Before Mr. Mclsaac came into this House, he was an honoured representative of the county of Antigonish in the local legislature, a member for many years of the Government of Nova Scotia, a distinguished member of the Bar of his province, a man of means, a man of affairs, and acquainted with the many vicissitudes in the progressive province of Nova Scotia.
He came here to give his time and attention to the building of this railway. And there is not a man living who can put his finger upon one spot in the character of Mr. Mclsaac. There are Nova Scotians here who are supposed to know something about Mr. Mclsaac and about Mr. Wade, now dead and gone, and I challenge them to put a finger upon one stain upon the character of these men in connection with any business they ever handled. As to the suggestion that lawyers should not be at the head of this business, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no class of men in the community who are better fitted for such business than lawyers, if you get the right kind of lawyers. It is all nonsense to say that a lawyer knows nothing but how to read statutes and give opinions upon points of law. If a lawyer has a wide practice-as these lawyers had -he has to deal with every kind of business. In a real estate case, he must know something about land measurements, he must know something of the cost of building, both the price of material and the price of labour. I will not go into all the cases; but if you have a practical, experienced lawyer, you have a man whose 146
training brings him into touch with eveTy kind of work. -For that reason, to sneer at lawyers being at the head of the work, is not doing the lawyers justice. The man trained as an engineer may know how to measure a rock cutting or estimate the quantity of material moved, but that is a small matter in comparison with the expending of many millions of dollars and in comparison with the whole work to be done on this road. The man who can deal with prices, men, and matters generally is better equipped for such a work as this than the man who is a specialist in one thing and knows little of others that enter into these projects. So, it is not doing justice either to the Government or to the men who were in charge of the work to sneer at those men because they weTe lawyers. Nor is it fair to sneer at them because the work cost more than it was supposed to cost at the beginning. An hon. member on the other side told us the other day that the commission appointed by the United States Government to build the Panama canal was composed mainly of engineers. Are we asked to believe that there was no over-expense there and that the work is being carried out within the estimate first made? I believe that the estimate given for the construction of that great work was .somewhere in the vicinity of $150,000,000. The expenditure has been $400,000,000, under this great and competent staff of engineers, and the work is not yet finished. If the Government of the United States, with a commission of engineers, naval and military, the best men that could be found, spends over $400,000,000 for a work that was estimated to cost $150,000,000, what have we to say against a commission here, because, forsooth, the work under their charge overran the estimate made in the first place?
The reason why we started this work in 1903 is very well known to you, Mr. Speaker, for you were then in the House at that time and a very active member. Those reasons are set forth in the preamble of the statute, which is as follows:
Whereas by reason of the growth in population and the rapid development in the productiveness and trade of Canada and especially of the western part thereof, and with a view to the opening up of new territory available for settlement, both in the eastern provinces and in the West, and the affording of transportation facilities for such territory, and for other reasons, the necessity has arisen for the construction of a National Transcontinental railway, to be operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion of Canada, from



ocean to ocean, and wholly within Canadian territory ; and whereas an agreement has been entered into, bearing date the 29th day of July, 1903, between His Majesty the King of the first part, and Sir Charles Rivers Wilson, G.C.M.G., C.B., and others, representing therein and acting on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, a company incorporated by an Act of the Parliament of Canada passed at the present session thereof, of the second part, making provision for tfoe construction and operation of such a railway; and whereas it is expedient that Parliament should ratify and confirm the said agreement, and should grant authority for the construction in manner hereinafter provided of the eastern division of the said railway between the city of Moncton, in the province of New Brunswick, and the city of Winnipeg, in the province of Manitoba : Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
As has been pointed out, this enterprise was fully discussed in this House at that time. I do not know that there ever was a subject before this House that received a more thorough threshing out than this. The people were asked to give their judgment upon it, and by an overwhelming majority they declared in favour of the Government carrying out this enterprise. The work was commenced. Then, in 1908, there was an opportunity again for the people to pass judgment; and again, the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was then Premier of Canada, received an indisputable and overwhelming mandate to go forward with this great undertaking to a satisfactory completion. These are the circumstances under which the Government undertook the work and were carrying it on. The hon. member for Kings-Albert told us that he was always opposed to this undertaking. It is possible he was. He says he was elected in 1904, and his opposition was well known. But when the people of Kings-Albert had an opportunity of understanding the subject, when they had the opportunity of knowing what the nature of this enterprise was and what it meant to the Dominion, when the hon. gentleman went back to his constituency in 1908, they defeated him by a sweeping majority. So, his own experience in his own county and in the province of New Brunswick is certainly no proof that the feeling in that great province is against this enterprise. If the hon. gentleman was opposed to it in 1904, I am not surprised that when the Prime Minister came to select his Cabinet he did not take in the hon. gentleman.	For the right hon. leader
of the Government (Mr. Borden) was in favour	of	building	the	road.
He proclaimed from the housetop- eveiv-
where in the province of Nova Scotia that he was in favour of the building of this road. Remarks to that effect were quoted from his speeches here to-night; what is the use, therefore, of a member coming here and telling us that he was against it? His leader, whom he supported and whom he now supports, was in favour of the building of this road from Quebec down to the Maritime provinces. When the right hon. gentleman was confronted with quotations from his own speeches this afternoon, made by the hon, member for Pictou, he took no exception to them, and we must take it for granted that these quotations were correct, that those were his views at that time and are his views to-day, and that he is in favour of the building of this road into the province of New Brunswick and down to the Maritime ports.
We are told by the hon. gentleman from North Ontario that this road should never have been built east of the Quebec bridge. If this road was not to be built east of the Quebec bridge, why should it be built to the bridge? No good purpose is to be served by building the road to the bridge, and stopping at that point. If the purpose of this road is to bring the grain from the West to navigable waters; if its purpose is to bring the grain to a point where it can get from the cars into the steamers, that purpose is accomplished the moment the road reaches Montreal. Why, then, should the road go to Quebec? For no purpose at all, but, in the face of their supporters from the province of Quebec, hon. gentlemen opposite do not dare to say that the road should not be built to Quebec. But why let the road go to Quebec when its purpose is accomplished when it reaches Montreal? If hon. gentlemen contend that the road is not to go further than Quebec; if the purpose, as has been pointed out, is to create a transportation route via Cochrane to the city of Toronto and to open up a canal system so that the traffic which is now going through	Montreal will go through Toronto, the logical conclusion at which we must arrive is that there will be no further necessity for building the road east of Cochrane; that Toronto should be made the central point of the route and that the rest of the road should be dropped. No road has ever been built on this continent on such a high standard as the Transcontinental, and that being the case we cannot compare the cost with that of any other road built in Canada or the United States. It is all very well to

say: you could have saved money by building wooden bridges; you could have saved money by having steeper grades; you could have saved money by having sharper curves. Of course you could. That reminds me of an advertisement of a milk seller which I saw in a newspaper some time ago;
' you can buy milk cheaper here, but it will be cheaper milk.' You could certainly build the road cheaper, but it would be a cheaper road. It would not be the kind of road we want; it would not be the road that would suit the circumstances and necessities of the provinces of New Brunswick Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and, indeed, Canada at large. What is the .purpose of the road? I have read from the statutes that the purpose is to connect the West with the East and to develop our seaports. If this road is not built in a way that-will make it superior to every other road and, by the completeness of its equipment and the nature of its grades, overcome differences in distance, it will not accomplish the purpose for which we have built it. It has been pointed out that there is a difference of at least one hundred or possibly one hundred and fifty miles in favour of Portland for traffic coming from the West. If we built a road of the same capacity and the same grades as the roads that are now going to Portland, why should we think that men who are routing grain from the West are going to route it to St. John and Halifax when they have the opportunity of routing it by the shorter and cheaper route to Portland? It is out of the question. Our only opportunity of competing for that trade and keeping it within 'Canadian lines is to have a better road. If we have a better road we can afford to run the trains faster, and we can afford to give cheaper rates. These are the things we are looking for, and these are the things we hope to accomplish by the building of this road. We are told, forsooth, that something which we thought would cost one dollar is going to cost three. Are we going to stop because of that? Is that the capacity of Canadianism, the capacity of the Government of this country? Because we find that a thing that is going to make a great commercial country of this Canada of ours will cost three dollars instead of one, are we going to stop there, throw up our hands, say we cannot do it, and allow this traffic to go through a foreign country? The statement that we should have only one road going into the province of Nova Scotia and into the province of New Brunswick is simply 146}
absurd. If it takes three great transcontinental railways ,to carry the present* traffic, how are we to get that traffic to the seaports of the Maritime provinces with one road, badly built, not in the proper place, with bad curves and bad grades? The Intercolonial was never made to pay properly; the fault must be somewhere, and when it cannot handle the present traffic, how can we hope that it will carry the traffic of the West, its grain and other great commodities, to the cities of Halifax, Sydney, North Sydney, Louisburg, and other cities that are waiting for that traffic? If three or .four railroads are necessary to carry the traffic across the continent to Montreal or Quebec, it is the greatest possible absurdity to suppose that one poor railroad is going to handle it from Quebec to St. John, Halifax or farther east, where we hope it will come when the greater development takes place. Traffic is something like a river that runs down from the glens and hillsides; it begins small, but as it flows towards the sea it gets bigger and bigger and only reaches its full volume when it enters the larger body of water. The same thing is true of traffic; it begins small, and as it goes on towards the great seaboards it gets bigger and bigger, and it requires better roads and better facilities to handle it. That being the case, if we hope to send to the ports of St. John, Halifax, Sydney, North Sydney, Louisburg and the other great ports of the Atlantic seaboard the great traffic which is being handled by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Canadian Northern railway, which is getting bigger as it comes east, we must provide sufficient facilities to handle it.
For that reason I submit that it is noanswer to the question to say that we are going to handle the whole trade by the Intercolonial. It cannot be done, and it was to overcome that difficulty that this project was launched and is being carried forward. For that reason it receives the support and sympathy, beyond question, of the Canadian people, and particularly of the people of the Maritime provinces. I watched with interest the speech of the hon. gentleman who preceded me, but he has not once said that he was opposed to the building of this road through New Brunswick and to the port of St. John. He simply said that he stood by the position which he took in 1903 and 1904 when this question was being discussed in the



House. We did not hear what that was, he may have been opposed to certain conditions, but I am not aware that he ever took the broad ground that he was altogether against the building of that road. What does the Prime Minister think of his Solicitor General, in view of the fact that the Prime Minister himself was in favour of the building of this road, not only from the West to Montreal and Quebec but into the Maritime provinces, and particularly to Halifax and St. John. He says he was in favour of its construction, and yet the Solicitor General, who was put forward the other night as the great champion of the Government, says that the whole thing is a pyramid of folly. He pays his leader, who was in favour of the building of this road, the great tribute of saying that his leader was supporting a pyramid of folly.
I would like to hear the Solicitor General or any other man, from the Maritime provinces or from this House, going to tell the people of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island that the building of this road, which is likely to give them the proper connections which they have looked for for years and which is going to bring to these great ports on the Atlantic the influx of trade and business that we have expected, that the stream of trade is to be cut short at the Quebec bridge or at Cochrane, and that we need not hope to receive in the future any of the great advantages which we have hoped for. We must yet enjoy these advantages, as neither this nor any other government would dare to go back on the promises made to the people in the past, and to dash the hopes raised by the building of this road. As I have said, it is no answer to say this is costing too much, if the money is properly spent, if we have value in the road, if the proper bridges are put in. Steel bridges are more expensive than wooden, but when they are built we have steel and not wooden bridges. Low grades are more expensive than higher grades, but when we have them we have the right kind of a road, a road that is going to pay and answer the purpose with which we started out. When the people have value for their money, they have nothing to complain of, and I am sure that they will not complain. We heard a good deal from our friends opposite a few years ago, during the last election particularly,	about	the	trade	of thiscountry	going	north and south

and not east and west. We were to keep our trade in our own lines, within our own borders; but what is the legitimate outcome of the theory that is now being put forward? If they degrade the road from Cochrane down to Quebec, smash it up so that it will be of no use, make its curves so sharp, its grades so bad and everything in connection with it of so low a standard that it will be incapable of carrying out the project we have in view, where will the traffic go? It is bound to go where the old Grand Trunk traffic always went, instead of going east and west to the extreme limits of Canada as it ought to go and we hoped it would go, it will be cut off at Cochrane or Quebec, and then this Tory theory and alleged Tory patriotism of bringing the traffic to the extreme end of Canada in the east will be of no more service, for we hear from our friends opposite that there is no intention and never was any intention of putting this road in commission beyond the Quebec bridge and that it is a pyramid of folly, as has been said by the Solicitor General who is, I suppose, voicing to some extent the ideas of the Government of which he is, if not a member, a very close ally. I wish to point out, as a Maritime province man, that the Intercolonial has never answered the purpose for which it is said to have been built. The Intercolonial railway is a part of the terms of Confederation. It was built for the purpose of creating traffic and trade between the Maritime provinces and Canada, as Canada was known at that time It was supposed that the Intercolonial railway would carry our fish, our agricultural products, and our coal to the markets of Montreal, Toronto and other western points. That was the purpose the Intercolonial railway was supposed to serve, but it was built in such a way, with such poor gradients, that that purpose was never accomplished, that trade was never created, and for that reason we were never satisfied that the terms of Confederation were fully carried out in that connection. Now, after a wait of forty-five years, we thought that this new road, would fulfil the conditions under which the provinces down by the sea had entered Confederation. But it appears that if hon. gentlemen opposite have their way that hope will also be blasted and we will not have our expectations in that regard fulfilled. At present there is no gTeat traffic from the west going further east than St. John and Halifax, but we are only at the commencement of the development of our

trade, we have not reached even ten or twenty per dent of the great development of this country. We have magnificent harbours on our Atlantic coast, such as Halifax, St. John, Sydney and Louislburg. Right in the island of Cape Breton we have six magnificent harbours. We expect that when.the full fruition of this undertaking is obtained, "when the traffic of the West is in full blast, these ports, the ancient port of Louisburg and the magnificent harbours of Sydney and North Sydney, will receive their share of this traffic. We have the right to expect that our magnificent fish and our other products such as iron and steel will go to the West on this road that will carry cheaper and better than any facilities we have had up to this time. That being the case we have always looked forward to the completion of this Toad up to the high standard which was set at the beginning and which I am sure will be carried forward to the end.
The Government and hon. gentlemen here representing the Government to-day may think that the appointment of this commission is a mere trifle, that they can appoint any kind of a commission they want and can put in their mouths any kind of a report. How is this commission appointed? It is not a haphazard affair, its appointment is based upon a statute of this country. Is it appointed by any one of the ministers? I do not think so. The commission is appointed as the representative of the Crown according to chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes of Canada:
The Governor in Council may, whenever he deems it expedient, cause inquiry to he made into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada, of the conduct of any part of the public business therof.
The Crown is called in. The Governor General appoints a commission but of course he has no responsibility. He takes the names of the men submitted to him and the responsibility rests directly on the Government. In 1912 that chapter was amended by the Government of to-day as can be seen by chapter 28 of the Acts of that year. I submit that the report that the commissioners sent here is absolutely illegal, absolutely improper, and absolutely in violation of the law put upon the statute books by this Government. ' The hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. S. Sharpe) specifically stated last night that there was a question of forgery in connection with this matter. It is very plainly hinted by the commissioners who committed that forgery. They hint that there was wrongdoing by some persons.
When they find that somebody is guilty of wrongdoing or suspected of wrongdoing, what are they called on to do? Chapter 28 of the Acts of 1912 says that if anything is discovered in the course of the inquiry which requires further investigation or which brings a charge home to somebody,
the commissioners may allow any person whose conduct is being investigated under this Act, and shall allow any person against whom any charge is made in the course of such investigation, to be represented by counsel.
Then follows the important part:
No report shall be made against any person until reasonable notice shall have been given to him of the charge of misconduct alleged against him and he shall have been allowed full opportunity to be heard in person or by counsel.
That is the law placed upon the statute books by the Government of to-day. The report before us simply bristles with charges of this kind, charges of theft, of squandering and fraud of every kind. Who could listen to the speech of the hon. gentleman from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) to-night and not believe that hundreds of cases of wrongdoing had been discovered by this commission. The very chapter under which these commissioners were acting says that if charges were discovered the persons charged must be brought before the tribunal to answer the charges. The chapter says further:
No report shall be made against anybody until the law is complied with fully.
I submit that this commission did not follow the terms of the Act under which they were appointed, and that they have made slanderous reports and charges against citizens of this country without giving 'them any opportunity of answering the charges made against them. I spoke of Mr. Cahan a moment ago. He describes himself as a Tory of the Tories, a strong follower of the leader of the Government and an associate of his in politics. He surely would not raise the hand of rebellion against the Government unless he had the strongest provocation. He evidently knew of this statute and of the power under which the commissioners were acting. Speaking in the city of Montreal a few days ago in regard to this matter, he said that the whole thing was ridiculous and absurd, that it was no better than an ex-parte trial before a magistrate. That is the kind of investigation upon which thousands of reputations are to be blasted in this country. That is the kind of report which the Government is spreading broadcast throughout the country.
