Mr. Speaker, at this stage of the debate one would almost need to apologize for offering any further remarks in regard to the matter which has now been under discussion for one full week in this Chamber. I promise that my remarks shall be rather general than detailed, and that I shall present to the House my own view of the findings of the commission, formed after a very careful perusal of the report and of the exhibits and the evidence which accompany it. I shall do this in as fair and impartial a manner as I can.
I, for one, do not think that the Government made any mistake in appointing a Royal Commission to investigate the affairs of the National Transcontinental railway; nor do I think they made any mistake in giving to that commission the wide powers they gave it; I suppose it was appointed under chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Opinions in Canada since 1903 or 1904 have conflicted a good deal in regard to various matters concerning the construction of the National Transcontinental railway. Charges and counter charges were made in the House, in the press and throughout the country, particularly on the occasion of two heated general elections in Canada, one in 1904 and one in 1908. I do not think that in the general election of 1911 the question of the National Transcontinental railway played much of a part. When the present Administration took office they made, no error in deciding that a Royal Commission should be ap-

pointed to investigate the affairs of the National Transcontinental railway. The initial mistake, the overmastering blunder which the Government did make was in its selection of thepersonnelofthatcommission. Had two or three individuals been selected in whose ability and non-partisanship the people of Canada had confidence, I doubt whether any discussion would have taken place in this House in regard to this report -at all events, there would have been little discussion. I do not believe that the Government or the Minister of Railways could have selected two men in whom the bulk of the people of Canada would have had less confidence in the matter of presenting an independent non-partisan report on the National Transcontinental railway. It was for the Government to choose the commissioners and in making the choice it did of Mr. George Lynch-Staunton, K.C., and of Mr. Gutelius, they made their initial blunder-a blunder that has shown itself in all the proceedings of that Commission down to the day the report was presented. The report is not the outcome of a judicial, independent, and non-partisan inquiry-exactly the reverse. I know Mr! Lynch-Staunton very well and esteem him very highly. I have met him in many cases and recognize his legal ability. I know that for the last six or seven years the Ontario Government has been his chief client. He has appeared on behalf of the Ontario Government before committees of this House time and again. He is a partisan from the beginning. As a campaigner at general elections, he is one of the most active men in the province of Ontario, never an election passes but Mr. Lynch-Staunton is to the fore in Western Ontario, in every little village where a number of Roman Catholic families happen to be gathered together you will find Mr. George Lynch-Staunton as a speaker.
Oh, oh.

That statement I know
to be correct not only with regard to the riding which I have the honour to represent, but as regards the riding of my hon. friend from North Wellington (Mr. W. A. Clarke) and other ridings in western Ontario. Mr. Staunton took an active part in the election of 1904 when the transcontinental proposal was probably the chief question before the electors. It was during that campaign that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister announced that it was better to have a government-owned railway than a railway owned government, and I remember a very
fine portrait of my right hon. friend with that quotation underneath. As I said, Mr. Staunton took an active part in that election and I have no doubt followed his leader in every respect. In the election of 1908 the Transcontinental was again the main issue though not the only one, and once more Mr. Staunton was one of the chief speakers of the Conservative party throughout western Ontario.

Would my hon. friend allow me to ask a question? Does he consider that because he is a Liberal that fact disqualifies him from giving now, or at any other time, a judicial and impartial opinion on this question?

No, I do not think it
does, for the reason that I am going to discuss the case solely upon the material which has been brought down by the commissioners. At the present time I am discussing the personnel of the commission. Following the election of 1908 there was not a great deal of discussion of this particular question. We drifted into trade and other matters until the change of Government in September, 1911. Very shortly after that, this Royal Commission was appointed. Mr. George Lynch-Staunton, fresh from the stump, with his preconceived ideas about the Transcontinental which he had heartily condemned, was appointed chairman of the commission to investigate the construction of that road. I submit that he was not a fit and proper man to place in that position. If he spoke what he believed in 1904 and 1908-1 am sure he did-he never believed in the National Transcontinental railway and he never believed that the eastern branch should be built. He was a prejudiced, biased commissioner from the first. I know little or nothing regarding Mr. Gutelius except what I have heard in the course of the debate, but I submit from what has transpired in the debate that we are bound to conclude that Mr. Gutelius was as greatly disqualified as was Mr. Staunton to act upon that commission, considering his preconceived notions and his record as a railroad man. There are some facts which are not controverted: he was an American railroad engineer; after coming to this country he was on the engineering staff of the Canadian Pacific railway for a number of years; later, he was made divisional superintendent somewhere in New Ontario, at North Bay, I think. There he came in contact with the Minister of Railways and Canals, and I have no doubt

that was their first meeting. He was taken under the wing of the Minister of Railways and Canals in regard to local politics in the province of Ontario. He was afterwards employed by the Minister of Railways, then a member of the Ontario Government, in connection with the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway. When the Hon. Frank Cochrane became Minister of Railways and Canals in this House he brought Mr. Gutelius along with him, intending to keep with him a man who had been so useful to him in the past and was likely to be as useful again in the future. Mr. Gutelius at present is filling a position worth, I believe, $20,000 a year. This prize has been dangling before his eyes for a long time, and at last he has landed it. A man occupying the position that Mr. Gutelius did should hardly have been appointed to a commission which was to investigate the Transcontinental, unless he was absolutely free from the influence of any minister of the Crown, and of all political parties.-I do not take very much exception to the fees which were paid to Messrs. Gutelius and George Lynch-Staunton. If the work was done I do not know that they were overpaid, although I am one of those who believe that the result of their work is practically useless as an independent report of what has transpired with regard to the road. When that commission was appointed, I fancy the Minister of Railways and Canals knew his men pretty well. There are many eminent judges in Canada who might have acted on that commission, there are eminent engineers who might have been chosen on that commission, unbiased and free from partisanship of any kind. There are eminent engineers, eminent lawyers, eminent judges in other countries, in the United States for instance, where conditions are very much the same, who might have been employed. Independent, practical, thorough men could have been found by the Government without difficulty had the Government desired to find them. The Government made the initial blunder of appointing two men who were of the most partisan character, one counsel of the Ontario Government, and who for the last eight or ten years had condemned this railway and its construction; and the other a man who had an office of $20,000 a year dangling before him all the time under the Minister of Railways and Canals.
Under these circumstances, could you expect an independent, unbiased report? 
I submit you could not, and I submit to my right hon. friend that if, upon any non-political question, he was called on to appoint a commission to arrive at fair and just conclusions, he would not select the men who were selected in regard to the National Transcontinental railway.	Had
he selected his commissioners	from
amongst the judges of Canada, we on this side would have had nothing to complain of. Had he acted as the former Government did-and	I have heard that
criticised during the course of this debate -there would have been no cause of complaint. When a report was brought up in regard to the Civil Service by Mr. Courtenay and two others, and there was a clause referring to some fraudulent dealing by some branch of the Civil Service, what did the late Government do? They appointed Mr. Justice Cassels, judge of the Exchequer Court, to examine into the question. As soon as he was named I think all parties were satisfied that it would be a full, fair and impartial investigation. Why did the Minister of Railways and Canals not pursue such a course in the present instance? I cannot tell, v I believe he knew or could assume what kind of a report he was going to get before his commissioners actually took office.
Now, there is a significant fact at the very beginning of the report which one must Tefer to. It is well known that the powers of the commissioners were very broad, and, as I submit, if the road is to be completed at the end of the present year, they should not have put in their report until it was completed, and this report should merely have been an interim report. While the powers of the commission were very broad, they have, themselves, limited the scope of their operations to the 1st October, 1911. In other words, all that they sought to investigate were the doings of the other fellows. What did the Liberal Government do in regard to the Transcontinental railway when they were in power? Under the Order in Council appointing them their duties were fuller than that, and they should still have been on the inquiry and remained on the inquiry until the end of the present year, when it is said the road will be completed. Who gave them instructions to stop at the end of the regime of the late Liberal Administration? It does not appear from the report. Did they take that upon themselves? I fancy they did;

that they thought they would look after what the Liberals had done and avoid what the succeeding Government has done without taking the advice of anybody on the subject at all, and without receiving any instructions. That thought came to them as the natural way of treating the affair. That showed the bias of their minds, and it is for that reason that I am pointing it out, and for that reason alone. The first clause in the report of the commissioners states that they only examined the work up to the first of October, 1911. What work did they examine? The surveys and preliminary work having been done, tenders were advertised for, but they were not advertised for until 1907. The first contracts were not let until 1907. The late Liberal Government was in power during the construction of that work during 1907, 1908, 1909, 1910 and a little over half of 1911. For the last two and a half years the work has been entirely in the hands of the commission appointed by the present Administration-four years or four and a half years under one Government and two and a half years under the other Government. Why, then, should not this commission have completed its work; why should it not have continued to tne end of the present year and shown us what had been done by the Conservative Government, or by the commission appointed by the Conservative Government, after the first of October, 1911? They did not do so, however. They had no directions, as far as I know not to do so. I am not concerned so much with that as I am with the fact that acting upon their own motion, following the prejudice and bent of their own minds, they were only concerned with the other fellows, in order to find out if they could show anything in regard to them, and they were not concerned with the commission appointed by the present Government.
There are certain minor features in regard to the report which I propose to deal with, and deal with rather briefly, because the commissioners in their report have rather epitomized their views in the first few pages. In the first instance, they say that the late commissioners of the Transcontinental railway, who were appointed by the late Government, caused a loss of $8,800,000 in connection with the letting of contracts. The commissioners state that had there been no sub-letting of contracts that money would have been saved to the people of Canada. I ask any one in this House to go over that report as carefully as I have and find the facts and the evidence to support that finding. You can add up all the various amounts that they say represent undue and unnecessary profit and they make only between $6,000,000 and $6,500,000. But then, what they state to be inordinate profits and improper allowances only form what may be called a matter of opinion at the best. The commission finds that a great mistake was made in letting these contracts in too large bulk. Let us see how that figures out. We have covering 1,800 miles, twenty -one contracts, or an average of 851 miles per contract. What they suggest is that contracts should have been let in blocks of fifty miles, and they say that if that course had been followed a great deal of money would have been saved. Would business men recognize the statement made by the commissioners as something they should act upon? Very often the cheapest way of letting a contract is en bloc, and then allowing the contractor to sub-let. That is the way in which a man will let a contract for his own store, offices, or house. There has to be some man of financial strength at the back of a large portion of the undertaking. If you let a contract in small blocks, you get a lot of small men in who have not the necessary financial strength; they at once go to the bank with the contract and ask the bank to finance them, and generally land in trouble before their contract is completed. What difference would there have been between letting these contracts at 85| miles on an average, as they were let, and letting them at 50 miles as the commissioners think they should have been let? Not a fraction of a dollar would have been lost or saved to the people of Canada by adopting either method. The usual rule, whether in the building of one's own house, of a canal, of a railway, or of any great public work is that the contract goes to one contractor who sublets it to the various trades. The most homely illustration is the case of your own house. You let a contract for $5,000, to build your house, and immediately the stone and brickwork is sub-let to one man, the woodwork to another, the painting and glazing to another, the plumbing and wiring to another man, and so on all the way down. The principle is that each of these sub-contractors will make a profit, and that the main contractor will make a profit also. That is what the late commissioners did in regard to the Transcontinental railway, and that is precisely what the present Government is doing in regard

to the Welland canal and the Hudson Bayrailway. It is also what the present Government will do in regard to the construction of the new departmental buildings. Sub-contractors, I believe, have already taken their sub-contracts in regard to the Welland canal. Was ever a railway, even a small one, built in Canada by a single contractor? I had to do with the building of a railway only sixteen miles long, which now forms a portion of the Canadian Pacific railway, and the contract was let to the firm of Booth and Company, well known contractors at that time, but three or four sub-contractors went in under Booth and Company, and then a second range of subcontractors were taken in to build that road. How would we have saved any money had we shortened -the blocks of the Transcontinental railway to 50 miles and let each block to an independent contractor? Would not that contractor have had his profit? Certainly he would; he would have sublet his contract and the men who had the subcontracts would also have had their profits. There would be those two profits and there might be middlemen mixed up in the transaction, because every ntan who enters into a contract does so with the intention of making a profit out of it.
1 have gone carefully over the twenty-one contracts let on the National Transcontinental railway; I have read the
4 p.m. evidence in regard to them; and I have seen the commissioners' statement. There is practically no evidence with respect to the letting of these contracts which would justify the bald statement of the commissioners that, if some other plan had been adopted, $8,800,000 would have been saved to the people of this country. Any one with any business judgment or common sense, who examines that statement, will see that the commissioners have only made an estimate of the saving. The commissioners take the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific and say that they took the contract and sublet it on the understanding that they were to receive 5 per cent profit. Then the commissioners say that the subcontractors let the work at a lower figure than that at which the Grand Trunk Pacific had received the contract and etill made a profit of from 20 to 25 per cent, and that consequently the country lost that money. Is not one of the very best tests of the genuineness of the tenders and of the contracts to be found in the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific were by far the largest tenderers? They tendered successfully on
[Mr. Guthrie.2
contracts Nos. 1, 3, 4, II and 14 at a total of $9,333,000, and sublet them all. They tried to force an assignment of contracts Nos. 16 and 17, which were two of the largest, on a basis of 10 per cent over and above actual cost, but they did not get tho?'>
contracts. They tendered altogether on 17 out of the 21 contracts advertised, and their tenders amounted in all to $38,436,789. Why did they do it? The reason that would suggest itself to the mind of any sensible man is that they desired to protect themselves, by seeing that the work was not being let at too high a figure. They had been building railroads in old Canada, and iD new Canada and they knew what railroads cost. They tendered on all the big contracts, first to protect themselves, and secondly, to ensure that there would be no extravagance and no wrong doing. All these contracts which the Grand Trunk Pacific obtained were sublet on a five per cent basis of profit to them, and the subcontractors made whatever profit they could on the prices at which they received the subcontracts. With these facts before us- can it be said that there is anything fair and just in the finding of the commission that on these twenty-one contracts, had different methods been purused, $8,800,000 would have been saved to the people? I believe that any judge reading this report, would say without hesitation, that there is not a jot or tittle of evidence to support the finding of the commissioners. The most one can say in regard to the finding is that it is guess work; it might have been or it might not have been.
What we on this side of the House say is, that the tenders were properly advertised; the contracts properly let, the profits, be they great or be they small, properly earned, and just as they would be earned in any other business organization entirely outside of the Transcontinental Commission. We say also that the Hudson Bay railroad will be built in precisely the same manner by this Conservative Government. The largest contractor on the National Transcontinental railway is the same Mr. J. D. McArthur who has obtained three very large contracts on the Hudson Bay railway, and has already sublet portions of them. He is not bound down in any way in regard to subletting on the Hudson Bay railway; he can sublet every yard of his contract, and on such terms as he sees fit. And the Minister of Railways and the Government have agreed to that, with full knowledge of what Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton have reported on that system in the case of the Transcontinental railway.

Why, the Government, as stated -by the hon. member for Soutih Renfrew, will not itself follow the advice of the commission. Summarized in one or two pages of this report is a plain argument that you should let your line in small blocks and thus avoid subletting. Have you done it? No, this Government has rejected that advice. They have let the whole thing, practically to one man who, I am informed, has immediately sublet the whole thing, and sublet at a profit to himself and to his subcontractors. How much will the people of Canada lose on that transaction if the standard set up by the Investigating Commission on the Transcontinental is to be accepted? Why, of course, it is not to be accepted. The Government has taken the correct way of doing business, it has gone about the matter of the Hudson Bay railway construction in a businesslike-way. And so with the Welland canal which, while short of mileage, is estimated to cost $50,000,000. Will the Government follow the advice of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton in carrying out that work? Indeed, they will not. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) says that the average contract on the Welland canal is $5,000,000, and the minister will not subdivide it. He says he wants men of responsibility, men of financial ability, men who are able to invest 'half a million or a million in a plant. These are the men he wants to deal with, and they can sublet to their heart's content if only they build according to contract and specifications. Has the Government done wrong in that transaction? Messrs. Staunton and Gutelius would say they have. Do the Government think that the report of Messrs. Staunton and Gutelius is a businesslike report in that respect? They do not or they would have followed it. As a matter of fact they have completely disregarded it in the case of the Hudson Bay railway and in the case of the Welland canal. And so, Mr. Speaker, this ridiculous point involving $8,000,000 or $9,000,000-forms a big item in this total of $40,000,000 which they say was extravagantly spent. What utter rubbish.
I will not deal at length with the $4,500,000 which these commissioners allege to have been improperly expended in the shops at Transcona. I noticed that in speaking of it the hon, member for South Renfrew puts it at $6,000,000, but the amount given in the report is $4,500,000.
They omitted the Quebec shops, intentionally, because their friends are building them.

I wish to point out to
the right hon. Prime Minister that this is another instance in which Mr. Lynch-Staunton has shown his bitter partisanship. He must have known that he was bound to follow the rulings of the engineers and the Department of Railways and Canals, as well as the rulings of the Department of Justice, which rulings were to the effect that these Transcona shops formed part and parcel of the construction of the road and should not be set down as part of the operating cost. This was brought to the attention of Mr. Lynch-Staunton time and time again. The law clerk of the commission, Mr. Atkinson, Mr. Newcombe, Sir Allen Aylesworth, the present Minister of Justice, all agreed on this point. And in the face of that Mr. Lynch-Staunton still has the audacity-on his own opinion and after noting the contrary opinions-to find that in this total of $40,000,000 the sum of $4,500,000 on account of the Transcona shops must be included. What was this man doing? What member of this House would do such a thing? What other commissioner would say so? In spite of the plain language of all these opinions and rulings, Mr. Staunton says: I give my opinion and I will put that $4,500,000 down as unwarranted expenditure. Surely, that shows the animus of Mr. Lynch-Staunton in this matter. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) in speaking on this subject, said that it showed the bona fides of Mr. Staunton that he had given in his report the opinions of other people and had given reasons for his own. In my humble judgment his bona fides would have been much better established if he had said:	In deference
to the opinion of the Justice Department, I will omit to place that $4,500,000 spent on the Transcona -shops among the items of wasteful expenditure. Let the Prime Minister take cognizance of another fact with regard to Mr. Lynch-Staunton-and I only mention this to show his animus, to show his frame of mind, to show that he was determined to come to a conclusion against the late Transcontinental Commission. In 1912 the question of the Transcona shops was being discussed by Major Leonard, the commissioner. It was urged that the shops were too large, that the railway would not require such shops for the next quarter or half century, and that too much money altogether was being expended, so that a large part of that expenditure was mere waste. They sent for an expert to the United States, Mr. Hodgins, of New York, a man thoroughly acquainted with



the requirements of railways and the construction of shops to be used in connection with them. No Liberal Oovernment had anything to do with the choice of Mr. Hodgins, no Transcontinental commissioner ever appointed by a Liberal Government had anything to do with it. The present commission sent for Mr. Hodgins and got his opinion with regard to these shops at Transcona. His opinion is on ' Hansard,' and I am not going to read it again. The Prime Minister heard the hon. member for South Renfrew read it, or I suppose he will do this side of the House the justice to read it himself. He will see that Mr. Hodgins complimented the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners in every way possible with regard to the construction of these shops. He said they were not too large for the trade present and expected on the road; he said they had been economically, constructed; he said their floor space was better used and their machinery more modern than almost any other car-ishops in the world. Yet, in the face of the report of this expert, Mr. Lynch-Staunton finds that $4,500,000 for these shops is unwarrantable expenditure. Another point I make is that he suppressed that report of Mr. Hodgins in his report as, commissioner. It should have been mentioned, or, at the very least, it should have been referred to. This all goes to show that Mr. Lynch-Staunton and Mr. Gutelius were not there to act fairly and squarely, but were prejudiced and biased in the extreme. It shows that they were men who under the circumstances were not able to bring in an entirely independent report. Their prejudice had become a ruling passion.
Then, there is the big question of momentum grades. I have not a great deal to say on that .subject. There is a tremendous sum charged as having been unwarrantably expended by the Transcontinental Commission on momentum grades. Well, what is the history of that matter? This was to be a railway of a very high standard, of the highest standard of railway across the continent. The conditions under which it was to be built, the standard to be employed throughout, was a matter of agreement between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific, who were to be the' lessees of the road for a period of fifty years, and to pay three per cent as rental upon the whole cost after the first seven years for which they used the road. It was directly to the advantage of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to

see that not one dollar was unnecessarily expended in the construction of that road. Their own engineer was on the work the whole time. If he could not agree with the commissioners' engineer upon any point, the matter had to be settled by arbitration. If the two engineers, one for the Grand Trunk Pacific and one for the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners, could not agree as to who should be appointed third arbitrator, the Chief Justice of Canada was to perform that duty for them. What could be fairer than that? They knew what they wanted; they wanted a road of a higher standard than any that crossed North America, and they were prepared to pay three per cent on what it was to cost. Nothing was said about momentum grades until very recently; in fact the first question in that regard arose during the time that Mr. Lumsden was chief engineer. Mr. Lumsden himself was not in favour of momentum grades. In his evidence, he says that he has not had much experience with them, but he does not .say that they would add anything to the usefulness of the railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was not in favour of momentum grades; they refused by letter to permit the commission to put momentum grades on the road between Winnipeg and Moncton. That letter, which was read in the House last night, and appears in yesterday's ' Hansard,' was written by Mr. Woods, assistant engineer of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, who was on the work, to Mr. Lumsden. His language was quite defiant. He said:	We object to your putting in
momentum grades; it is not part of our bargain. We want the actual grade of four-tenths against eastbound traffic, and six degree curves-no greater grades and no greater curves. That surely is sufficient notice to the Government and to the Transcontinental Commission as to what the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company want, and as to what the commissioners could do and could not do. Nothing more was heard of momentum grades until Mr. Lumsden's retirement in 1909, I think it was, and Mr. Gordon Grant's appointment to the position of chief engineer. It is true that in a letter written by Mr. Gordon Grant the assertion is made that in certain places momentum grades might be used, and the commissioners have stated in their report that according to Mr. Grant's evidence the use of momentum grades was quite proper.

Hon. gentlemen can look over Mr. Grant's evidence from beginning to end without finding a single statement on the subject of momentum grades. To Mr. Grant's letter recommending their use, the company replied that they would not have them. Time has gone on; the commission has changed. Major Leonard, appointed by the present Government, is now sole commissioner. He seems to be a stickler for momentum grades, but he should bear in mind the letter which he received in July, 1912, from E. J. Chamberlin, president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, stating that the company would not permit the use of momentum grades. The last clause of that letter is as follows:
I beg to say if this work is done in accordance with what I understand to be your recent instructions it will not be in compliance with the agreement or satisfactory to this company, and cannot be accepted.
Surely that is positive language. But what has been done? Hon. gentlemen, in defiance of the warning of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, have proceeded to put in from thirty to thirty-five momentum	grades-for what purpose I know not, unless it be to give the Grand Trunk company an opportunity to get out of their contract to operate the road under a fifty-year lease. If they make that salutary change; if they degrade the road, and put in something which has not been agreed upon by both sides, when the road is completed and they ask the Grand Trunk Railway Company to execute the lease for fifty years, the company can say: you have not kept your agreement; you have not lived up to your contract. We warned you and your engineers and your proper officers, and you did this in defiance of our warning. The same is the case too, I am informed, with respect to steel bridges-The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is entitled to a first-class road. It does not want wooden trestles, it wants steel structures; it is willing to pay for them, and it is agreed with the Government that they shall be installed. Yet these commissioners assume to find that the late commission did wrong in living up to its agreement and in erecting steel structures on the railway. They state that in their opinion the Government might have saved $6,200,000 if they had adopted momentum grades, which the Grant Trunk Pacific railway say they will not accept. That letter of Mr. Chamberlin's was, no 1471	...
doubt, before the commissioners; why did they suppress it? Why did they not put tt in their report? They may offer the excuse that the report covered a period which ended in October, 1911, and that the letter is dated June 12, 1912, but I notice that in many of their calculations of payments the figures are given to December 31, 1912. There is a good deal of dispute about the question of momentum grades, and it would appear to me to be a controverted question. I heard a New York railway man say that his company were spending $20,000,000 this year to establish actual grades and cut out curves. I know that certain western roads in the United States are doing the same thing; I believe the Canadian Pacific and Grand Trunk railways are doing the same thing-the Grand Trunk did it at Guelph, anyway. I believe that the best railway practice to-day is to get rid of wooden structures and momentum grades as rapidly as possible, and to put in actual grades and steel structures. That is evidently what the Grand Trunk Pacific Company want, and that is evidently all the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are going to take when the road is completed. How do the commissioners make up the amount of $6,200,000 which it is alleged we would have saved if these grades had been put in? Their estimate is the wildest kind of a guess; they have arrived at the amount by taking 10 per cent off $62,000,000 worth of fill and excavation. They have no reason for taking ten per cent off that amount; none of their engineers show any reason for doing so, and one engineer, Mr. Berry, of Chicago, whose remarks were quoted by the hon. member for South Renfrew7, says it is a wrong practice .to go upon. That is an indication of the material of which this report is made up.
I shall not take up the time of the House by going into many other questions, but I am going into the matter of the classification of the work. It is alleged that a large amount has been overpaid by reason of over-classification and in connection with overbreak.
The commissioners say:
The amount charged for excavation of solid rock or assembled rock which is described as ' fragments or rock cemented together by interstitial material ' was improperly introduced after the contracts were signed, and though $1,835,051 was paid for 'assembled rock,' there is no material on the line which can possibly be marshalled under that head.
It was paid before Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton signed the report.

I am aware of that, because the report was not signed until last February. I believe myself that the finding of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton was wrong, and that they made a pure guess at the amount, and that is apparently what they did on nearly every point of their investigation. I do not believe for a minute that McArthur got anything more than fair treatment. What reliance can we put on this report when the Government say: We will knock 75 per cent off Gutelius and Staunton's estimate, and deduct only the other 25 per cent; whereas our commissioners found a payment of $640,000 unwarranted, we will cut that down to $150,000. Personally I think that was a fair settlement. But what does the Government think of the report?
I cannot go through all the items as I have taken up too much time, already. There is absolutely no foundation for the findings in this report. They are repudiated by the men who, we hope, are going to take this road over. What about their statement as to the $6,200,000 for momentum grades and the $8,800,000 because we let the work out in big contracts, unreasonably large sections? It is the purest kind of buncombe when you come to read it. Then in regard to overbreak; competent men say that you cannot properly examine that, after a lapse of a year or two, and certainly the commissioners could not examine iton contract 21 in the neighbourhood of Winnipeg where the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) lives, and knows what is going on. The Government would not take the Gutelius-Staunton report on that, and indeed it is uncertain on what points they will endorse it, probably on none.
I blame the Government not because they appointed a commission, but because they appointed such commissioners. If they had appointed independent men who were not biased politically they would have done a service to the country, and such commissioners would have found that the road had been well and economically constructed and at the highest standard of any transcontinental railway in America. We have heard about Mr. Fielding's estimate of $61,000,000 and how before the election of 1908 the road had cost $112,000,000, the estimate being almost doubled in four years. But the cost of labour and material had gone up and we were building a better and more expensive road than was perhaps originally anticipated. Under the late commission appointed by the Liberal Government the road was kept up to standard, and there was no attempt to degrade it or to substitute wooden trestles foT steel bridges. We tried to carry out the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific to the letter and if the company should repudiate the contract it will be the fault of Major Leonard, of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton, and of the Government which backs them.

We did rather understand that each one would look more particularly after individual sections: for instance,
I was on ' D ' and ' E.' . . .
Q. Were you present at La Tuque at the time the contractors and Mr. Lumsden were there? -A. No. I never was on the work with Mr. Lumsden.
Q. Was Mr. Lumsden in the employ of the commission while you were there?-A. No. Mr. Grant had been chief engineer for some time before I came on.
On page 615, to show the thorough grasp Mr. Calvert had of the duties of the commissioners, I read:
Q. What is the difference between actual and virtual grades on a railroad?-A. I do not know that X can just answer that properly.
Q. Did you ever hear that matter discussed? -A. No, not if you put it that way. In fact,
I may say I was not very conversant with momentum roads until this question came up.
Q. Do you know anything about curvature in railroads? Did you ever hear it discussed at the time you were on the board?-A. Oh, well, sometimes, I suppose, the question was discussed, but not very much at board meetings.

Q. You never became very familiar with it?
__A. I would not like to say so.
Q. You could not form any judgment as to curvature?-A. X would not like to give an opinion on a thing like that.
There is a letter here that will go to show what Mr. Calvert thought primarily was his business. It is signed by Mr. Mattice, the district engineer, and reads as follows:
Mr. Calvert is asking that no appointments be* made to the staif in future without his consent, and these instructions must, be carried out, except in so far as cooks and building gangs are concerned.
Even the district engineer thought that Mr. Calvert's knowledge was so restricted as to the requirements of a railway that he was not even to have the recommending and selection of a cook.
With such a commission as a starting point; Mr. Parent, a discredited and discarded politician of Quebec, according to the reports of his own friends, Mr. Mclsaac, a decent, honest, inoffensive citizen, who had never been in the capacity of commissioner before, and Mr. Calvert, who frankly admits his utter inability to cope with the situation, what a playground it was for the Minister of Railways and Canals and the contractor? who loomed up in the gloaming to go after the public treasury! When the Liberal party went out of power, their nightmare was: what will turn up in regard to this railway and all that has been done in the past, and the Liberal press took up the cry. From the outset it was announced: Here was a wonderful railway, and, even if it had cost a great deal of money, it was a first-class railway no matter what it had cost. But the public were becoming a little dubious about that, knowing that even a good thing can cost too much. These gentlemen had to try to square themselves by showing that this was a judiciously built road. So, the hon. member for South Renfrew was to be immortalized, and the proper medium for his immortalizing was found, of course, in the Toronto Globe. They gave him some special advertising, with a view to helping these gentlemen out. It so happened that in the year 1912, Mr. Charles M. Hays died and a vacancy was created in the presidency and general managership of the Grand Trunk railway. Mr. Smithers, the vice-president, was coming on to Canada, and it was announced in the Toronto Globe in its issue of the 15th of May, 1912, in effect:	Hon. George
P. Graham has been asked to accept the position of president and general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It
said this is a striking tribute to his ability and worth, to his practical knowledge, his powers of initiation and his thorough understanding of the railway problem in Canada. These were given as the reasons the Grand Trunk management sought his businesslike administration. I do not think that surprised Mr. Graham, and if the truth were known, probably it would be found that he was in Toronto on the day when that report was given circulation. But, as with a good many other reports, that was the end of it. However, it served its purpose; it went from one end of the country to the other that Mr. Graham had been offered the presidency and general managership of the Grand Trunk railway, and this gave him a good advertisement before the people. Mr. Smithers arrived on the 24th of May, and the $50,000 per . annum salary of the position which they said had been dangled before Mr. Graham faded away, 'and Mr. Graham, naturally did not get the position, I merely mention that to show that these gentlemen had been anticipating the troubles that were to beset them, and so this cheap advertising in the Globe was given the hon. gentleman.
As to this letting of contracts in large sections I wish to make one point here. There is a vast difference in the letting of these contracts and the letting of an ordinary contract for a public building. Suppose that tenders are called for a public building and one is accepted at $25,000; you have there the total amount involved. But the tenders on this Transcontinental were of a more far-reaching character. As an example, take the tender of McArthur Brothers on section 1. That tender was for about $13,000,000, but when it was moneyed out, they received $20,000,000. The reason is that the work was done by schedule, and the work being so done, it was to the advantage of the contractor to do as much work under his contract as possible. We can understand how, under such contracts, immense sums were obtained by these men in addition to what is was originally intended should be paid to them.
A great deal has been said about the question of the 'additional deposit which might be called for. I shall not deal with that at length, for to do so would be to trespass on the good nature of the House. But I wish to endorse everything that has been said which went to show that this system was in the interest of the big contractors and of these alone. The contractors

knew, and so did the board when a tender put in at $13,000,000 might ultimately money out at $20,000,000, both contractors and board knew that all tenders were of a very large order. So we find the very unfair proposition laid down that the tenderer should first put up a certain sum as a deposit, and then be subject to the will of the board to increase that amount. This prevented many men from putting in tenders. There was this further: under the terms, the successful tenderer, if not able to comply with the increased demand made upon him, stood the chance of losing what he had put up in the first place, Mr. Mclsaac placed himself on record as objecting to that condition. There was another gentleman who objected to it, and the treatment of his objection showed the futility of entrusting men with power which they were not able to use. At page 603 of the evidence contained in this report, we find that the Finance Minister of that day protested to the board against this condition regarding a further deposit. The letters of Mr. Fielding and the evidence of Mr. Mclsaac are set forth in the report What superhuman power, if we may so term it, intervened to balk the wishes of the Minister of Finance, the man who above all others is charged with the custody of the public money? But, in any case, the result of his being overruled was that those who wished to tender were subject to these onerous terms.	.
I wish to deal for a few moments with some of the gentlemen who tendered. Mr. M. P. Davis tendered for a number of these contracts, and it is needless to say that he secured a large proportion of them. The Quebec bridge, which was referred to last night, netted him a quarter of a million dollars. He had had the Cornwall canal of unhappy memory, from which, it is said, he made so much money that he himself could not estimate it. Then he had that priceless gem, the water-powers on the Soulanges canal, granted him when the present leader of the Opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was Prime Minister and acting Minister of Railways and Canals, and granted by him in defiance of the report of the chief engineer -_>f that branch. What was the Soulanges canal deal? In 1902 Mr. Davis made application for powers on what is known as the Cedars section of the Soulanges canal. He asked for a twenty-one year lease, at a Tental- no, I will deal with the rental in a moment. In due course the matter was referred to fMr. W. H. Bennett.]
Mr.' Thomas Munro, engineer of that system of canals. Mr. Munro reported on the 18th of February, in the course of which he said:
If trade is to grow it will be advisable to adopt means of electrical traction to facilitate the passage of laden barges. The whole question is of much importance, so much so that it should have the fullest investigation before any action is taken, at least, such is my humble opinion.
That report of Mr. Thomas Munro was before the right hon. gentleman, who in the absence of Mr. Blair was acting Minister of Railways and Canals. On that report an Order in Council was passed in the month of April giving Mr. Davis, for the paltry sum of $3,000, that enormous water-power for sixty-three years from that date, for the term of the lease was twenty-one years with two renewals of twenty-one years each. I have heard eminent contractors and engineers say that the rights given to Mr. Davis were worth not a paltry $3,000 a year, but over $250,000 a year. Is it to be wondered that Mr. Davis was right in the foreground, and that he was able to deal with this Government on very advantageous terms?
Let us examine these twenty-one tenders. Nine contracts embraced half the line, and for these there were only five tenderers. These were secured by Davis, O'Brien and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and the return made to Mr. Davis on the section which he sub-let-let it be remembered that Mr. Davis did none of this work himself, as the contracts were handed over to others-amounted to the neat sum of $3,500,000. It is a striking, fact that when Mr. McArthur tendered on contract No. 1, he was forced by the board to deposit with the department over $1,000,000, but when Mr. M. P. Davis tendered they asked him for a small payment only, and did not request a second payment at all. The right hon. leader of the Opposition may be in a position to explain how Mr. McArthur was compelled to deposit more than $1,000,000, while Mr. M. P. Davis got off scott free. Another firm, Hogan and Macdonell, who did not seem to be on friendly terms with the commissioners, were compelled to deposit $794,000 when their tender was accepted. If a man could get hold of Mr. M. P. Davis and in solemn and quiet stillness, ask him what he thought of the whole thing,
I should think that he would say, like Warren Hastings of old, * that he was amazed at his forbearance when he considered his opportunities.'

Let us now take contracts 16 and 17, with which Mr. M. P. Davis was most concerned. It is well for the House to bear in mind the dates which I am about to give. The contracts were let on October 29, 1908. The work on contract 16 was to be completed by December 3, 1910, and the work on No. 17 by March 11, 1911. In September, 1909, they had not commenced work on these sections, and on September 16 Mr. Davis assigned the contracts and cleared up $740,000. What was happening in the meantime? Mr. Hays had written a letter to the commissioners on October 8, 1909, protesting against the contract being allowed to stand any longer, and asking, in view of the fact that nothing had been done, that new tenders be called for. There is no doubt that Mr. Hays felt very strongly on this question, and that he had his own opinion of the board. He knew that the man in authority was Mr. Parent, and as he and that gentleman evidently were not on good terms-my own opinion is that Mr. Parent would be more or less closely linked up with M. P. Davis, considering what Mr. Parent's reputation has been in the past- Mr, Hays addressed no less a personage than the then Prime Minister, asking for an explanation, and for an arrangement. He wrote:
My Dear Sir Wilfrid,-
On the 29th day of October, 1908, the National Transcontinental Railway Commissioners awarded two contracts for the construction of about 204 miles on sections ' D ' and ' E ' of the National Transcontinental railway. The first section starting on the west end of Fauquier Brothers' Abitibi contract, in the province of Ontario, about 100 miles west of Cochrane, for a distance of 104.24 miles; the second contract commencing at the terminations of the first and joining Fauquier Brothers' contract north of lake Nipigon, a distance of 100 miles. By the terms of these contracts the work was to commence immediately after the execution of the agreements to be proceeded with continuously and diligently under the personal supervision of the contractor until completed, the date of completion being 31st December, 1910.
This work is remote from rail transportation, the closest point being 100 miles west of Cochrane. The prices at which the work was awarded were very high and consequently sufficient to allow contractors to build tote roads or some other means of transportation and getting in supplies so as to immediately commence work. To the best of our knowledge no attempt has been made as yet to open this work, and the indications are that while the work, as before stated, was let at very high prices on account of the difficulties of transportation, it Is now the intention of the contractors to haul their material over a portion of the Fauquier Brothers' work track, on which will be completed the present season, say about 50 miles, and haul along right of way to their own section 50 miles distant.
This delay will add largely to the profits of the contracts with no commensurate advantage so far as the National Transcontinental railway is concerned, and under the circumstances I will ask that the Government arrange for the cancellation of existing contracts and ask for new bids which can undoubtedly be obtained on very much reduced schedule prices, particularly so if it is known that the contractors will be enabled to haul their, material and supplies over such portion of Fauquier Brothers' work as track has been laid upon.
Considering that this was such a large question, one would have expected that the then Prime Minister would have answered Mr. Hay's letter. No answer was made, however; the letter was referred to Mr. Parent, and he was instructed to look into the question whether or not, in the interests of the Government of the country and of the Transcontinental railway, the suggestion of Mr. Hays should be carried out. As a result, what happened? Davis turned around, sold out the contract and made $740,000. In the innocence of his heart the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals the other night asked what difference it made to the country whether or not Davis made a profit of $740,000-the country had to pay it anyway. But had there been honest and straightforward competition, the McDougall firm would have been quite willing to do the work at $740,000 less than the tender that Davis had made. It is computed by the investigators that upwards of $8,000,000 would have been saved to the country had these contracts been let out in smaller sections and had more favourable terms been given. If on that contract $740,000 could have been saved, is it not a fair inference that a large amount could have been saved on the others as well? By applying this percentage of loss to the gross amount that was paid out, it may be seen that the report has proved that a large amount of money might have been saved.
Hon. gentlemen on the other side-and I give them credit for it-have taken up for discussion in connection with this matter points which may be largely questions of judgment. 1 am free to admit that at a public non-partisan meeting of fair-minded men it would be a fair question to argue whether or not momentum grades are a desirable thing to be used in any railway. I quite admit that hon. gentlemen opposite are sagacious and wise when they bring the question of momentum grades to the foreground with a view of attempting to discredit the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton. I am not going to say that all engineers agree upon this question and,

if they do differ, the first point to be considered is what is the ordinary practice of railway companies. The most important part of the Grand Trunk Pacific road is the part that runs from Graham to Fort William, as that part of the road will carry the greatest amount of traffic. No hon. gentleman opposite can successfully deny the statement made by gentlemen on this side of the House time and again that that section of the road from Graham to Fort William has a large number of momentum grades. I invite any hon. gentleman on that side of the House to show that that is not the case. No part of the Canadian Pacific railway is used more than that part between Winnipeg and Fort William, because the bulk of their traffic is carried between these points. By a statement of the Canadian Pacific railway authorities in the House the other day, it was established that there are no less than eighty-five momentum grades on that section of the Canadian Pacific railway.
Why, then, if it is good railway engineering for the Canadian Pacific railway to have on the best part of their line a large number of these momentum grades, should they not be used on the main line of the Transcontinental?
The opinions of one gentleman have been cited time and again on all things pertaining to engineering. I shall quote the opinion of this gentleman, Mr. Gordon Grant, on this question. He says, at page 615:
Disregarding ordinary sags in long fills or fills over soft ground, it has been considered inadvisable to bring up to profile grade, at present, and contractors' prices for the unnecessary work. There are, as you will see, only two places where virtual grades have been adopted, and the saving effected with this slight change amounts to $27,797. They are both well within velocity limits, and will not affect the hauling capacity of a locomotive to the extent of a single pound. The introduction of virtual grades in railroad construction, for the purpose of economy in first cost and subsequent economy in operation, by reason of reduced interest charges, cannot be considered other than a good business proposition.
There is the answer of Mr. Grant; and the hon. gentleman will not deny that on this Grand Trunk Pacific road there is a large number of what are called pusher grades. With a pusher grade the alignment is not preserved. One of these so-called momentum grades cannot affect the running of trains more than a pusher grade would. The estimate by the commissioners of the unnecessary expenditures in that respect is $6,200,000
We now come to a point somewhat analo-

gous to the question of momentum grades. I refer to the grade at La Tuque. Mr. Lumsden submitted to the Transcontinental Railway Commission a proposal in reference to the grade at La Tuque. The proposition of Mr. Doucet will be found at page 100. His proposal was to'have a so-called pusher grade instead of preserving the line as was done; and his estimate was that there would thus be a saving of one million dollars. A reference to the evidence of Mr. Mclsaac will show that he gives as one reason for the imposition of this second unascertained amount to be paid by the contractors was that they were guided by Mr. Lumsden's advice in that respect. If they were to be guided on purely financial questions by the engineers why should they not have been, guided in matters of engine eering? Here was the position. The engineer had recommended that a pusher grade should be substituted and had advised that one million dollars would be saved in that way. In defiance of that the commission, at the instigation of the Government-because the evidence shows, that they consulted the Government of the day through the then Minister of Railways and Canals- set the engineer's opinion at defiance and at La Tuque 'alone one millioini dollars was lost to the country.
One subject on which the hon. member for South Renfrew dwelt with pleasure, was trestles. He quarrelled vigorously with the estimate of the commissioners that $5,500,000 was wasted on bridges, embankments and trestles; and he gave a great many opinions of his own. At page 2179 iof ' Hansard,' the hon. member said:
The reason for not using wooden trestles is that they are not reliable and they are not modern railway construction through a country like ours and everybody knows it. . . . It would have been absolutely wrong, next to criminal, (for the Government to have done anything else, and still this Government is distributing a report saying that we could have saved on wooden trestles $2,947,000-and they dare not attempt to save one farthing themselves. I challenge this Government to show me where they have adopted a wooden trestle or a wooden bridge in preference to a steel structure. In modern railway construction, where the Government is taking over a completed road and not where the company itself is going to operate the road and is going to do the filling, it would have been, I say, nearly criminal to put in these wooden bridges. . . . The Grand Trunk Pacific is the company that owns the road west of Winnipeg and it can fill its own line at any time; but it will be compelled by good railway practice to fill it inside of eighteen months.
There can be no doubt that the hon. member for South Renfrew made the point strongly that good railway practice would

necessitate dispensing with wooden trestles, *and I suppose he still sticks to that. It has been repeated by other hon. gentlemen on his side. The hon. member had better travel a little through Ontario if he wants to find wooden trestles which have stood, not for eighteen months as he says, but for eighteen yeaTS. Between Peterborough and Lindsay, on the Grand Trunk railway, where hundreds of millions of bushels -of grain have been hauled, where fast passenger trains pass every day, there are wooden trestles to a height of 75 feet; and jet the hon. gentleman says that good railway practice would have abolished them long ago. I suppose he will admit that the Canadian Pacific railway is a fairly well managed road, perhaps not as well as the hon. member himself would manage it, although I do not think he has been offered the management of the Canadian Pacific railway as they say he was that of the Grand Trunk. I assert that there is no better piece of Tailway, no higher-priced construction, than the road from Port McNicoll to Bethany, near Peterborough. There the hon. gentleman will see a trestle a quarter of a mile long which was built by the Canadian Pacific railway four years ago, over which they are carrying trains of [DOT]60 loaded cars, each containing one thousand bushels of grain. And yet this great expert, this sought-for gentleman who was asked to take the place of the late Mr. Hays, says that good railway management will fill in wooden trestles within eighteen months after construction. The hon. gentleman should travel a little. He will admit that the Pennsylvania is a fairly well run railway. On that line near Washington, I think over Chesapeake bay, there is nearly three-quarters of a mile of trestle work; and yet trestles are condemned by this Solon of railway building, this greatest expert on railways in Canada. The hon. gentleman is publishing a speech, which, although it extended over seven hours, is being sold at the low price of one cent a copy. When people read that speech, in which he says that good railway practice compels the filling of these trestles within eighteen months, the people of this country, especially Tailway men, who do the hon. member the honour of reading his speech, when they come to his remarks on trestles and see the crass ignorance displayed by him on that question, will say: If that is all the hon. member for South Renfrew knows about
trains it was high time that the control of the Railway Department was handed over to some person else. I hope that we shall hear no more about trestles after that. If there was any one scheme that lent itself to the cupidity and greed of contractors under this board, it was the construction of trestles. See how it worked out. In the first place, they were paid by the foot for the trestles used in constructing the road. Then the contractors were to be paid 55 cents a yard for all fill, and they were to be allowed for all over-break. What a prospect that was, under this kindly and benevolent board, for a railway contractor !
In the first place, instead of breaking down on either side to the extent of twenty per cent, which is good railway practice, the contractor was allowed to break to the extent of forty per cent. And what was thfe result? His train was there, he had to stop and load the overbreak on the cars and as there was a double quantity he was successfully handling it that much cheaper. This overbreak on which there was a large profit was then taken to the dump and used for filling around the trestles. How these contractors must have smiled knowing that they were getting fifty cents a yard for dumping this overbreak in the fill while the Grand Trunk railway were only getting twenty-five cents a yard. Is it any wonder in the face of these facts that the commissioners report that there was a waste of $5,500,000 on trestles and embankments?
Then as regards sidings. Some hon. gentleman opposite laboured the other day to show that the building of six miles of siding was permitted under the Act. Commissioner Mclsaao disagreed as he understood that the specifications called for a single track. Was there any sense or reason in parallelling the main line with six miles of siding? I can understand as every man can, the necessity of having a siding long enough to pocket say a couple of trains. But why a siding of six miles? I will ask the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) whether he can give me any reasonable explanation for that six miles of siding and I will be pleased to sit down while he answers.

Where was this six
miles of siding?
I think it was at Trans-cona.
That is only four miles.
Was it not near Graham?
There is no place where there was six miles of siding. The six miles is made up of siding at different places.

My recollection is that
at some place there was six miles, hut as I cannot lay my hand on it just now I will take the hon. gentleman's statement that . it was four miles. Fancy the management of a railway company putting four miles of siding alongside their main track! What did it mean? It meant that it was necessary to pocket four miles of trains there, in order to allow the trains on the main line to go by. The thing is absurd on the face of it and I tell the hon. member for South Renfrew that he cannot find a siding of four miles in the whole system of either the Grand Trunk railway or the Canadian Pacific railway. It is apparent that the reason those sidings were put in was to enable the contractor to make more money. Take the McArthur tender for instance. The tender was for $13,000,000 but when finished out it amounted to $20,000,000. Hon. gentlemen are well within their rights in discussing cases in this report involving a question of judgment, but there are cases of reckless expenditure which they do not attempt and will not attempt to discuss, because they are so palpably absurd that no man would have the temerity to stand up anywhere, much less in this House, and attempt to defend them. Take the case, cited time and again of the farm offered to the board for $3,500. The commission refused to buy the farm and deliberately built a culvert connecting the two parts of the farm. As a result of that, and of the expenditure incurred in connection with the other farm crossing case, the country had to pay $60,000.
Hon. gentlemen opposite also assailed the commissioners for saying that the portion of the line east of Levis should not have been built and that the $35,000,000 spent thereon, was wasted. In answer to that I say that the commissioners' finding is justified by every inference than can be deducted from the .situation, as it presents itself to-day. There is nothing in the whole contract between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific to compel the Grand Trunk to send a single bushel of grain or a single pound of freight over that eastern section. That was shown when the contract was up some years ago. In the meantime what have the Grand Trunk railway been doing? Have they made preparations for traffic at St. John or Halifax by spending a single dollar?

Not at all. The very moment the contract was entered into and construction commenced, the Grand Trunk started operations to deflect this trade to Portland; and all the time this railroad was under construction it must have been known to the then Government that such was the case. What was the first step the Grand Trunk took. The town of Midland is their principal port for shipping grain either to Montreal or Portland. Directly the contract was signed, the Grand Trunk spent a large sum of money, probably about $3,000,000, in the construction of docks and elevators at Midland to accommodate the traffic that would come from the Northwest and be carried to Portland in the winter and to Montreal in the summer. A glance at the map shows that that traffic never can go to the ports of St. John or Halifax. In the first place, the Grand Trunk will do what the Canadian Pacific railway are doing; they will have a port on the upper-lakes, from which they will ship their grain in the fall of the year to Montreal, and when navigation closes the grain will be taken to Portland, and the Canadian Pacific railway will do as they are doing, and continue to take their traffic to St. John. Moreover the situation is such today in the Maritime provinces that after the grain for export has gone by, no grain at all will go to the Maritime provinces in the winter months. The grain will leave the Grand Trunk Pacific at Cochrane and by an arrangement with the Ontario Government will come down to the province of Ontario and be distributed for use in the flour mills, just as is being done to-day. And here will stand this railway, unused in the winter months. There will not be any large trains of immigrants coming in who might travel over that road because it is the shorter route. Passengers will travel either by way of Chicago, or by the Canadian Pacific railway to North Bay, or passing up to Cochrane they can take the Grand Trunk Pacific there if they want to patronize that road. The whole thing stands as a monument of blundering incapacity on the part of the late Government. Worse than that, by reason of the enormous sum the railway has co-st, the rates will for all time to come be so abnormal that it will not be a paying road for the Grand Trunk Pacific.
My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) said:	look at the position
of Mr. Chamberlin; Mr. Chamberlin protested against momentum grades. I have no doubt that Mr. Chamberlain protested

against momentum grades, and I think he was a wise man to protest against them. Why? Mr. Chamberlin knew the enormous expenditure that would be incurred in the construction of this road and when the present Government came into office he was seeking for an opportunity to put up some excuse in order to try to evade the bargain of taking over the road as the company are bound under the contract to take it over. I assume that was the reason he wrote that letter. It was good business and good policy on his part as the representative of the Grand Trunk railway.
These hon. gentlemen may go before the public of Canada and discuss this report on its merits. They may assail Messrs. Lynch-Staunton and Gutelius, but the bold fact will stand out that after the late Government had stated that they had complete surveys, that they had employed competent engineers to make these surveys and that it was a fair estimate to say that the road would only cost $61,000,000, it will have cost 300 per cent more than that. That is a fact that cannot be gainsaid, and that they cannot get away from. The report discloses a condition of blundering incapacity-I fear I must almost say of idiocy- that is without precedent in the administration of public affairs. The public will consider the stamp of men who composed the commission and, having regard to their reputations, their special unfitness and incapacity to deal with the construction of this road. The Government were well within their rights when they instituted this inquiry. The gentlemen who conducted the inquiry and made the report bring the facts out so boldly and so strongly that hon. gentlemen opposite, being shy of argument, at every turn have endeavoured to justify themselves by the assertion that the questions dealt with are only questions of ordinary opinion and judgment. I am prepared to vote against the amendment proposed by the hon. member for South Renfrew for the reason that I believe the Government have done right in having the investigation and because I believe that not only have the investigators brought to the task ability and a conscientious regard for the faithful discharge of a public duty, but that they have produced a report which will be of great interest to the people of Canada, one which will be a source of information to them and one which amply justifies the Government in employing them to conduct this inquiry.

Mr. Speaker, if powers of vituperation and a low order of abuse will pass current for argumentative skill, then I think my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) has earned the congratulations of his friends who gathered so quickly into the House the moment he undertook to speak. My hon. friend's speech has been very much indeed like the report-the alleged report-which is involved in the motion of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). There is in it a poverty of argument and of fact, but it is resplendent in assertion. I do not feel that I am called upon to follow my hon. friend in that line of argument. Were I to attempt to do so I know that I must ignominiously fail because I have neither the inclination nor the ability to follow in the trail blazed out by my hon. friend. It seems to me that my hon. friend, in taking that course, has given away entirely the case of hon. gentlemen opposite. I was not very much surprised that my hon. friend did take that course; I rather anticipated it. The gentlemen on the other side who have taken part in the discussion are for the most part rich in such powers, and in the absence of any fact or argument, they have indulged to the full in vituperation.
There has been circulated throughout this country a .document called the Federal Press Bulletin, and in the copy which came into my hands, I find a repetition, perhaps the original, of the speech of my hon. friend from East Simcoe, of my hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) and of my hon. friend from Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler). I find this document full of headlines, in glaring print, and it goes through the country as a substitute for facts, but entirely impoverished as to argument. It gives us a clue as to the object of the report. This report has been characterized as a partisan and non-judicial report upon a great national undertaking, and as a campaign document to be circulated broadcast throughout the length and breadth of Canada.
