The secret of the obtaining of running rights over the Temiskaming and Northern railway from Cochrane to North Bay was divulged but recently in connection with the great delegation that came here. I will not enter into the details, but this report emanated from an ex-official of the Canadian Pacific Tailway, a gentleman whom I should fairly suppose to be in close communion with that great railway. That gentleman advocates, as did the Grand Trunk Pacific originally, stopping at North Bay and having the traffic come down through the American seaports because that would be the natural channel. The present Minister of Railways is wrapped up in that proposed railway centre, North Bay. The scheme is openly proposed; true, it is but visionary, but speculators in land around North Bay are trading on the idea that the traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific will find an outlet through North Bay, that it will come down through Toronto, and that a portion of it which does not seek an outlet through Montreal and Quebec will find its way to the seaboard through American ports. ' The scheme is against the Maritime provinces seaports; it is against the Canadian seaports, and I make the assertion that every movement of the chessboard since October, 1911, has been carefully planned and is in the direction of the consummation of that scheme. This report is brought forward to bring aid and comfort to those who wish to carry out that idea. Let us not sail under false colours; let it be recognized that if the traffic goes via North Bay we aTe going to be an adjunct of the United States, in so far as our export business is concerned, in winter at least. My right hon. friend the leader of the Liberal party has certainly received the support and commendation of the people of eastern Canada because they believed that he was determined that the products of the West should find an outlet through Canadian seaports, and every act of his and of his Government gave strength to that idea. Had he continued in power the people of eastern Canada would have had confidence in his carrying out that idea to its fullest fruition. But there is a sense of alarm in eastern Canada with Tespect not merely^ to the traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific going down as I have -stated, but with respect to the destiny of the Intercolonial railway. It, too, will be made contributory to the companies that have had the monopoly in this land for too many years. This Government seem to be lending their aid to the idea, and I hope that it is not too late to have the movement arrested.
I would wish, Mr. Speaker, that I could have had more time to deal with this subject, because in its many phases it is a big one. There are many things connected with the matter that can only be explained at some length, but time will not permit me to deal with them.

One word as to the cost. They say that this road has cost over $100,000 a mile. Have the people of Canada forgotten the construction of the St. Charles branch ? Do they not know that the Government of that day, under Sir Charles Tupper as Minister of Railways and Canals, constructed a line from St. Charles junction down to Levis, a distance of about fourteen and a half miles, and that the cost per mile of that railway was nearly $125,000 per mile ? Yet our friends of the Conservative party to-day stand horrified at the thought that a transcontinental line of railway of an entirely different and much higher standard, has been constructed for an amount per mile of about $100,000. If that road had been completed up to the standard designed for it, it would have been without a peer on this continent.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the amendment of my hon. friend from South Renfrew is sustained by the evidence, by the facts, by the circumstances, by the actions and attitude of the Government of the day, and I shall have a very great deal of pleasure in voting for that amendment.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Quebec East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although this debate has lasted now for more than a week, everybody will agree that the time which has been spent upon it has been time well spent. It has already cleared the atmosphere, it has already removed and dispelled many misconceptions which were floating in the air and which were darkening the fair name of Canada. But the discussion has taken so wide a range, and so many issues have been brought into it, which, although connected with it are entirely irrelevant to it, that it may not be out of place that I should recall to the attention of the House what is the true question now before it. My hon. friend who sits beside me, (Mr. Graham), in concluding the powerful indictment which he brought against the Government and the commission, asserted that the report which has been laid upon the table by the Government was so wilfully partisan and misleading as to be wholly unreliable. This is the effect of my hon. friend's amendment, and this is the question which is now before us. Is this report reliable or not reliable ? Is it true or is it not true ?
Is it partisan or is it fair ? That is the only question with which we have to deal at this moment. The volume in which the commissioners have placed their views as to the construction of the National Transcontinental railway bears upon its 
first page these pompous words:	' Report
of the National Transcontinental Railway Investigating Commission.' It has pleased Messrs. Staunton and Gutelius to place upon the volume which they have placed before us this high sounding title ' Report of the National Transcontinental Railway Investigating Commission.' Of course, as we know, paper is impassive, and has to receive everything that is put upon it; but, Sir, if, according to the fitness of things, there should be some connection between title and text, no title could be worse chosen than that which has been placed upon this book. It would be more in accordance with the fitness of things, looking at the report itself and the evidence connected with it, to call it ' The Comedy of Errors, by Messrs. Lynch-Staunton and Gutelius,' for, Sir, in that so-called report there are so many misstatements of fact and so many mis-statements of law, that the book should certainly be called a comedy, or something worse. The counterfeiter who tries to palm off a spurious coin upon the community places upon it the visage and the inscription of the true coin of the realm, and for some time he may deceive the community; but sooner or later the fraud is detected, and the counterfeit is revealed. So it is already in respect to this report. The fraud is discovered, the counterfeit is fully revealed in all its hideousness; and to that counterfeit the Government have been accessories both after and before the fact. They became accessories after the fact when they circulated that report; they became accessories before the fact, when they appointed commissioners who, it was well known from their antecedents, were notorious partisans and could not give us any other report than the distortion of facts which they have placed before us as their opinion on the construction of that railroad.
When this Government came into office they were besieged by their followers and friends to have an investigation into the construction of the National Transcontinental railway. The press of the party had repeated again and again that in the construction of that railway there had been, to the detriment of the community, not only gross errors but fraud. There were assertions that millions of dollars had been diverted from the purposes for which they should have been employed, and had gone into the pockets of individuals for private gain, or still worse. Under such circumstances I am not at all surprised that the Government should have

come to the conclusion that a commission should be appointed. If they believed all that had been said in the press, then, like the rest of the party, they must have worked themselves into a frenzied conviction that their opponents had been as dishonest as had been represented. But even if they did not believe anything of the kind, for my part I do not blame them for having appointed a commission. A (work of that magnitude might well have been the subject of investigation so that the public might know the whole history of the transaction from first to last, but, Sir, while I dio not attach any blame whatever to the Government for the appointing of a commission, I blame them- and this is a ground of complaint which they cannot avoid-because in the selection of the commissioners they did not do justice to their opponents, to themselves, or to the community, at large. Every consideration would seem to require that the Government should have appointed men who, from their well known character, from their reputation in the land, from their antecedents, would have afforded to the community a guarantee that the investigation would be fair and honest, free from fear and free from favour; that the commissioners would disguise nothing, that they would 'naught extenuate nor aught set down in malice,' and that they would make a true deliverance according to the evidence. Is that the character of the two men who were appointed as commissioners? I do not hesitate to say-and I believe upon this I can appeal to the fairness of every man who sits in this House, whether on this side or on that-that in a court of justice these two men would have been challenged for cause, and would not have been allowed to sit upon the jury. As to Mr. Gutelius, I do not want to say anything of him but what is known to the community. In 1911 he was, I believe, an employee of the Canadian Pacific railway in a minor capacity; he did not hold any high office. It is said of him, and I have heard it on good authority, that he took an active part in the election of 1911. Be that as it may, the fact is that no sooner had the present Government and the Minister of Railways come to office, than Mr. Gutelius became the close adviser of the Minister of Railways. From the humble position which he occupied in the employ of the Canadian Pacific railway, and which, as I am told, commanded but a very modest salary,
he was hoisted into the office of general manager of the Intercolonial railway; hoisted, I say, and at a salary of $20,000 a year, which Mr. Gutelius is now receiving. That position had been occupied for more than thirty years by Mr. Pottinger at a salary that at no time exceeded $6,000 a year. Without saying anything derogatory of Mr. Gutelius, I say that it would be a lucky day for him, if, when he leaves the position he is now occupying and which has been occupied by his predecessor, he carries with him one-half of the respect which is now surrounding the white hair of Mr. Pottinger. It has been said that it is not fair to any man to put him in the position to choose between his salt and his duty-not fair to the man who earns the salt and not fair to the man of whom the duty is demanded, because sometimes there will be strong temptation when a man has to make such a choice. After having read the report which I now have before me, it seems to me that I am not doing an injury or an injustice to Mr. Gutelius when I say that, in my opinion, in this investigation he was truer to his salt than he was to his duty.
And what of Mr. Lynch-Staunton? If Mr. Gutelius was not known in 1911, the same cannot be said of Mr. Lynch-Staunton. Mr. Lynch-Staunton was very well known. I have nothing to say against him personally. He is, as I understand, a good lawyer, though in my opinion there are better lawyers than he. He is a partisan, but I do not find fault with him for that. I do not know of a man in this House who would disclaim being a partisan. I would not, for my part, but, partisan as I am, I say there are some offices to which a partisan should not be appointed. My hon. friend the Solicitor General dealt with that question; he anticipated the reproach. I have said before, and I am glad to say again, that I am an admirer of the subtle intellect of my friend the Solicitor General, but on this occasion it was hard for him to defend the appointment of such a partisan as Mr. Lynch-Staunton. This is the way, however, that he attempted the task. Speaking in answer to my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), the Solicitor General said:
The hon. member knows that in our selection of judges, whose office doubtless compares in dignity and in consequence with that of a commissioner, we are compelled to resort to party lines on one side or the other for appointees; and so the same objections which the hon. member hurls against Mr. Lynch-Staunton

could be hurled against every man appointed to the bench by the Government of which he himself was a member.
It is not exact to say that we are compelled to resort to party lines on one side or the other in making appointments to the Bench. But we have held on both sides that party affiliation was not a bar to the appointment of any man, I believe that experience has shown that though we have appointed men to the Bench who have been actively engaged in politics, of very few, if any, can it be said that they were political partisans when on the Bench. On the contrary, I have no hesitation in saying that in many instances the experience obtained in political life has been of good .service to a judge. We expect that as soon as a man ascends the Bench he shall ignore altogether party lines, and if we thought *he would remain a partisan we would not think of appointing him. The moment a man has been called to' the high functions of arbiter between man and man, if he is worthy of the office, he ought to forget that he ever belonged to a party, and honour his oath that he will administer justice without fear and without favour. Is that the oath that was taken by Mr. Lynch-Staunton? No, Mr. Lynch-Staunton took no oath at all. But even if he took no oath, at all events according to the tenets of our morality, the moment Mr. Staunton received his appointment, if he was to act in a judicial 'spirit, it was his duty then and there to cease to be partisan. Can that be said of Mr. Lynch-iStaunton? It is known that he remained so much a partisan after his appointment, that he left his duty at Ottawa as commissioner to take part in an election. It is obvious that Mr. Lynch-Staunton remained a partisan to the end, and when he wrote that report he was fresh from the campaign in South Bruce. Such were the commissioners.
Let us see how these commissioners performed their duty. If their object in this investigation had been to have the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, one would imagine that the investigation *would have taken place in the full light of day, and that all the proceedings, would have been in open court. It is a maxim of law, it is a maxim of justice and it is a maxim of fair play, that there is no fair trial except free and open and public trial. Is that what was done? No, Sir, the commissioners sat in camera. The public were not admitted to their sittings, the press was excluded.	They shunned the
light, and no light was allowed to filter

through except such light as suited the good-will, or the caprice, or the intent and purpose of the commissioners.
If you want to see the immense distance which separated >the Cosnsetrva/tive party in 1913 and in 1880, look at the investigation that took place jn 1880 upon a very similar matter. If there is one man in the history of Canada whose name stands emblazoned as the very incarnation of righteousness and honesty it is Alexander Mackenzie. Alexander Mackenzie, dead, is a model for all men, but Alexander Mackenzie, living, did not escape the fangs of calumny, and when Mr. Mackenzie left office in 1878 there were some accusations against him as there were accusations against those who lost office in 1911. The accusations had reference to the! construction of the Intercolonial railway by Mr. Mackenzie, and a commission was appointed by Sir John Macdonald in 1880. Who was the commissioner? The commissioner was not a partisan of the class of those who "were appointed in 1912; the commissioner was Mr. Frank Shanly, an eminent engineer of that day. There is no greater name, I believe, in the engineering history of this country than the name of Frank Shanly, unless it be that of his brother, Walter Shanly. Mr. Frank Shanly was absolutely disconnected with politics. The sittings were open, the public were admitted, the press were there and from day to day the public could follow the history of the construction of the road as it was told by the witnesses. No obvious cross-examination was avoided, and everybody knows that there is no evidence which can be accepted as a final expression of truth until the evidence has been subjected to the supreme test of cross-examination. Nay, more, I believe, and I assert, that if this investigation which we have to-day, and the result of which is set forth in the report of Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton, had been in the open, and reported from day to day by the press, the results of the investigation would not have been expressed in the terms in which they are expressed in this report.
As to the manner in which the report, ox the result of this investigation, was submitted to the pulblic, I h-ave a word to say. Tn this the commissioners showed themselves not only to be experts, but to be artists as well. The proceedings were behind closed doors. Nobody was admitted, but by some mysterious process which has

not been explained yet, from time to time statements appeared in the press as to what was going on in this investigation. It was stated in the first paragraphs that were sent sent to the press that these commissioners were making awful discoveries. Later on the insinuation was to the effect that millions of dollars were discovered to have been abstracted from the public treasury in connection with the railway. Then the report was to the effect that $40,000,000 had been taken from the treasury in the construction of the road. At last the report was placed upon the table, in manuscript, or to be exact, in typewritten copy. It could not be taken possession of, it could not be read, it was not printed, but an abstract was placed in the hands of the press which could not have come from any other source than from the commissioners themselves, for they alone knew the contents of fheir report, and in the press of Canada, on the day following, it was stated that as a result of the investigation, the commissioners had discovered that $40,000,000 had been robbed from the public of Canada in the construction of the Transcontinental railway.
We have the report in our hands to-day; we have been able to study it, and, Sir, what is it? It is an unblushing partisan libel. From every syllable partisanship oozes out in an endless flow of misrepresentation and distortion. But, amid all these insinuations, amidst this mass of suppressed and distorted fact, one feature stands out clear and true, and that is that there has been no graft in the construction of the National Transcontinental railway. You say that it cost $160,000,000, but not one dollar has been diverted from the object for which it was voted by Parliament. If it be a fact that it has cost $160,000,000, -every dollar of that amount has gone ini to the construction of the road. The only fault that they charge against us is that we have built too well, too substantially, with too much hope in the future, and too great faith in Canada. Mistakes there may have been; I am prepared to say that mistakes there were, but there is no cause for any man who supported the late Administration to blush at the construction of that road. Our faith in the country was great, but not greater than it should be. Our expectations were high, but not higher than they should have been, and to-day I say that the railway will realize everything that was hoped from it provided that it be not degraded by
the men into whose charge it has passed. The commissioners having sought, and sought in vain, for scandals, determined to establish the theory that there had been extravagance and unlawful and fraudulent expenditure.
This report is divided into two parts. The second part contains a detailed statement of all the cases in which it is asserted that there has been fraudulent or extravagant expenditure. The first part is simply an epitome of the second and this is how the commissioners summarize their findings:
We And that the Transcontinental Railway Commission, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and those having charge of the construction of the railway did not consider it desirable or necessary to practise or encourage economy in the construction of this road.
We find that without including the money which was unnecessarily expended in building the railway east of the St. Lawrence river $40,000,000 at least was needlessly expended in the building of this road.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

How these
hon. gentlemen cheer! How happy they would be if that statement were true! But, if that statement is false, is there a term strong enough to characterize the calumny which has been perpetrated by the commissioners against the fair name of Canada? I call upon these gentlemen who pretend that this report is true to show us how the commissioners have been able to make up that sum of $40,000,000. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) stated yesterday that, on their own figures, they fall short by at least $10,000,000. Torture the figures as you will, take the detailed statements given by the commissioners themselves, and you cannot make up to $40,000,000 what they charge as losses of Canada. I say more; I say that in that report there are statements as to illegal expenditures made by the commissioners which not only cannot he maintained, bult which are untrue and dishonest. As an example of this, I call the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to the finding of the commissioners in regard to the Transcona shops:
The country has been committed to the expenditure of $4,500,000 for the erection and equipment of the Transcona shops at Winnipeg, which, in our opinion, are not authorized by law and which are, in any event, twice as large as are required for the purposes of the eastern division.
It is stated that this sum of $4,500,000 spent on the Transcona shops has been spent contrary to law. This is the opinion

of Mr. Lynch-Staunton, given in this report, which has been circulated to the extenit, I understand, of a quarter of a million copies. According to Mr. Lynch-Staumton, this $4,500,000 has been illegally spent. When Mr. Lynch-Sftaunton issued that statement he knew that that money had been spent according to law and not contrary to law. Mr. Lynch -Sit aun ton, later on in his report, at page 121, discusses for some ten pages his legal opinion that this expenditure was not according to law. Before I proceed further, I will show how my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) has dealt with that subject. In answer to my hon. friend the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), he made use of this language to which I call the attention of the House:
The hon. member for South Renfrew says that the Transcona shops are another source of great pride to him; that if he had to build them again he would build them just as they are now; and that Mr. Lynch-Staunton is entirely wrong when he argues that the building of the Transcona shops, as a plant for repairs, was beyond the powers of the commission and should have been done by the Grand Trunk Pacific. I was aware, before the ex-Minister of Railways rose, and I think most of us were aware, that Mr. Staunton in that opinion did not agree with the deputy Minister of Justice who gave the late Government his opinions and who gives this Government his opinions. We knew that Mr. Staunton was running counter to the opinions of eminent lawyers in tins country, and we knew it was the duty of the Government to heed the opinion of the Department of Justice, but I was not aware, and I am not yet aware, that it was a crime on the part of Mr. Staunton to give his own opinion even if it did differ from that of the deputy minister.
No, it was not a crime for Mr. Lynch-Staunton to give his opinion and to defend it, but it was a crime for Mr. Lynch-Staunton to give to the public his opinion that this money had been spent contrary to the law, when Mr. Lynch-Staunton knew that the courts and competent
10 p.m. authorities had decided against him. Lawyers will differ. That truism is as old as the first day there were two lawyers in the world. But when lawyers differ, there must be competent authority to settle their differences, and there are only two ways in which differences of lawyers can be determined, and that is either by having recourse to the tribunals established by law or by voluntary arbitration. In this case it is quite true that Mr. Lynch-Staunton was of the opinion that the shops at Transcona should have been charged to the Grand Trunk Pacific and not to the Government. But
this was a case in which Mr. Lynch-Staunton was of one opinion and all the other lawyers were against him. The Deputy Minister of Justice was against him, Mr. Atkinson, the counsel of the commission was against him, Sir Allen Aylesworth was against him, Mr. Brown, the battonier of the Bar of Montreal, was against him, and I think I may say that the Minister of Justice was also against Mr. Lynch-Staunton on this matter. But this, after all, is of no great consequence. The matter had still to be decided between the Grand Trunk Pacific on the one side and the Government on the other, and what took place ? The Minister of Railways himself took pains to have the difference of opinion settled. The Solicitor General said the other day that the Government were bound to abide by the opinion of the Department of Justice. So they were; but on this occasion they did not do so, because, while it is true that Mr. Lynch-Staunton was of one opinion and his opinion had been contradicted by the Department of Justice, the Department of Railways did not follow the advice of the Department of Justice, but the Minister of Railways asked Sir William Whyte to act as arbitrator and to decide the question between the department and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. On the 4th of December, 1912, the following joint telegram was sent to Sir William Whyte by the Minister of Railways and Mr. Chamberlin. I need not say that if there is a man in Canada who is accepted as an authority on railways, it is Sir William Whyte, former first vice-president of the Canadian Pacific railway. The telegram is in these words:
Will you act as sole arbitrator between the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway to fix the rental to be paid for use of that portion of the Transcontinental railway line between Winnipeg and lake Superior junction pending completion of the entire line through to Moncton. If so, necessary information will be sent you directly and arrangements made with the Grand Trunk Pacific officials at Winnipeg to furnish train so that you can go over the line and make the necessary examination; also any other information.
Upon the assent of Sir William Whyte, the reference was given to him, stating the point for decision, and that point was:
Are the shops at Transcona and repair shops at divisional points or, any of them to be regarded as a portion of the eastern division, -within the intent and meaning of the agreements of July 29, 1903, and of February 18, 1904, and Acts affirming the same?
If not, what is the proper rental for the use of such shops, or any of them by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for any railway purposes they may desire?
fSir Wilfrid Laurier.]

This is the form in which the matter was submitted to Sir William Whyte. And the judgment upon the matter pronounced by Sir William Whyte put an end to all contention upon this point, whatever may have been the previous opinion of Mr. Lynch-Staunton. Sir William Whyte's judgment was:
With respect to the shops at Transcona, considering their location and the circumstances under which they were produced and furnished, and the specifications; and interpreting the said agreements and Acts in the light of modern railway practice, and considering the contemplated use of the said eastern division by other railways, I award, order and determine that the said shops are to be regarded as and are a portion of the said eastern division within the intent and meaning of the said agreements of the 29th of July 1903 and the 18th of February 1904 and Acts confirming the same.
I further award, order and determine that all repair shops at divisional points are to he regarded as and are a portion of said eastern division within the intent and meaning of the said agreements of 29th July, 1903, and of the 18th February, 1904, and of the Acts confirming the same. I consider these are a material part of the railway and necessary convenience for its proper, and efficient operation.
In the face of this, I say it was dishonest on the part of Mr. Lynch-Staunton and Mr. Gutelius to say that this was still a matter of legal opinion. It was no longer a matter of legal opinion; the matter had been settled, and it was settled against the opinion of Mr. Lynch-Staunton. If the matter was still a matter of legal opinion, the Government could go before the courts to have it determined, but the Government know that they are precluded from that course, and that the matter is closed forever. Yet, Sir, the report has been sent broadcast throughout the country that in this matter the Transcontinental commissioners illegally spent $4,500,000.
Now, what about classification? The investigating commissioners say that about $3,200,000 has been illegally spent through over-classification. This matter also is no longer in issue; and it is no longer in issue because, so far as the Government and the Grand Trunk Pacific are concerned, it was arbitrated and decided. The arbitrators in this case were men of the highest eminence -Mr. Kelliher, for the Grand Trunk Pacific; Mr. Gordon Grant, for the Government, and the third arbitrator, a man of eminent respectability, one of the best men in his line that we have in this country, Mr. Collingwood Sclireiber. So far as the Grand Trunk Pacific, who objected to this classification, are concerned, the matter is at rest. But what about the contractors?
Can the opinion of Mr. Lynch-Staunton and Mr. Gutelius be raised against the contractors? My hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) answered that yesterday, when he told us that the Government had actually paid these contractors. The Government have not confidence enough in the opinion of Mr. Lynch-Staunton to follow it in matters of law, but they are quite ready to distribute his opinion for partisan purposes.
Before I leave this part of the subject, there is one thing as to which I feel particularly bound to say a few words, I refer to the contracts on sections 16 and 17 held by Messrs. M. P. and J. T. Davis, and with which my name has been connected. It is quite true, Sir, that in the month of August, 1909, I received a letter from Mr. Hays complaining of the delay of Messrs. Davis in carrying out their contract. I do not know that it is necessary that I should read that letter-the House is familiar with it. Suffice it to say that in that letter Mr. Hays called my attention to the fact, as he alleged, that Messrs. Davis had done nothing at all towards the completion of their contract, that they were in default, and that therefore the contract ought to be cancelled. This afternoon my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) rather took me to task for not having answered that letter. How does he know I did not answer it? He could not know from the report, because the commissioners did not ask me. It so happened that at the time this letter was written to me I wias mat in Ottawa, I was in the country, but the letter was forwarded to me from my office, and I answered it in this way:
Arthabaska, P.Q., August 12, 1909.
Dear Mr. Hays,-X am in receipt of your avour of the 2nd instant. I propose to return o Ottawa before the end of this month and if lOssible will see you in passing through Mont-
Oh, oh.
And I saw Mr. Hays when passing through Montreal.
Oh, oh.

What more
could I do than discuss the matter with Mr. Hays? Will any one suggest what else I could have done? I did one other thing, I referred the matter to Mr. Parent, the *chairman of the commission. I have to take issue with some of the statements that were made in that letter of Mr. Hays advising me that Messrs. Davis had done nothing at all towards the completion of

their contract. Having been appealed to, I thought it might be my duty to make some inquiry as to how the matter stood and I learned that it was contended on the part of Messrs. Davis that they had taken steps towards proceeding on their contract. Everybody knows that in railway construction in those distant far-north parts of the country which were then without communication, it was the first duty of a contractor, and perhaps the most difficult, to get supplies to the scene of his operations. Generally, this could only be don'e in the winter. Messrs. Davis had two lines by which they could try to reach their contract; one of which was by the Temiskaming railway, and then taking advantage of the railway westward towards Cochrane which was then under construction. The other course was to take the supplies by the Canadian Pacific railway to Nipigon, then use Nipigon lake, carry supplies to the northern shore of that lake, and then use rivers which flow from the north, or, if the rivers could not be used, build a line across. I was told that Mr. Davis had sent a party of surveyors to Nipigon to survey the country and to ascertain whether or not he could take his supplies over that line; I was told that he was engaged in that work during the entire winter, and that he found that- there would be no advantage in using this line in preference to the Temiskaming railway, and there the matter stood. It was represented to me that the snmmer was lost and that they had to wait for the next winter. It was a question whether Mr. Davis was in default; I came to the conclusion that it would be a very risky thing to attempt a lawsuit under such conditions, and that when the contractor had done what he could it would not be fair to him to take any such course. Messrs. Gutelius and Staunton., however, take a different view. On page 52 of their report they say:
This letter does not contain one reason-
That is the letter of Mr. Parent in answer to Mr. Hays.
which justified the commission in its refusal. The contractors were clearly at that time a whole year in default and could have no legal or moral claim to any consideration from the commission.
The commissioners say that Messrs. Davis were clearly in default. Where did they get that evidence? The commissioners examined Mr. Davis under oath, and examined him upon this very contract. If they believed Mr. Davis to be in default, should they not, in justice to him, have asked him whether or not he was in de-

fault and to have asked for his reasons? We have here the evidence of Mr. Davis; every hon. gentleman has it in his hand, and can read it-and not a question, was put to. him upon this point-., I shall read to the Hou.se all the questions which were put to Mr. Davis with regard to contracts 16 and 17, and which will be found on pages 658 and 659 of the report:
Q. In connection with contracts 16 and 17, there were two contractors tendering, M. P. and J. T. Davis and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway. Was there any arrangement between you and the Grand Trunk Pacific railway in connection with these contracts?-A. No, sir.
Q. You sub-let these contracts to Mr. M. J. O'Brien and his associates?-A. Yes.
Q. Was there any arrangement between you and M. J. O'Brien in the tendering for these two contracts?-A. No, sir.
Q. M. J. O'Brien did not know he was going to get that contract if you secured it?-A. No, sir.
These were all the questions asked by Mr. Gutelius on that particular point. But the chairman took a hand in the matter, and proceeded to examine Mr. Davis. These are the questions which were put to the witness by Mr. Lynch-Staunton:
Q. I want to know whether of not there was ever any pressing by the commission to you to commence the work on contracts 16 and 17?- A. No, we got that contract.
Q. Yes, but I am just asking you that. I inquired from Mr, Ryan and he tells me there was not. I just want to have a confirmation of It on your part.-A. I do not think so.
Q. Do you know whether or not there was ever any pressing or urging by the commission to O'Brien and Company to speed the work after they obtained assignments of the contract?-A. No, sir.
One would have imagined that the chairman would have asked Mr. Davis: you have had that contract since October, 1908; what steps did you take towards the performance of your contract? One would have thought that in this way Mr. Davis would have been given an opportunity to state whether or not he had taken any steps to carry out the contract, and if in the opinion of Mr. Staunton the steps taken had not been sufficient, he could have asked Mr. Davis to give reasons to justify his default. Not a question was asked Mr. Davis along this line; yet the commissioners have the audacity to say that Mr. Davis was in default.
I ask every hon. gentleman who sits on the other side of the House: is that the kind of justice they would like to have meted out to them? Is that the kind of treatment they are pleased to call British justice? Is it not a principle of British justice that a man is given an opportunity to state his case and give his reasons before a judge

finds him guilty and passes sentence upon him? I say that the very element of simple, ordinary justice was denied to the man who was reported by the commissioners as being in default. I call this not justice, not fair play, not honesty; I call it partisanship, pure and simple.
But it is in the conclusion of their report especially that the commissioners show their animus and disclose the spirit which has inspired their conduct in this whole matter. In that part of the report they attack the construction of the line from Levis to Moncton. What was their authority for doing so? The construction of the line was a pure question of policy, within the exclusive jurisdiction of Parliament and of the	Canadian people.	Can we conceive of the Government asking these two men to report upon a question of policy which had been twice submitted to the	Canadian people?	No, Sir, the
Canadian Government knew better; they did not confide such authority to the commissioners. The Order in Council called for one thing and one thing alone, and that was the investigation into the construction of the road. The Order in Council asked:
For an investigation in respect to the Transcontinental railway between Moncton and Winnipeg, now being constructed under commissioners in accordance with the National Transcontinental Railway Act of 1903, chapter 71, and such investigation should be of a full and comprehensive character, covering all matters bearing on the actual construction of the railway and expenditure thereon, whether direct or indirect, the system adopted for such construction, and the management of the undertaking generally.
Their mission was to investigate how the money had been expended; whether it had been expended economically or otherwise, fraudulently or otherwise, extravagantly or otherwise, but they had no authority whatever to pass judgment upon a question which was one of policy-whether it was wise or unwise, politic or impolitic, to construct that radway or any part of it. Having no authority, then, to do so, why did they go into that question? Not content with that, they made a comparison between the Transcontinental and the Intercolonial. What was their authority for that? They had none whatever. Where did they get their information? They examined fifty-eight witnesses, and, speaking subject to correction, for I do not pretend to know the depositions of these fifty-eight witnesses with such minuteness as to be able to risk a definite statement, I submit that they did not get their information from
anything that was deposed under oath by any one of these witnesses.
But, Sir, the source where they found the condemnation of this part of the railway is not far to seek. That was an echo of the speeches of Mr. Lyneh-Staunton in 1904 and 1908. He simply put in condensed form what he had been stating in more extended form on many platforms in the province of Ontario. I say in Ontario because we must remember that, as far as that part of the line is concerned, the Conservative party was not a unit upon it. There were those in the Maritime provinces who were in favour of that extension of the line; but in the province of Ontario, on the contrary, every member of the Conservative party was against the construction of the line not only from the St. Lawrence to Moncton, but from Cochrane to Quebec as well. In this very debate the Minister of Customs, now acting Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid), gave us the benefit of his opinion. On the day this debate commenced the Minister of. Customs said:
I believe that if the Grand Trunk Pacific had been permitted to carry out the charter as proposed by them when they came to Parliament, namely, to build a line from North Bay through to the Pacific coast, at least $100,000,000 would have been saved to the people of Canada.
Of course, if the Grand Trunk Pacific had been allowed to build only from North Bay westward probably the country would have saved $100,000,000, and if the Grand Trunk Pacific had not been allowed to build at all,, the country would have saved $200,000,000. Not very long ago the Minister of Finance condemned the building of the line east of ' Cochrane. He said:
If a fraction of the money that has been spent on the National Transcontinental railway between Moncton and Cochrane had been spent for agriculture, I do not believe this question of the high cost of living would have been to the front to-day.
I am sorry that my hon. friend the Finance Minister is not in his seat, if he were, I would recall to him that in these words of his there is a little bit of demagogism. Let that pass to-day, we can meet again at. Phillipi. But there is the opinion of my [DOT]hon. friend the Minister of Customs, reflecting that of the whole Conservative party of Ontario, that the line should have been built from Cochrane westward, and that the whole line from Cochrane eastward should have been set aside. In dther words, .the opinion of the Conservative party in the province of Ontario was that we should have built the railway from the West to Cochrane, and.

then let the Grand Trunk Pacific bring the trade to tthe old Grand Trunk system with Portland as its terminus. We would have saved $100,000,000, says my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, but how much would we have lost of national honour, national profit and nationhood. I have to say to my hon. friend the Ministter oi Finance that there were overwhelming reasons why this road should have been built east of Cochrane, reasons of a local nature, and reasons of a national character. When we started the idea in 1903 there were many misgivings as to the character of the country which we would open north of the Laurentian mountains. It was supposed that that section of the country, which had up to that time been uninhabited, was uninhabitable, that it was a desert and could be nothing else. We had information, also, that in that section of the country there was a high plateau equal to any portion of the valley of the St. Lawrence or of the valley of the Great Lakes. We now know, the fact is beyond dispute at the present time, that there is a valley east and west of lake Abiti'bi, 700 miles long and between '60 and 100 miles in width, of the most fertile soil there is on this continent of America, which will grow everything that is grown in the valley of the St. (Lawrence or the valley of the Great Lakes except pears and peaches. We know that there are immense rivers flowing from the mountains towards Hudson bay with immense capacities of water-power development. We know, further, that the resources in pulpwood are incalculable, and that if the Governments of Quebec and Ontario are wise and understand how to husband their *wealth, these resources will be inexhaustible for all time. It is not a rash prediction to say at this moment that within the life of men now sitting in this [DOT]Chamber the greater proportion of the paper manufactured on the continent of America will be manufactured along that line of railway.
Sir, this being the character of the country, and for local reasons alone, setting aside for the moment any reason [DOT]of a national character, I ask the Minister *of Finance would it have been fair that we should have built that railway west -of Cochrane and left undeveloped that portion of the territory from the St. Lawrence to Cochrane? Would it have been fair that the province of Ontario

should have had the benefit of that development, and that the province of Quebec, which contributes its share to the revenue, should have been left behind? Sir, that would be intolerable to think of; and if the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs will reflect upon their language of the past, they will henceforth come to the conclusion that this line is one of the best portions of the Transcontinental railway.
What of the portion of the line from the St. Lawrence to Moncton? I had better first quote at length the conclusion
of the commissioners:
This commission does not think that the National Transcontinental railway should have been constructed east of L6vis, which was done at a cost of $35,000,000 first,-because the Government at that time had a railway in operation between L6vis and Moncton, the Intercolonial; second,-because the Nations* x ranscontinental railway would only be 33 miles shorter; third, -because the gradients on the National Transcontinental railway are greater than those on the Intercolonial railway; and fourth,-because the grades on the Intercolonial railway can be reduced to four-tenths per cent eastbound and six-tenths per cent westbound, whereas it is practically impossible, according to the construction of the National Transcontinental railway, to reduce the 1.10 per cent grade at 146 miles west of Moncton and the 1.10 per cent grade at lake Pohenagamook.
The traffic on the Intercolonial railway is such that it will in a short time be a business proposition to reduce its gradients which when completed will make it the low grade line between L6vis and Halifax, rather than by, way of the National Transcontinental railway, and it is inconceivable that the grade revisions on the Intercolonial railway above referred to will cost more than half of the amount of money expended in the construction of this portion of the National Transcontinental railway.
This is very positive language; but truth and justice will in the end prevail. Justice did prevail in the end, and the end is not far off. It comes in the next paragraph to which I invite the attention of the House. After the building of that section of the railway has been absolutely condemned by Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton, they go on to say:
While there may be some reason for the construction of a railway through the timber districts in the eastern portion of the province of Quebec, the construction of the railway from Edmundston to Moncton was not justifiable because of the lack of local business along this line which two years of operation has already proved.
After all, there was some local reason for building a railway through the timber districts in the eastern portion of Quebec. While there was some reason for the con-

struction of a railway through that portion of the province of Quebec, the railway should, according to the commissioners, have been left in the fields as the Intercolonial was at Levis years ago, and should not have been prolonged to a point where it could become a transcontinental railway. What sort of reasoning is that in the mouths of these commissioners? If I were to ask these commissioners what local traffic there is on the Canadian Pacific railway between Sudbury and Port Arthur on the lake Superior line, they would have to tell me that there is not one dollar of local traffic on that section of the road. But is that any reason why the Canadian Pacific railway should not have been built? If I were to ask these commissioners to show me one of the many transcontinental railways on this continent every inch of which is productive of local traffic, they would have to admit that there is not one. Could there be anything more partisan than this condemnation of the Transcontinental railway because 99 miles of it, or something like that, would not be productive of local traffic?
The commissioners have admitted that there might be some reason for the construction of a railway through the eastern portion of Quebec, and so there is. Many years ago a charter was given by this Parliament for the construction of a railway in that very section of country; and many years ago that very road was subsidized by the Parliament of this country. It is well known in Quebec that a respectable and powerful company, the Quebec Central Railway Company, was ready and anxious to build a railway in that district. Was it not better if there was need for a local railway that we should make it a part of the Transcontinental? But	all these
reasons of a local nature are superfluous in this debate. The day is past for criticising that enterprise. To-day the necessity of a railway from ocean to ocean and on Canadian soil is no longer disputed, it is admitted everywhere. It is not disputed in the city of Halifax, which has never received from the Intercolonial the share of the traffic of this continent to which it is entitled. It is not disputed in the city of St. John, which, to bring to its port the western trade, has made sacrifices of almost heroic proportions. It is not disputed in the city of Quebec, which has built its hopes of a new birth on this transcontinental railway. It is not disputed in Montreal, which is anxious to be 149
connected by branch lines with the trunk lines. It is not disputed in Winnipeg; it is not disputed in the western provinces, whose stupendous production is seeking an outlet in all directions, north, south, east and west. When we remember, as has been stated more than once on the floor of this House by my hon. friend from Edmonton, that this year we have
400.000.	000 bushels of grain with only
18.000. 000	acres under cultivation, And when it is remembered that we have
150.000.	000 acres immediately available for tillage, 'and another 150,000,000 fit for tillage with but little preparation, it is evident to any man who has a proper conception of Canada that we must have that railway in order tO' do justice to all parts of Canada. Such were the views which influenced us and such were the views which were not accepted by our opponents. If the Conservative party could not rise to the height of this conception perhaps it was more their misfortune than their fault, but it is their fault to-day if they degrade that road from the original conception of the Transcontinental railway simply to make it from Cochrane a local road; a branch for the *Canadian Pacific railway.
Some time after the Conservative party came into office we learnt that the character of the road was degraded, and momentum grades had been substituted for the uniform grade specified in the contract. I do not propose at this moment to enter into technicalities as to the effect of momentum grades, but there is one thing which I am going to state to the Government and upon which I impeach them, and it is that they have made those changes without consulting the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and have thereby given the Grand Trunk Pacific power to repudiate their part of the agreement.
When Major Leonard was appointed as commissioner of this railway we were told that at least we had a man of railway experience capable of dealing with these matters. His, it was said, was an experienced hand. We had a right to expect that when Major Leonard decided to change the grade of the railway and the character of the *road, he would take the trouble of getting the consent of the Grand Trunk railway which is to lease that road and have joint supervision of it. But we know from a letter addressed' by Mr. Chamberlin to the commission that no such precaution was taken. On the 18th day of July, 1912, the following letter was addressed to Major Leonard by Mr. E. -T. Chamberlin:



July 18, 1912.
Major E. W. Leonard,
Chairman, Transcontinental Commission, Ottawa, Ont.
Dear sir,-I learn from our engineers that the standard of work on that portion of the Transcontinental railway between Lake Superior Junction and Cochrane, which was at the outset adopted and has so far been complied with, is being departed from, and that instead of four-tenths grade and permanent structures, you have authorized grades up to one per cent and the erection of temporary wooden structures. In regard to this I would call attention to clause 7 of this agreement of the 29th July, 1913 which provides that the work of construction of the eastern division shall be done according to the specifications approved by the company and shall be subject to the joint supervision, inspection and acceptance of our chief engineer and the chief engineer of the commission. I beg to say if this work is done in accordance with what I understand to be your recent instructions, it will not be in compliance with the agreement nor satisfactory to this company and cannot be accepted.
Mark the words, and cannot be accepted! So, according to this, the Grand Trunk Pacific is at liberty to refuse that part of the road and the consequence will be that the traffic will go as far as Cochrane, then, instead of going to Quebec, will he turned to the right towards the old Grand Trunk system whose terminus is at Portland in American territory. We have had no reason yet assigned to show why this change should have taken place, except the reason of economy. How much has been economized upon that? We have not yet learned. The commission have told us that if momentum grades had been adopted, $6,000,000 would have been saved, but the commission has not told us, Major Leonard has not told us, the Minister of Railways and Canals has not told us, how much this change of grade has saved to the country. It would be a very small sum after all and for that small sum the future of the road is put in jeopardy.
Nor is that all. Since the commissioners set out to find fault with what has been done by the old commission and to show their extravagances, how is it that they have not set down as one of the extravagances of the commission the purchase of 300 acres of land at Cap Rouge at $350 an acre for the purpose of putting the workshops of the Transcontinental railway at Quebec? This selection was made at Cap Rouge as a site for the workshops. It is no longer an issue now. The Government is bound to build workshops upon that section of the road. That has been settled by the arbitration of Sir William Whyte. The old commission was to build the shops at Cap Rouge, but now Major Leonard has changed

the site to St. Malo. Two or three days ago the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) asked me if I was opposed to the transfer of the shops from Cap Rouge to St. Malo, and I understood the point of that question very well. The point is that St. Malo is in the constituency which it has been my pride to represent in this House for more than thirty years. I .could not very well understand the animus oi the hon. member but, Sir, my answer to his question is that if this transfer of the site is in the interests of the railway I am for it; if it is against the interests f the railway I am against it. The only guide I have in this matter, the only guide my electors, whom I know well, have in this matter is that we should do everything that can be done to make that railway a success and to give the city of Quebec the opportunity of having the trade which must come from the West over the road. That is the first, last, and only consideration. Whether the change is right or wrong I await the opinion of the engineers, and I want to know what the reasons are which induced the engineers to change the shops from Cap Rouge to St. Malo. Reasons there must be since we have now at the head of the commission an experienced railway man,-Major Leonard. I am sure that Major Leonard will explain to us what advantage there is to this railway in moving the shops, which are projected on the railway at Cap Rouge, a few rods only from the St. Lawrence, and putting them in the valley of the St. Charles at least eight miles from the railway. The shops to-day are not on the railway. Somebody may say: surely you do not mean to tell me that these shops destined for the Transcontinental railway are not upon the line of railway? I say they are at least eight miles from the line of railway and to get access to them a new line has to be built, or, as I am told, a tunnel has to be built. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) told us one day that he wanted to have a tunnel in order to find the heart of Quebec, and know where it is, and the Prime Minister told us also when he was in Quebec that we were to have a tunnel to communicate with the shops and the station. If this tunnel is built I understand that the distance will be shortened and that the shops will not be eight miles from the railway, but only about half a mile. At all events, that is the condition of things. But we must presume that it is all right, although it sounds very absurd, because it was done by a man of railway experience.
If it is all right to take these shops eight

miles away from the line of railway and put them in the valley of the St. Charles instead of in the valley of the St. Lawrence, then, Sir, we must condemn the commission for having spent $100,000 in buying the site for the=e shops at Cap Rouge.
But that is not all. There is also to be a station somewhere in Quebec. The late commission had selected the Champlain market site for the station, a site at the very point where the line reaches the St. Lawrence, and if the station had been put there, passengers could leave the station and walk directly on the steamer. Now it appears that a new arrangement has been made with tiie Canadian Pacific Railway Company whereby there shall be no station on Cham plain market, but the station shall be at the Palais, in the valley of the St. Charles, a considerable distance from the Champlain market. The site of the Champlain market had not been selected at haphazard; the commission had taken every precaution to select the proper place for the station. In the month of October, 1906, the following circular was issued by Mr. Parent:
Ottawa, October 2, 1906.
Dear Sirs:-
Re Quebec Terminals.
1 have the honour by direction of the board to advise you that the commissioners have had under consideration the matter of terminals at the city of Quebec for the National Transcontinental railway, but consider it desirable, before making a recommendation to the Government of Canada on this important question, to obtain an expression of opinion from the accredited representatives of the railway and steamship companies having interests in the city of Quebec, the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, and the Quebec Board of Trade, on the question of joint terminals.
The commissioners have accordingly arranged to be in the city of Quebec on Friday, the 12th instant, and would be pleased if your corporation would have a representative present to discuss the matter. The meeting will take place at the Transcontinental railway offices, 147 Mountain Hill, in the city of Quebec, at 10 a.ni., Friday, October 12 instant.
Besides the Quebec Bridge and Railway Company, the following corporations have been invited to send representatives to the meeting: The Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk railway, the Intercolonial railway, the Delaware and Hudson railway, the Great Northern railway, the Quebec Central railway, the Quebec and Lake St. John railway, the Quebec Railway, Light and Power Company, the Allan Steamship Line, the Dominion Line, the Leland Line, the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, the Quebec Transport Company, Limited, Mr. E. C. Fry, Lloyds agent, etc., the mayor of the city of Quebec, the chairman of the Quebec Board of Trade, the chairman of the Quebec Shipping interests, Mr. Power, M.P., Quebec West, and Arthur Lachance, M.P., Quebec Centre, have also been invited to be present.
149i
All the parties here invited, except the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, were present on the day mentioned, and a motion was passed referring the matter to a large committee, which in turn appointed a sub-committee, which consulted agents, and made a report. On the 20th day of November, a month later, the committee met again, and on that occasion the Canadian Pacific railway was represented by Mr. McNicoll, and the following resolution was then adopted:
Recommended that the Champlain market be made the passenger and freight station for the present, at the same time contemplating that at a future date a passenger station be built on the upper level of the city. Recommended that a terminal company be formed by the different railways using the terminals to take over the bridge and its approaches and all the terminals. That part of the cost be assumed by the Government and part by the railways interested as may be agreed upon hereafter, and that legislation be passed at this session of Parliament to sanction such an agreement.
Acting upon this unanimous resolution of all the interests of the city of Quebec, the Champlain market was determined upon as the station, after numerous and complicated negotiations with the city of Quebec. When we went out of office, plans were ready, tenders had been asked for and the contract was signed for the completion of that station. That contract has been cancelled by the present Government in order to have the station not in the valley of the river St. Lawrence but in the valley of the river St. Charles in conjunction with the Canadian Pacific railway. What reason can be assigned for such a change ? I have yet to hear a single valid reason why the Transcontinental railway should lie made an adjunct, a branch line, of the Canadian Pacific railway. If there is to be a joint station, I could understand why the joint station should not be in the valley of the St. Charles river, but in the valley of the St. Lawrence river, in the vicinity of the Champlain market; but to carry the station from the St. Lawrence river over the other side of the hill, into the valley of the St. Charles river, is putting a blemish on this great national enterprise.
What lias been done since then ? Three years or more have elapsed, and to-day, if I am correctly informed, the plans are not yet prepared for the building of a station at the Palais. Two days ago the following paragraph appeared in the Quebec Daily Telegraph:
Quebec may secure the desired union railway .station-some time.
That is right.
