speechtext:
I wish to tell the hen.
gentleman who made that statement, whoever he may be, that Messrs. Gutelius and Lynch-Staunton are equal in character, reputation, and record to any hon. gentleman on the other side of the House, bar none, from the highest to the lowest; and, that their character, their reputation and their record can be compared favourably with those who have assailed them in this House.
Now, just one or two observations with regard to these gentlemen. There are some
hon. gentlemen in this House, I do not know whether they knew better or not-my right hon. friend did not go quite that far, but he did carry an insinuation along the same line-who sought to impress the idea upon the people of this country that ordinary usage had been departed from in that these gentlemen had not been sworn to the faithful performance, of their duties. The right hon. gentleman avoided saying that directly, though he endeavoured to insinuate it, but he knew better, as did others on that side of the House I desire to say that the statute under which these gentlemen were appointed makes no provision for having them sworn, and my right hon. friend knew that when he made the insinuation. I challenge my right hon. friend to name one Royal Commission appointed during his fifteen years of office the members of which were sworn, and so I hope we shall not hear more of any such suggestion.
The character and record of these gentlemen have been condemned, hut the highest tribute that could be paid to the thoroughness of their work is the bitterness of the attack that has been made upon them. We were told by the hon. member for South Renfrew that the report is so contradictory and partisan on its face that it condemns itself and requires no refutation, and yet the hon. gentleman spoke for seven hours in a most unsuccessful and vain attempt to refute it. The character of the two gentlemen is called into question by hon. gentlemen opposite. Mr. Lynch-Staunton is a lawyer in the province of Ontario who, in the eyes of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, hears the unspeakable disgrace of being a member of the Conservative party. That, of course, was enough to condemn him in their eyes from the first, but, so far as I am aware, no suspicion of a reproach has ever been levelled against George Lynch-Staunton in respect of his personal or professional career. Mr. Gutelius was in a still more perilous position, ior he had to endure the misfortune of having been horn in the United States, and, .according to the expressed assertion or direct insinuation of many hon. gentlemen opposite, his report is absolutely untrustworthy for that reason. There are in this country many thousands of citizens of Canada -men in the East and men in the West-who were born in the United States

of America,- and I do not think we have any better citizens than the hundreds of thousands who have come to Canada from the United States during recent years. [DOT]But, according to the conception of hon. gentlemen on the Liberal benches, these men are to be regarded with disdain and to be looked upon as objects of abuse; and their statements are to be considered as absolutely untrustworthy because originally they were citizens of the United States, although they have seen fit to become good citizens of Canada, and to participate with us in the abundant opportunities which here reward their industry and intelligence. When hon. gentlemen in this House, whoever they may be, descend to argument or suggestion of that kind, it is very evident to me that their case is overwhelmingly weak.
It has been suggested that these two gentlemen were particularly under the influence of the Minister of Railways and Canals. One hon. gentleman told us that Mr. Gutelius was a personal friend of the Minister of Railways and Canals, and that therefore he would be sure to do whatever the Minister of Railways would desire. As a matter of fact, Mr. Gutelius had never met Mr. Cochrane until he was called to his office for the purpose of inquiring whether he would take up certain duties in connection with the Intercolonial railway, and undertake the investigation which has been carried out by Mr. Lynch-Staunton and himself.
Reference has been made to the supposed partisan character of this report and to the fact that Mr. George Lynch-Staunton. being a member of the Liberal-Conservative party, could not be supposed to be capable of making an impartial and judicial examination of this question. I would like to remind hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House that when certain matters were under discussion in 1908 and again in 1910, and when we moved for a Royal Commission, on both occasions the whole question was relegated to the investigation and consideration and report of a committee, first upon the Hodgins charges, and then upon the Lumsden charges. The majority of the Committee in both cases was of course composed o.f Liberal members. May I ask those who have put forward this charge whether or not the hon. gentlemen on the other side who constituted the majority of that committee and made the majority report, were partisans, and if so, 
whether their reports were absolutely untrustworthy? Hon. gentlemen are on one of the two horns of the dilemma; either the investigations which they held in 1908 and 1910 were, according to their own statement, a mere mockery, or, on the other hand, their assertion that Mr. George Lynch-Staunton's report is partisan because he is a Conservative, does not stand. I desire to add in this connection that so long as hon. gentlemen opposite remained in power, they deliberately and successfully attempted, from first to last, to burke every investigation demanded by the Conservatives. Investigation was burked in 1908; it was burked again in 1910; and when, after it was burked in 1910 before a Committee of this House, we came solemnly before Parliament and asked that a Royal Commission be appointed to investigate the matter, what was the answer? Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House stood by and voted it down, and if these gentlemen who are now in the shades of Opposition had remained in power there would never have been any investigation of the Transcontinental railway. No one knows that better than my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). It is somewhat amusing to hear these hon. gentlemen talk now. All this story of overbreak, of excessive classification, of waste, extravagance and unjustifiable expenditure, was put forward by the officials of the- Grand Trunk Pacific railway; put forward over and over again through the letters of Mr. Woods, their chief e-ngi-neer; put forward over and over again and brought to the attention of the Government, and now, after the work has been almost wholly completed, what answer is given to us by some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House? The answer is, that the hour is past when any effective investigation can be held. Vote down an investigation when there is an opportunity of doing it in the most effective way, then, when the time is past when it can be done effectively, stand up and say: it is too late now; we voted you down when there was an opportunity of holding an investigation, and now the facts can never be disclosed. If hon. gentlemen on the other side are satisfied with their attitude in that regard, I for one cannot congratulate them upon it.
My right hon. friend has not gone so minutely into this report as did the hon. member for South Renfrew, but he said sufficient to make it clear that he possesses very much less knowledge of the evidence and of the report itself, than even he

possessed in 1903 with regard to the cost of the National Transcontinental railway. My hon. friends on the other side of the House do not agree very well among themselves. Some of them say there should have been no investigation; some of them say there should have been an investigation; some of them say there should have been an investigation by a committee of the House, although in 1908 they burked any such investigation for the alleged reason that it should be carried out by experts, and not by a committee of the House. Some of them say it should be by a Royal Commission, and some of them say the contrary. Thus it will be seen they are not very well agreed among themselves; but I suppose I may accept the statement of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, who told us frankly to-night that in his judgment there ought to have been an investigation, although he finds fault with the personnel of the commission. May I ask him why he did not appoint a commission in 1908 or 1910 when these charges were brought to his attention? To-night he says there should be an investigation, and is it not a fair question to ask him: Why did you not give the investigation when in 1910 we asked you to investigate, and when you had the power to name the personnel of the commission yourself? My right hon. friend is silent. Let me give the answer for him. It is that he never intended, had he been returned to power, to have any investigation.
I think that hon. gentlemen opposite, after all, should be rather grateful to this commission, and I shall tell them why. They ought to be grateful because the commission has shown that if proper care and supervision had been exercised, and if the Transcontinental commissioners had been of the right stamp, the right hon. gentleman and his Minister of Finance would have been out in their estimate of the cost only 200 per cent instead of 300 per cent. The commission have shown that this road might have been built for $120,000,000 instead of $160,000,000, but of course there does come the sting that the commission assert that the remaining $40,000,000 was needlessly spent and represents the waste and extravagance that was practised by their commission; and practised, as it would appear from the record, entirely with their concurrence and approval. The situation
reminds me of an incident that once took place in a Nova Scotia court. A solicitor had put in a defence in an action against him upon a promissory note. He declared that he had signed the promissory note as accommodation for another person and under an agreement by which the plaintiff had agreed to give to him all his legal business in consideration of his becoming surety upon the note. The judge who tried the ease decided as a matter of fact that no such agreement had ever been made. The case went on appeal before Mr. Justice Thomson, who, in giving judgment, dilated upon the disgraceful character of the defence, and said something like this: The learned judge, in his effort to save the defendant from the disgrace of his defence, found it necessary to disbelieve his evidence on oath. And so, this commission, in its endeavour to show that this road could have been built for only double the estimate of the late Government, found it necessary to show that that Government had been guilty of a great deal of waste and extravagance and negligence, to say the least.
What were the conditions in 1903 when my right hon. friend undertook to build the Transcontinental railway? We had the Canadian Pacific railway, a well established transcontinental road; we had in the West the Canadian Northern railway, recognized as a considerable system with no connections in the East; we had the Grand Trunk railway, a great railway system in the East with no connections in the West; and we had the Intercolonial railway, connecting Quebec, and, to a certain extent Ontario, with the Maritime provinces. The Canadian Pacific railway had experienced many vicissitudes but it had then become firmly established. My right hon. friend has paid himself the compliment of saying that he undertook the project of building another transcontinental railway. I will go a little fartner and say that in 1903 or 1904 or thereabouts, he embarked upon the project of building two additional transcontinental railways. I say that, because, in 1903, 1904, 1905, 1906, 1908, 1909, 1910, and last but not least 1911, the Canadian Northern railway, under legislation passed by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, had acquired the status of a transcontinental railway, and they expressly and definitely recognized it as such in an Act which they passed in 1911. The Canadian Northern railway had established itself in the western part of Canada.

and had four thousand or five thousand miles of line. The Grand Trunk railway in the east of Canada had many lines of railway, and a great mileage, but it had no connection in the West. Thus the question arose as to another national transcontinental railway, and as to the connection of the Canadian Northern railway with the East, and as to the connection of the Grand Trunk railway with western Canada. My right hon. friend embarked upon his policy, and I then suggested to this House, on more than one occasion, that whatever was done with regard to the development of further transcontinental railways in Canada, the six hundred or eight hundred miles north of lake Superior ought to be eliminated, so far as the cost of carriage was concerned, so that the West would be brought close to the East, in the way of transportation; and the tolls otherwise payable over that six hundred or eight hundred miles of uninhabited territory, affording no local traffic for the present at least, would be absolutely abolished. My right lion, .friend has referred to that mileage here to-night. Let me say to him that while it was undoubtedly necessary to have one railway through that country, I would think that any government might very well pause before embarking upon the project of building three railways across eight hundred miles of such territory. When my right hon. friend speaks of binding Canada together by transcontinental railways, no project could have more usefully served that purpose than to have acquired one national transcontinental railway across that area of eight hundred miles, double tracked, if you like, as traffic developed, and to have that line of railway operated free of cost to the producers of Canada, whether in the East or in the West. By such a policy it was entirely open to my right hon. friend to have' done infinitely more to build up the national ports of Quebec, St. John, and Hailfax, and to bring the East and West of Canada together, than by the plan he did decide upon.
Let us leave that for a moment and see [DOT]whether there was any need for an investigation into the proceedings of the National Transcontinental Railway Commission. My right hon. friend, in 1903, and his followers throughout the country, said that Canada was to have a national transcontinental railway for $13,000,000.
My right hon. friend did not mean that the cost of the road would be $13,000,000, but he did intend to say that the actual cash outlay to Canada, for interest during the seven year period of no rental, after 
the completion of this road, would be no more than $13,000,000.. I have in my hands one of the campaign documents, issued in the election of 1904, wherein it is boldly stated that Canada under the policy of the Laurier Government was to have a transcontinental railway for $13,000,000. If at that time my right hon. friend had said $300,000,000 instead of $13,000,000 his followers would not have cheered so lustily. What was their estimate? His Minister of Finance estimated the .cost at $61,415,000 for a road with 0.4 per cent grades and 6 degrees of curvature. It has cost $100,000,000 more. Why? I would have thought that the hon. member for South Renfrew, and particularly the right hon. gentleman himself who boasts of being the author of that project, would have taken some portion of their time tonight in explaining to the people of Canada why that road exclusive altogether of interest has cost $100,000,000 more than they said it would cost. Mark you, there was no question about it -in the House, and there was no question about it in the country. Let me quote from that campaign document :
The feature of the bargain in regard to which most of this is done is the financial arrangement. It is an actual fact, an indisputable fact, that $13,000,000 will cover every cent of the country's expense in connection with the railway.
An indisputable fact indeed! It has cost in all $300,000,000. It has cost without consideration of interest or rental $100,000,000 more than their estimate. My right hon. friend sat down after a two-hours' speech in which he gave not a single word of explanation as to the increased cost. It is right that the people of Canada at the present time, when this Administration has a certain responsibility for that which has been bequeathed to them as a legacy from their predecessors, should know just what this road is costing Canada, and what it is likely to cost Canada in the future. My hon. friend boasts of the bargain as a monument to his wisdom and foresight. The road from Moncton to Winnipeg, according to the engineers appointed by my right hon. friend, will cost $161,307,800. The construction will cover a period of eleven years and for the purposes of estimating interest I take four and a half years as an average which, at 3| per cent amount to $27,220,670, or a total of $188,528,470. I have taken my estimate of the rate of interest from the permanent officials of the Department of Finance. Everything here that does not appear in the record I have taken from the

report made to me by permanent officials of the Government of Canada who were also permanent officials under the Administration of my right hon. friend. Add to the $188,526,470, seven years' interest during which no rental is payable, which amounts to $47,488,729, and you have a total cost, when the road is taken over and interest begins to be payable, of $238,017,199. this country under the bargain made by my right hon. friend must pay without recourse on the bonds guaranteed on the mountain section ($56,342,000), interest at 3 per cent for seven years, which amounts to $11,831,820. The country must also pay the cost of implementing the bonds under the agreement of 1904, clause 8, which will probably amount to to about $12,000,000, but which I am placing at the lowest estimate, $10,000,080. This gives a total of $259,929,019, which does not include the Quebec bridge, the cost of which has been placed at $17,000,000; it does not include the interest for three years on $188,528,470 at 3^ per cent in case the net earnings of the eastern division are not sufficient to pay that rental, which would amount to $21,209,343, these two amounts totalling $38,209,343. Thus we have a grand total of $298,138,462 as the actual cost to the country of a road that was to be built at an actual outlay to Canada of $13,000,000. If the seven years' interest during the non-rental period were capitalized at the end of that period, the last item of interest would be $26,766,937, bringing the grand total up to $303,70o,976, and that would not be an unfair method of computation.
I have not taken into account the fact that there will be in future a one per cent loss on the rental, because while we receive 3 per cent we must pay 4 per cent, and, that being capitalized, as pointed out by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), would amount to $4o,000,000.
I have not taken into account the loans, $25,000,000, and the guarantee Am the western section, $70,000,000.
So I think under the circumstances my right hon. friend will agree that the estimate which he made in 1903 was very misleading to the people of this country, and that he carried the general election of 1904 upon statements which have been absolutely and wholly falsified by the actual facts.
Under these circumstances, is there any man in this House, or is there any man in Canada, who will say to me that it was not the absolute duty of this Government
upon obtaining offioe to make a thorough and impartial inquiry as to why the cost of this road was so enormously in excess of that which my right hon. friend declared in 1903. And. let it be borne in mind that when we suggested in 1903 that no survey had been made, that the country had not been explored, and that my right hon. friend was taking a leap in the dark, his only answer was to point to a number of documents on the table and to inform us on this side of the House that we had mountains of information. The mountains of information were evidently not of a very reliable quality.
I place the situation before the country to-night, as one for which the present Administration is not responsible. We raised our voices against it in speech and by vote; we declared that before this project was undertaken there should be a reasonable businesslike inquiry, and that the highest eloquence and the most glowing periods of my right hon. friend in his speech in 1903 were a poor substitute for the reasonable businesslike inquiry which any reasonable man in this country would have insisted upon in respect of his own affairs.
My hon. friend the member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) has gone into the question of responsibility. He said that for everything but $98,000,000, I think, the present Administration is absolutely responsible. As I understand him, $105,000,000 had been paid out before we came into power, and, further, a great deal of work had been done which was not paid for. But does the hon. member for Pictou or any other hon. gentleman in this House suppose that the mere fact of a change of Administration enables the Government of the country to destroy or nullify contracts which have been solemnly entered into by their predecessors? Let us look at that idea for a moment. Suppose the directors of a bank undertook to erect a very expensive bank building, and made a contract for its erection, and that at the next meeting of the shareholders they were turned out of office as hon. gentlemen opposite went out of office in 1911; and suppose that the new directors said to the persons with whom the former directors had made a binding contract: We will not pay you, we were not the directors at that time. Could any one, whether lawyer or layman, have so little comprehension of the binding effect of a legal contract as to put forward any such argument? Yet that is precisely

the argument that was put forward by my hon. friend from Pictou. Absurdity can -go no farther. When these hon. gentlemen, in 1905 and 1906, made contracts and bound this country to these contracts, it would be absolute repudiation if we attempted to get rid of them, and, even if we attempted to repudiate, the courts of the country would not permit us, as the hon. member for Pictou and his friends know perfectly well-
The hon. member for Pictou and other hon. members have referred to the personnel of the old commission. I was going to say a word or two with regard to that, but the hour is late and I shall refrain. All I have to say is this: If Sir Thomas Shaughnessy and Mr. Chamberlin when commencing to build a railway should employ a dry goods merchant, a druggist, and a barber to supervise the work, they would be pursuing very much the same course as was pursued by the late Administration!, for the Minister of Railways and Canals stood in the same position in regard to the National Transcontinental railway as Sir Thomas Shaugh-nessy would stand in regard to the construction of any new line of the Canadian Pacific railway. These hon. gentlemen have attacked Mr. Leonard on the ground, forsooth, that lie had had no experience.
I have a letter under my hand which shows that Mr. Leonard, for twenty-five years before he undertook this work, was engaged continuously in railway construction and operation, and I doubt if you could find any morn in Canada who has had a longer experience in that work than the man whom my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane) selected as chairman of the National Transcontinental Railway Commission.
I did intend to go into this report to some extent had time permitted, but my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro), my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) and other hon, gentlemen on this side of the House have dealt with it very fully indeed. I have read this report carefully, and I have listened patiently to the criticisms that have been made on it. It may be that here and there yon may be able to put your finger on some trifling error or inadvertence, and it would be singular indeed if such were not the case, as these commissioners, like all the rest of us, are merely human. But in the [Mr. Borden. J
face of everything that has been stated to the contrary by hon. gentlemen on the other- side of the House, and after listening most carefully to what they have had to say, I assert most confidently, and I am prepared to back this assertion by argument wherever necessary, that the report from begining to end, is substantially correct in every important particular. I am not now referring to questions of law or questions of policy, into which the commissioners have gone to some extent, but to the findings of fact. In so far as questions of law in regard to the Transcopta shops are concerned, the commissioners have stated frankly the opinion of the Minister of J ustice, and Mr. Lynch-Staun-ton has disagreed with it. My right hon. friend and the hon. member for South Renf-ew seem to think that if Mr. George Lynch-Staunton entertained a conscientious opinion in regard to that he should have suppressed it, but I say that it was his duty to state it. In regard to the line from Quebec to Moncton, Mr. Lynch-Staunton has differed from views which I have publicly expressed in this House and on the platform but, I do not hold Mr. Lynch-Staunton in fault for that, in so far as he has felt himself called upon to make any statement in regard to the matter. I point out, that this very fact shows that these gentlemen were not under the control or influence of the Government, and that they iwere free to express their own thought and belief.
My right hon. friend and the hon,. member for South Renfrew reproached us for circulating and publishing this report. What were we to do with the report when it came in? Were we to hide it? It might have been very consoling to them if we had adopted that course, but was it, or was it not, our duty to bring it down and lay it on the table of the House? What is behind this cry about our circulating the report and publishing it? These hon. gentlemen are very mucn concerned about the report because it justly reflects upon their administration of public affairs, and they can be excused for being a little insistent and a little angry. But. I would like to say that if there was in the report, from first to last, as glaring a mis-statement as I heard from my right hon. friend to-night, I would send that report back for correction, or I would suppress it. He has stated that 250,000 copies of the report have been printed by the Government and circulated throughout the country. The actual facte are that

10,000 copies in English and 4,000 copies in French have been printed and my right bon. friend is only about 2,000 per cent out of the way in his statement.
Some reference has been made to the McArthur payment. While I had intended to go over some other mattters, I will not detain the House farther than to deal with that. It has been stated that the commissioners should be condemned because the Government have made a certain settlement with Mr. McArthur, who had contract No. 21. I am very g^d that, first, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), secondly, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and, lastly, the right hon. leader of the Opposition have made some allusion to this, because it enables me to give a certain object lesson to the country and to the House, as to the actual results of the policy carried out by the late Administration. After certain questions had been raised as to over-classification and overbreak, an arbitration took place between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government. If I remember correctly, that arbitration was carried out by Mr. fcelliher, Mr. Collingwood Schreiber, and Mr. Gordon Grant.
As a result of that arbitration deductions were made in the contractor's estimate- of February, 1911, amounting to $512,821.16. It appears from some figures given by my right hon. friend that the deduction in respect to the work done up to the arbitration was only some $429,000, and I suppose the increased amount of $512,821.16 was due to some further estimates made afterwards in respect to which a like deduction was made. Mr. Gordon Grant, on January 23, 1913, submitted to the commissioners Mr. J. D. McArthur's final estimates on that part of the contract extending from mile 2.8 to mile 242. On the same date the board passed a resolution, which I have here, and as it is a matter of some importance, I think I had better place it upon 'Hansard.'

/I will not go into the report. I had intended to do so, but the hour is late. Let me say in conclusion: The Government finds itself confronted with the problem of seeing to the completion of two transcontinental railways which were initiated, supported, subsidized and guaranteed by our predecessors in office. We are confronted with the question of seeing them completed or of leaving them uncompleted. The responsibility for initiating the policy which has brought about that condition and for imposing this problem upon the country rests upon those who were then in office and are now in Opposition. But the responsibility for dealing with the situation which they created rests, as it presents itself to-day, upon the Administration. We are not afraid of that responsibility, and we shall deal with it as best we may. In dealing with it, especially in so far as it involves contractual or semi-contractual obligations affecting the public interest, we have to take into account the fact that as ' the King never dies,' so the King's Government never ceases though one party may go out of power and another party may come in. We shall give to the situation, which we did not create and which was brought about against our vote and our protest, the best of our energy and the best of our efforts with a full and abiding sense of the responsibility that rests upon us as trustees for the people of Canada.

Post Office Department-Contingencies- Clerical and other assistance, $15,133.32.

Before the minister takes up his main Estimates, he ought to respond to the Orders of the House and bring down the returns that have been ordered. The returns that are brought down from his department are different from those of the other departments. Every one of his returns is carefully edited; somebody goes over them carefully and abstracts letters which are frequently necessary in order to carry on the sense of the correspondence. Where the Postmaster General is shown by the file to have written a letter, the letter in reply to which it is written is frequently not on the file. Often these missing letters contain the essence of the whole matter, and the file becomes absolutely unintelligible owing to their absence.
Of course, the standing instruction^ are that private correspondence should remain on the private file, and public correspondence on the public file.
You did not observe that rule in the Department of Labour; you did not observe it in regard to me, but brought down letters marked private when it suited you to do so.

I cannot follow what my hon. friend says as regards the Department of Labour. I am informed by my friend the Prime Minister that the right hon. leader of the Opposition has made a general complaint about that. Hon. gentlemen behind my hon. friend will bear me out that if they write about any return which is incomplete we try to supply the information required. In a large department like the post office, a document may be easily overlooked, but we are always glad to supply any information that may have been omitted by the officers preparing the files. If *my hon. friend will let me know what returns he particularly wishes, I shall take special trouble to press the matter and have the returns prepared. A member of the Opposition has a right to receive returns containing information desired before the Estimates are discussed. Owing to the large number of returns ordered from my department, we have not yet taken up my Estimates. We are well under way in that respect, and hope to take them up before very long. If there are any special files not yet brought down and especially needed, I shall do my level best to meet the wishes of hon. gentlemen.

I quite agree that it it not expedient, when an Order of the House is issued, that private correspondence and communications from representatives in Parliament should be brought down. I merely wish to observe that when the hon. gentleman's colleague the Minister of Labour produced to this House certain private letters I wrote to a previous' minister, that exemplary rule was broken. I made no complaint at the time because I had no objection to the correspondence being made public, but several hon. members in this House regarded it as a very peculiar circumstance. When my hon. friend brings down a return in answer to an order of this House and produces a letter written by himself, or an official of his department referring to another document which he has received from somebody, when that latter document is not brought down the whole thing becomes unintelligible. Whoever in the hon. gentleman's department is responsible for this matter should comply with the order of the House in making the return.

Since the Postmaster General is willing to revise some of the incomplete returns brought down, might I ask him to add to the return brought down the other day about the-purchase of a parcel post and rural mail boxes a list of the

members of the House who were canvassed by 'the department in regard to the choice of boxes. I understand that about seven boxes were inspected in the office of the superintendent, Mr. Bolduc. Mr. Bolduc says that he took a canvas of ninety-two members of the House and the majority reported in favour of a certain box. I would like to know the names of the members consulted. I have asked several members on this side of the House but they have not been asked to pass judgment upon the boxes. I think Mr. Bolduc should give a list of the names.
I understand my hon. friend to say that Mr. Bolduc said so many members were canvassed,, but that he did not give the names.

Yes. He said that over ninety members had been consulted. I do not object to that, it is only fair that the members should see the boxes. Some years ago we had the boxes in room 96. where all the members could see them. Mr. Bolduc says in this case that of the ninety odd members canvassed, seventy-five were in favour of a certain box.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Regarding these boxes I may say that I was not invited to go in to see them, but I happened to be in there one day and Mr. Bolduc asked my opinion.
Perhaps ' canvas ' was not the proper word for me to use. I meant that the opinion of the members was invited.

I told Mr. Bolduc, who is the head of the rural mail branch, that as the boxes were for the benefit of the farmers of the country he might show them to members coming into his * office in order to get their opinions as to the best box. I did not ask him to keep a list of the members who saw the boxes. I simply asked him to take their opinions so as to find out which box suited them best.
Will the hon. gentleman take the opinion of members as to the establishment of rural mail routes, or does he confine himself merely to our opinion as to the value of the boxes ?
I am always glad to hear opinions on both matters. What is the complaint about the routes P

Rural mail routes are in the interest of the whole community, Liberal and Conservative alike, and I want to know why members are not consulted 150
as to the establishment of these routes, since you are willing they should be consulted as to the kind of boxes. In my constituency the member was not consulted, but a man not even a candidate, was consulted. I wouild not like to give my opinion on the rural mail boxes at least, if I am not to be consulted as to routes.

The choice of a route is left with the inspector or one of his officers. He is supposed to consult the gentlemen who have signed the petition to have the .route. I have not had any complaint, so far, that the members have not been consulted.
1 a.m. Mr. MARCIL: If you do not
want the members to take any interest in the adoption of these routes, you are going the right way about it.
Might I be permitted to say that previous to 1911 the Liberal Government did not consult the member of a constituency as to mail routes, if he happened to be a Conservative.
You have now the opportunity to improve on that.

I am glad that my hon. friend thinks that method could be improved on. I am just giving my hon. friend the facts.
Administration of Justice-Further amount required, ?3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is required on account of the expenses incurred in connection with the penitentiary investigation.
I understand that an investigation was conducted into the fire at St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, and that there was also an investigation at Kingston. To which does my hon. friend refer ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This bears on the investigation at Kingston.

I think the minister
might leave this item over if it is to do with the commission appointed to investigate conditions in our various penitentiaries. The hon. minister said he would leave one item over until the report came down. I do not feel like voting an amount to pay the expenses of this commission before I .see that report. I think I am taking a reasonable ground in making that objection. I am very doubtful if the commission. will b,e entitled to any pay. Of course, that is not an opinion in which a great many would concur. If this item fixes the amount that these men are to be



paid for their work I do not think it should (go through. I would like to know what amount these commissioners are to receive?

Does my hon. friend
want it struck out?

No, I do not feel that it should be struck out but I think that I am perfectly entitled to ask that the item which goes to pay the expenses of this commission should not he passed: until the commission has completed its work and presented its report.
Unless the report is satisfactory to you, you are not satisfied that the commissioners should' be paid?

The hon. gentleman
need not put words into my mouth that I do not utter. I will say all that I have to say without his assistance.
I put that question in the tone of inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There can be no possible objection to affording ever opportunity for discussing any question in connection with the penitentiary investigation. There are items in the main Estimates that are yet to be dealt with and they will afford that opportunity. This particular $3,000 is asked for as an addition to the sum voted for miscellaneous expenditures. The reason why our $10,000 vote for miscellaneous expenditure proved insufficient was that the expenses of the commission had to be met and they were not expected. The expenses of the commission have been incurred and have, in large measure, been paid in the course of the past year and we are dealing with the Supplementary Estimates for the year which has just expired. That is the only reason Why there is any desire to pass this item now.
The passing of this item would have nothing to do with fixing the amount they will be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The amount that they were to be paid was fixed at a. certain rate per day together with a certain allowance for travelling expenses.
What was the per diem allowance of the commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
$15 a day and $5 a day
for living allowance in addition to actual travelling expenses.

I do not think that is an exorbitant amount to pay commissioners 
if they are any good, but in this pirticular case I do not think these men are worth 15 cents a day.
What are the names of the commissioners?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. G. M. Macdonnell,
K.C., Dr. Etherington, Kingston, and Mr. J. P. Downey, Orillia.

And they are not worth
15 cents a day?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I can say that I am not willing to concur in that suggestion.
Mr. Downey is the superintendent of the Orillia asylum?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

How much has the commission cost? There is some reason for the request of the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edvrards) although I would not be prepared to say that these commissioners were not worth 15 cents a day when the Government paid these other two gentlemen $65 a day. You are closing up the arrangement with these commissioners as I understand it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The report of the commissioners has not come in, so that their work is not absolutely completed. This is to cover the expenses incurred in the year that has expired.

How much have they
received?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
When will this report
be brought down? Will there be an item in the minister's Estimates under which we can discuss the report and the remuneration of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not actually received the report yet. As soon as I have received it and have had time to take communication of it it will be brought down.
I am expecting it every day. I was told that I might expect it about the middle of the month of March but it has not reached me yet. I understand that it is actually in process of being typewritten. As to there being an item, I have no doubt there will be some balance to be paid to them which will, of course, be in the Estimates for the coming year. In any event there.are Estimates dealing with the expenditure on penitentiaries and I can assure the hon. gentleman that there will be no objection to his discussing this matter fully on any item.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I anticipate that they will be expected to be paid for the time that they actually devote to the preparation of their report. I have not yet seen the report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It covers simply what has already been paid to them in the past fiscal year.
Paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That means the amount paid against the appropriation for the expenses of the commission, that is to say for their per diem allowance.
What further amounts will be required to meet the expenses of this commission? It seems to be a pretty' large amount for so unimportant an item as it appears to be 150i

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I cannot give any
amounts that would be accurate enough to be worth while. When the hon. member speaks of this as an unimportant item, he does not realize that the work of this commission was not merely an investigation of the conduct of the officials in one penitentiary, although that was an important feature of it. The commissioners were charged with making a general study and investigation of penitentiary systems in addition to that, and to make a general Teport of possible improvements to penitentiary systems.
Have the commissioners been to the Dorchester penitentiary? If not, is it their intention to go there?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They have not been to the Dordhester penitentiary, and there is no intention that they should go there. They are investigating the conduct of officials in the Kingston penitentiary.
What was the cost to the country in connection with the Harry Thaw case at Sherbrouke?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not the information. It would not come within the business of the Department of Justice to deal with that cost. [DOT]
Exchequer Court of Canada-Contingencies,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A lawsuit was taken against Judge Clement and we were given judgment for the amount.

Does the
fact of having had a judgment against Judge Clement free him from criminal proceedings being taken against any individual under the same circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The fact that he is a judge does not free him from his responsibility; but whilst the case was being tried, before the Supreme Court, it has been shown that it was by some kind of a mistake that the amount had been drawn by Judge Clement.

Dominion Police-Retiring gratuity to constable E. Spenard, '$1,764.17.
Does that item indicate a new principle?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, the law does not
provide a gratuity for the Dominion police, but it is the established custom to pay one. This particular man has served for almost thirty years and is now pronounced physically unfit for duty.
Penitentiaries, $120,000.

I think we are entitled to some explanation on the various amounts.
. .Mr. DOHEIRTY: The supplementaries are larger than usual, because the requirements for the last fiscal year have been considerably under-estimated.
Mr,. BUREAU:	In what particular
branch? I just want to know if it is salaries, repairs, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In connection with the estimates of the cost of living, providing food, fuel, etc. The estimates last year were made by a gentleman who is not now an inspector, who, although he has been an Inspector for a number of years, has not usually prepaied these estimates and who apparently under-estimated the expense of providing for the food of the prisoners, for the heating of the premises, etc.
Is there not for each of these institutions a fixed annual cost to which the minister must adhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Our population is sometimes larger one year than another year and sometimes we get certain articles cheaper [DOT]one year than another year. It is quite [DOT]impossible to say it is going to cost so much a year to feed the inhabitants of a penitentiary.
That does not explain the whole of the $120,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I pointed that out as one reason. At Kingston penitentiary very considerable works have been carried on. At St. Vincent de Paul there were paid for retiring gratuities some $8,000, and the renewal of the electric plant and increased cost of supplies account for the balance.

That hardly covers the
first explanation of the minister that the amount is supposed to be for the increased cost of living and fuel. So far as the feeding of the prisoners is concerned, it is hard to get that to a cent because of the varying population. I do not think an increase in
IMr. Doherty.]
the population would account for the increase in the cost of fuel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not say that the whole of this was caused by those things. I have pointed out another thing at Kingston and another very particular thing at St. Vincent de Paul. I mentioned food and fuel, the prices of which are not identical every year, and you may have one winter that calls for a greater consumption of fuel than another.
My hon. friend has misunderstood me or else I did not make, myself plain. As I pointed out, at St. Vincent de Paul there were gratuities of $8,000 and expenditure for renewal of part of the electric plant, while increased cost of supplies accounts for the balance. In Dorchester there was increased cost of supplies. An hon. member asks explanation with regard to Saskatchewan. When the institution was taken over* by Inspector Hughes the conditions necessitated an exceptional expenditure. A new building containing 106 cells had to be constructed, also new quarters for the deputy warden, a cement and concrete granary and storehouse, stables and pumphouse, and a new water system to replace the one provided by the Public Works Department in 1910.

Is there any special
reason why we should remain here all night? The hon. minister has mentioned the purchase of additional land at Dorchester. I reside there, and I have not heard of any transfers. I see an additional amount of $5,000 for that penitentiary. I would like to get some information with respect to the additional offices created in connection with this institution during the past year and consequent additions to the salary list. Cannot this stand until to-morrow? If there is no special reason, I do not see why we should be asked to remain here all night.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These supplementary Estimates are for the year which ended the 31st of March.

They should have
been taken up sooner.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Possibly, but the debate
on the Transcontinental has taken up the time. I postponed my Budget because of that. I think there should be accommodation on both sides. It would oblige us very much if we could get these Estimates through together with one-sixth of the main Estimates. In connection with these supple-plementaries, the expenditure has all been

incurred, the parties are entitled' to their money and they are waiting! for it.
I do not wish to be obstructive, but there is one item in these Estimates relating to railways which will certainly take some time if it is what I think it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Senate adjourns tomorrow.
Why should we be kept all night for the Senate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is something to be said for that-
A good deal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We wish to get the Supply Bill to-night if possible, and get the Senate to pass it to-morrow, and have the assent of the Governor General.

There are some items in these Estimates concerning which I should like to ask some questions and have some discussion. It seems hardly reasonable to place before us $3,000,000 of Estimates relating to every department of Government, and ask us to put them through without discussion, besides voting one-sixth of the main Estimates. This last, perhaps, is not so serious because we shall have further opportunity to discuss each item. So far as our friends of the Senate are concerned,
I should be sorry to see them discommoded, but I do not know that their work is so onerous or the time they give to it so great that they should not stay here as long as is reasonably necessary to do the work for which they were sent here.

The understanding was that one-sixth of the Estimates was to go through to-night, that the items already passed in Supply should be concurred in, and also that any of these Supplementary Estimates that were non-contentious should go through. I take it that these supple-mentaries can be gone over, but that any item that any hon. member asks to stand should be allowed to stand. There are several items in these supplementaries that will have to stand over. They cannot go through to-night unless we are to stay here until daylight.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That position seems perfectly fair. The Government is not asking that any item in these Supplementary Estimates about which information is asked should be passed. But I would ask that items that are non-contentious should b*
passed that we make the Supply Bill accordingly and proceed in accordance with the understanding outlined by my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee).

To cure the matter, I
think I would say that they are all contentious.

Penitentiaries will
stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, penitentiaries stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gen tleman would be willing to discuss on the main Estimates any matters which he wishes to bring forward, and allow these items to pass.
The only item I mentioned was Dorchester, and as to that I wish information which, of course, I do not insist upon having to-night, if my hon. friend will be prepared to give it later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly, I shall be
glad to.

No doubt, it is the wish of members on both sides to be as courteous as possible; but the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) will understand that we have had experience with hon. gentlemen opposite on this point of allowing things to go through reserving discussion for some other time. I have a distinct recollection that last year we passed something like $150,000,000 in two nights after twelve o'clock. I see the hon. Minister of Militia (Mr. Hughes) smiles. He gave us two hours of his time last year, and then we had to put through about $10,000,000 of his Estimates and he did not even do us the courtesy of being present. Along between four and five in the morning we had to put these items through without even having opportunity to ask a question.

Hon. gentlemen knew
that these Estimates were all right.

I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that he ought not to ask us to put ourselves in that position. But I would like to say, that if it were only the Minister of Justice, then, personally, I would favour letting them go through. But it will hardly do to make fish of one and flesh of another, and so I think we must stand upon our legal rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will try to carry out the arrangement outlined by the hon. member for West Lambton. Any item that any hon. gentleman asks to stand after considering it, I think might stand. But it is very

desirable that these Supplementary Estimates us far as possible should pa3-s.
Arts, Agriculture and Statistics-Experimental Farms-Further amount required to defray expenses arising out of losses sustained by fire at the Central Experimental Farm-Governor General's warrant, $25,000.

This -comes within the category of items with reference to which I sent to the Minister of Finance a note this evening saying that I expected this would come up this afternoon and asking him to bring down certain reports. The items to which I refer are covered by Governor General's warrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not received that note.

We had to get the Governor General's warrant, because we had absolutely no funds. The main barn at the Central Experimental Farm was burned last October, and we lost ' all the machinery and equipment, all the feed produced on the farm, and all the material which was to be used to feed 175 head of cattle, as well -as sheep and swine.

For what was the
amount expended?
$16,000 worth of feed was destroyed, and a portion of the appliances and machinery. We had to make immediate provision for that, as the stock was there and had to be attended to.
Was there any insurance?
I think not; the Government usually carry their own insurance.

I do not wish to start a discussion on this item, but a rather important principle is involved in connection with these Governor General's warrants.
I have no objection to this item going through if another be allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of fact, it has not been usual in the past to insert in the Estimates amounts in respect of which Governor General's warrants have been issued, but I think it is a proper practice, and we .have adopted it this year. There is no objection to this item being allowed to stand if the hon. gentleman so desires.
What principle does the Government follow in regard to the insurance of its buildings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They carry their own insurance.

I know for a fact that the Federal Government carried insurance on certain buildings in my riding. For instance, there is insurance on a school building on the Munsel Indian reserv-e. Perhaps the Minister of the Interior can tell me something about it?
Mr. ROCiHE: I will inquire about the matter, and give my hon. friend the information.

I know the facts, but I should like to know the principle followed by the Government.
,, For the administration and enforcement of the Meat and Canned Food Acts-further amount required, $30,000.

After the Estimates had been prepared early in the year it -was found that the expansion of the work necessitated about twenty-two -extra inspectors in connection with the abattoirs throughout the country, and this is to pay their salaries and expenses.
How many of these inspectors are there?

We cannot tell the
exact number; that will depend on the expansion of the whole business.

Does the hon. minister
insist upon the inspectors being veterinary surgeons?

Yes, all inspectors have to be veterinary surgeons, and in addition have to pass the departmental examination, which is a pretty stiff one. If my hon. friends will allow this item to pass I will giv-e them all the information they desire when my main Estimates com-e up for consideration.
Militia and Defence-Dominion arsenal further amount required, $60,000.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	In the investigation of the Dominion arsenal, it was found -that a great deal of material had been overrun, and on the 1st of November there was a shortage.

What does over-run
mean?
I do not want to go into the details of the matter to-night, but the $80,000 is for wages and material.
Is any part of this amount to be used for the purchase of property?
None whatever.

Surely the minister can give some information as to the necessity for this vote. We might as well let the minister understand that if there has been something wrong in his department there are no secrets in Parliament, and we might as well have the whole of it.

The hon. gentleman will have everything; he will get all the details that are asked for. It is to my advantage that everything should be brought into the open. On November 1, it was found that the $300,000 vote for the arsenal was practically exhausted, there being only $54,000 of it left with which to carry on work until April 1. I do not want to go into the details as I have not all the papers here. It concerns' the investigation into the arsenal.
A great deal of material had to be destroyed and quantity of material had been purchased in excess of requirements.
Improperly used.

Overproduction, purchasing raw material that was required. I do not wish to say anything against the former manager of the factory, who has since retired; tout he has expended more in purchasing material than he had ca culat-ed upon. It left the factory in this position that we would require $80,000 for the salaries and wages of employees and $30,000 for material, leaving a balance of $60,000 to be provided. There is $14,000 revote out of the $60,000.
These figures stagger one. How much is the minister spending on that factory ?
$300,000 thrown away, worse than wasted; and now the minister wants $60,000 more in order to make good the blunders of some of his officers. It is a wonderful record.
This is the same vote as for years past.
Why not close the whole thing down anyway, what is the good of it?
I think it is a very good institution and that it serves a useful purpose.

Why not turn it into a fertilizer factory and make something that would be of service to the country ?
National Transcontinental Railway-Refund of security deposited by George Goodwin on tender, station building between Cochrane and Superior Junction. $27,500.

This is a refund to Mr. Goodwin of $27,500. He tendered for some work on the National Transcontinental and that was the amount which he put up. He was the lowest tenderer, but was so low that he could not go on with the work and we are giving him back the money.
I do not remember seeing a vote of this kind for a refund.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would not have been necessary if the refund had been made within a year, I know something about this personally, and I really think that Mr. Goodwin is entitled to get his money back. I think they were too sharp, they gave him notice within the time in which he might accept. I believe he stated orally that he would not accept, but his formal notification was too late and he was notified that his deposit would be forfeited. I think he is within his legal right. In view of this, I think he is entitled to have the money back.
Is it the practice to make refunds to tenderers who' for any reason refuse to enter into a contract ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It depends altogether on the reason. Sometimes they are forfeited, sometimes they are not. The circumstances in this case appealed to me very strongly on behalf of Mr. Goodwin and I therefore spoke to the minister about it.

I have in mind the case of gentlemen in Halifax who put in a tender in connection with the Prince Edward Island car ferry, whose deposit, a very considerable sum,' is at present in the hands of the Railway Department. An application has been made for a refund. Has any action been taken ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have had that under consideration also. I discussed it with the Minister of Railways. The minister holds a rather strong opinion on it, but I think, there is something to be said for the other side of the case. I hope to take it up with the acting minister.
It seems to me a pretty dangerous precedent to establish, to give back the deposit put up by a contractor because he is supposed to be too low. It is a question how far that should go.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think cases of that kind should always be submitted to Parliament.
Board of Railway Commissioners-To pay expenses in connection with cases before the Further amount required, $35,000.

This is a vote for the Railway Commission. Much of the expenditure will be made in connection with cases coming before the board in which the public are interested, such as the western freight rates and the telephone inquiry.
It includes travelling expenses ?

Oh, yes, everything.
Experimental Farms-Tobacco curing stations, $12,091.65.

At Indian Head.

Has the Government purchased Port Credit Harbour?
I think we did, but I am not quite sure.
How much was paid for it?

I can get my hon. friend the information, and let him know tomorrow.
