We are not making him a present. $500 is the amount 2 a.m. required to settle the whole account between the contractors and the department.
Does the minister know whether the department furnishes the wire and cable?

That was in the contract.
Investigating claims in regard to Pelagic Sealing Treaty, $7,000.
What is that for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend is aware that under the treaty entered into with the United States, with Russia and Japan pelagic sealing is done away with. Canada is paid 15 per cent of the sealskins thrown [Mr. Borden, j
upon the shore by the United States, 15 per cent by Russia, and 10 per cent by Japan. The United States has paid us $200,000 as an advance payment. Pelagic sealing is now abolished.
That has been received. Claims were made by those who were engaged in the sealing business and in order to arrive at the amount which would be paid to those whose living and occupation have been interfered with, Judge Audette of the Exchequer Court was appointed a commissioner to investigate. Some 1,500 claims have been submitted. We had a sum placed in the Estimates for the year ended March 31, of -$10,000. Judge Audette has been proceeding with the work and it was found that the $10,000 was insufficient. Only a comparatively small amount will have to be voted in the Supplementary Estimates for the year commencing April 1, in order to finish the work which is now well under way and which will be finished during the summer. It is to make provision for this work that this amount is required.
Dominion Lands and Parks-To pay expenses connected with water power investigations and reports in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Railway Belt in British Columbia, $20,100.
Is this a new item, or a further amount required?
This is a further amount required.
What is this water-power investigation?
We had a vote of $114,003 and we require $20,000 to complete the service.
Who compose this commission?

It is not a commission. We have a water-power branch in connection with the Interior Department of which Mr. Challies is the head. Mr. Hendry is one of the water-power engineers.
Miscellaneous-British Columbia Better Terms Commission, $3,500.
What is that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
A commissioner was nominated on behalf of the province of British Columbia and one on behalf of the Dominion. The two men were appointed by Order in Council. The British Columbia case has been filed. The case for the Dominion has not yet been filed but it is in course of preparation. In the meantime a third commissioner has not been appointed as it is undesirable to bring him

from England before he is actually needed here.
Who are the commissioners on behalf of British Columbia and of the Dominion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The commissioner for
British Columbia is Mr. Bodwell, K.C., and for the Dominion, Mr. Lash, K.C.
Expenses under the Canada Temperance Act __Further amount required, $20,000.
What is this for?

The expenses are very much increased. This is to cover the expenses already' incurred in the Tecent elections under the Act in the counties of Huron, Peel and Welland, and the cost of preparing the voters lists in the unorganized districts of Ontario. There was very little interest shown in the Canada Temperance Act for many years, and elections under it had become comparatively infrequent, hut it has been the custom to place in the Estimates $500 or $1,000 to meet the expenditure. This year the expenditure has been much greater on account of a kind of revival of the Act.
To provide for the purchase of 600 copies of the Parliamentary Guide-Further amount required, $600.
What is this $600 for?
For many years the Government have bought 600 copies of this guide, but through a clerical error only $600 was provided for in the Estimates, and this is to correct the mistake.
What becomes of the 600 copies?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are distributed to members and senators.
Mr. CaRVELL: Is that annual?
Annual.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Formerly, I think, it was only every other year. But I think it is now carried on every year, in accordance with the practice of other parliaments.

It is a very good work, and I did not intend to criticise it, but I merely wanted to know what becomes of the extra copies. There are about 210 members and 80 senators, and that would leave about 300 copies unaccounted for.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I could not give my hon. friend the correct information as to that. I imagine that some are sent to provincial authorities and exchanged for [DOT] documents of a similar character.
To provide for the expenses of commission to prepare plans relating to the cities of Ottawa and Hull, $8,000.
Can we have some information about this?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Government during the year appointed an honorary commission consisting of Mr. H. S. Holt, of Montreal, who is chairman, the other members being Sir Alexander Lacoste, Mr. Home Smith, and Mr. Frank Darling, of Toronto, t-he Mayor of Ottawa, and the Mayor of Hull. The Government took the matter up in co-operation with the two corporations, the city of Ottawa and the city of Hull, on the basis that plans should be prepared of Ottawa and Hull and their environments, including the laying of boulevards and squares, the location of public buildings, and generally to deal with the town-planning in the two cities upon the understanding that the Government would pay one-half the expense, the remaining half to be defrayed in proportion of population by the two cities. Both corporations agreed through their municipal authorities to that arrangement. This commission is . now engaged in the work of town planning. Engineers and a staff have been engaged. This amount of $8,000 represents- substantially the expenditure made up to the 31st day of March.

This commission is
separate from the Ottawa Improvement Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
Is the work of this commission to cease as soon as these plans are made and a general scheme outlined, or does their work continue?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This commission is appointed only for the purpose of making the plans; it does not interfere in any way with the work of the Ottawa Improvement Commission.
Will either of the cities be called upon to contribute to the preparation of plans anything further than the amount they have already contributed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not in respect of this particular commission. The joint arrangement between the Dominion Government and the two cities was that this commission should cause plans to be prepared, and the expenses of the commission and the preparation of the plans to be borne half by the Government and half by the two cities.

Nothing further is in contemplation so far as this commission is concerned. After the plans are prepared and the work done, what we have in mind is that all parties concerned, the Dominion, the two cities of Ottawa and Hull, the railways and other interested parties will all work together in the carrying out of those plans.
Have any plans been prepared yet?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are in process of preparation.
It is a matter of mutual agreement whether these plans will be carried out or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The commission is charged solely with the duty of preparing the plans.
To provide for cost of liquidation and inquiry into the affairs of the Union Life Insurance Company, $20,000.

This is a large sum with so far varying unsatisfactory results. It seems that warrants have been issued for the arrest of certain people. I understand that Mr. Harry Symons is awaiting trial, and I venture to say that he was the most innocent man in connection with the matter and that the really guilty man, Mr. H. Poll-man Evans, is still at large.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am entirely willing that the item should stand, because it is an item of an unusual character. So far as expenditure is concerned, I think I can satisfy my hon. friend, although not to-night, that it has been well spent in the interest of the public. The Dominion Government has had nothing whatever to do with the prosecution of the parties in question.
Who has?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Ontario Government, which is charged with the administration of justice. The liquidation was for the purpose of enabling about 160,000 policy holders throughout the Dominion, for the most part poor people, paying five, ten, or fifteen cents a week, to obtain reinsurance. Otherwise they would have lost all that they had in this company. The inquiry was further prosecuted in Toronto under the Winding Up Act, with the view of ascertaining how the funds of the company were lodged. The inquiry was widened to take in some of the companies whose affairs were connected with the affairs of this company. So far as the matter to which my hon. friend has referred is concerned, the Dominion Government has nothing whatever to do with the prosecution of any one in connection with

the company. The liquidation was carried on in the city of Toronto before a referee, and he being an officer of the court and the inquiry being public, the Dominion did not consider it to be any of its duty to consider the mattter, of laying an information.
How much did Mr. Masson get?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think about $7,000. My hen. friend as a lawyer, I think, will be entirely satisfied with the account of the liquidator here presented and the expenses of liquidation.

It is a pretty stiff price to the liquidation.
Item stands.
Grant towards relieving distress caused by storm on Great Lakes-Governor General's warrant, $25,000.

That comes within the category of the items to which I referred my hon. friend earlier in the evening; but, on the understanding that we can discuss this on some other item dealing with Governor General's warrants, it may go through.
Mr. J. I). REID: All right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will make me repent of putting these items in the Estimates. It is a new departure.

It is not that, but it is the Governor General's warrants.
To provide for the settlement in full of the claim of Government of New Brunswick, for loss sustained owing to the leasing by the federal government of angling privileges in non-tidai waters of the province from 1875 to 1882, the province having disputed the right of the Dominion to issue such leases in 1875 $66,382.
Is this a final settlement of the fishery claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This settles both claims.
Customs-Expenses of inspectors of ports, etc., $35,000.
Does this include Mr. Carstair?

He was not an extra
officer.
Is he a permanent officer?
Yes. He is an inspector. We had one or two deaths on the inspection staff and we put him on.

Does he do any political
work?

No.

Customs-Miscellaneous-Printing and stationery, subscriptions to commercial papers, flags, dating stamps, locks, instruments, etc., for variouB ports of entry, express charges on samples, stationery and forms, legal expenses, premiums on guarantee bonds and uniforms for customs officers, $40,000.

Are the customs officers put in uniform now?
Mr. REID . I insisted that more of them at the different ports should have nice uniforms. I thought it better in the case of the officers who have to meet the public. We pay $5 extra on each suit, and it makes a considerable item.
Railways and Canals-Chargeable to collection of revenue-Railways-Prince Edward Island railway-Working expenses-Further amount required, $65,000.
Did you lose that last year?

They lost $150,000 altogether.
Public Works-Chargeable to collection of revenue-Telegraph lines-British Columbia- Further amount required, $30,000.

Why is the Dominion
building telegraph lines in British Columbia? I can understand it in the Yukon.
We build them not only in British Columbia tout in the Maritime provinces.
I know there is a little Dominion line running along the Miramichi river.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And some in Cape Breton. Mr. REID: And in Queibec too.

I should have thought
that arrangements could be made with the telephone companies. Thirty thousand dollars is a pretty large amount, and naturally raises the question whether the Government is not launching out in a general scheme of telegraph lines. I could understand some lines having been built in the Maritime provinces or on the lower St. Lawrence for some reason or other and now we have to keep them up. But so large an amount as this would seem to indicate a general scheme. I should think that a fairly good line in British Columbia could toe built at $100 a mile. This is a 'further amount required.' How much is being spent altogether?

Last year through some
mistake a sufficient vote was not taken to cover the operation and repairs of the telegraph lines. At that time I took much the same ground as the hon. gentleman
takes, thinking that the Dominion had no business to go into telegraph lines. I was trying to bring about a settlement between the different provinces that they should take care of these lines themselves. This sum is required for the repairs and working expenses of the British Columbia system.
Land and Cable telegraph lines-Lower St. Lawrence including working .expenses of vessels required for cable service-Further amount required, $44,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This matter has been up for discussion many times. As I understand it the telegraph system was first extended into the thinly settled portions of the seacoast largely as a means of getting prompt news concerning marine disasters. For instance there is such a line through the thinly populated portions of Cape Breton and also on the north shore of the St. Lawrence. Then there is a cable somewhere in the Maritime provinces. Extensions have been made to these lines, I believe, for the convenience of the people in places where the telegraph companies would not establish stations. I do not know that it has been upon any distinct principle, but rather as a matter of expediency and for the convenience of the people.

It must have been a
large sum before when your ' further amount required' would build about four hundred miles of new line.

The statement supplied
by the department shows that this $44,000 is required to complete payments for the fiscal year on the working expenses of the land and cable telegraph lines in the Lower St. Lawrence and the Maritime provinces and the working expenses of vessels employed in the service. The amount includes such items as $7,800 for the steamship Tyrian, $6,000 for the Cape Breton and special amounts for the various telegraph lines.
It is not for extensions then according to that?
No.

I desire to put my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) right on his statement that a telegraph line should be built in British Columbia for $100 a mile. It is evident he does not know the conditions in British Columbia. There are many hundreds of miles of telegraph lines in that province that could not be built for less than $225 a mile. If there is one thing more than another that this Government, or any government can do to benefit the public of British Columbia it is in providing these telegraph lines.

That has all been
done.

Not yet.
Trade and Commerce-salaries of commissioners and officers and other employees; rents, day wages and contingencies under the Inspection and Sale and Canada Grain Acts, further amount required, $75,000.

Certain officers are appointed to carry out certain duties; is it not known at the time of their appointment what salaries they are going to receive? Have additional officers been 'appointed since the main Estimates came down, requiring a further sum of $75,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the explanation desired by the hon. member may be found in the concluding paragraph of a statement which the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce sent me this evening, and which is as follows:
For the ten months of the current year to January 31, 1914, there was an increase in the cars inspected over the same period during the fiscal "year of 25,385 cars, and all previous records were broken.
A rather complete summary follows, showing just why this amount is required.

Tile sum of $75,000 is
required for salaries of commissioners and officers and other employees, rents, and so on, not heretofore provided for. As I understand it, under the Civil Service Act these men are appointed by the year, and their salaries are known, to the department. Are these officers men who have been appointed since the main Estimates came down? I do not understand why there should be any extra amount, because the department should know just what their officers are going to cost year by year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a permanent
staff and they should, and usually do, know what the salaries will be, subject to reasonable increase if business develops in the course of the ensuing year. I think the more important items, those of day wages and contingencies, are due to increase of business at the ports, and the extra permanent staff would tend to increase the amount to $75,000. I would suggest that, with the unanimous consent of the House, we might take concurrence for all the items in the main Estimates em bloc.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The suggestion is made to the House that these resolutions be concurred in en bloc without naming the items. These are the items already passed at previous sittings of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And one-sixth of the remaining items.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
As the resolutions are
of different dates they could not, in my judgment, be put through on one motion; but by putting through the resolutions without calling the items afterwards much time will be saved and I understood it was agreed that the items should not be called.
Progress reported.

The House proceeded to consider resolutions reported from Committee of Supply.
Resolutions concurred in.

Mr. SPEAKER read a communication from the Governor General's Secretary, announcing that the honourable Mr. Justice Idington, acting as Deputy of His Royal Highness would proceed to the Senate Chamber on the 3rd instant at four o'clock for the purpose of giving the Royal Assent-in certain Bills.
On motion of Mr. Borden, the House adjourned at 3.05 a.m. Friday.
Friday, April 3, 1914.
